Probably derived from the Old High German word beraht meaning "bright", this was the name of a goddess worshiped in Austria, Baveria, Baden, Swabia, Switzerland and Slovenia.

A variant of Perceval, the knight most closely associated with the Quest for the Holy Grail. Early legends have him raised in the wilds of Wales, but others state he was the only surviving son of Evrawc, Earl of the North. There was a real Peredur, who was king of York between 560-580 AD.

Portuguese form of Percilia, the name of a genus of perch-like fish native to Chile. It is a diminutive of Latin perca, from Ancient Greek πέρκη (perke) "perch", cognate with περκνός (perknos) "dark-spotted".
Derived from Latin percipere meaning "to obtain, to gain; to perceive, to learn, to feel".
Variant of Bertarid. Perctarit was the name of a 7th-century king of the Lombards.
The thunder goddess mother of Perkūnas, in Slavic mythology referred to as Percunatele mother of Perun, which is probably derived from the Balts.

A variant of Perceval, the knight most closely associated with the Quest for the Holy Grail. Early legends have him raised in the wilds of Wales, but others state he was the only surviving son of Evrawc, Earl of the North. There was a real Peredur, who was king of York between 560-580 AD.
Means "first" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रधान (pradhāna).
in classical Indonesian, perdani means treasurer. while the other meaning of Perdani is the feminine form of "perdana" which mean the first
Respelling of Perdita which might have arisen based on a dialectal pronunciation.

Meaning unclear. This was the name of a Macedonian general who served as regent of Alexander the Great’s empire after Alexander’s death in 323 BC, until he died in Egypt in 321/0 BC. It was also borne by several earlier kings of Macedon.
Basque form of Fernanda and Fernande.
Combination of Per and the Norse name element dís "goddess", first used in the early 1900s.

Means "partridge" in Greek. In Greek myth Perdix or Talos was a nephew of the inventor Daedalus, to whom he was apprenticed. His teacher became jealous of his skill and pushed him headlong off the temple of Athena on the Acropolis, but before Perdix hit the ground, the goddess turned him into a partridge.
Either a diminutive of Perdita or a variant of Purdie.

column5: Pe re ah su wor deh
column12: Means "wealth has entered me" in Ijaw.
Taken from second part of Dognat-Peregnat. Usually used for twin of Dognat. Means "overtake" in Russian.
English variant of Peregrine as well as the German form of Peregrine. Peregrin "Pippin" Took is a character in J.R.R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings.
Spanish and Galician feminine form of either Peregrino and Slovene feminine form of Peregrin.
Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of Peregrinus.
The name for the planet Venus, in the novel of the same name by C.S. Lewis.

Perëndi is the Albanian word for "God", "the sky" and "heaven". Perëndi is thought to have been a sky and thunder god in the Albanian pagan mythology, and to have been worshiped by the Illyrians in antiquity.

Old French form of Petronilla borne by Perenelle Flamel (1320-1402), wife and fellow alchemist of Nicolas Flamel. They are known for their quest to discover the philosopher's stone, a legendary substance said to turn any metal into gold and to make its owner immortal.Today, Perenelle is most commonly known for her mention in J.K. Rowling's fantasy novel Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone, in which she and her husband have succeeded in creating the stone and have lived to be in their mid 600s.

Derived from the name of the old Roman deity of the circle or "ring" of the year, Anna Perenna. The name itself is derived from Classical Latin perennis "perennial; everlasting, perpetual" (ultimately from Latin per- “throughout” and annus “the year”).
Daughter of King Pelles of Corbenic and mother of Galahad in La Tavola Ritonda.She is known as Amite or Elaine in French romance.
From the word perfection, referring to the quality or state of being perfect or complete.
Derived from the name of a citadel in Troy, possibly related to Ancient Greek πύργος (pyrgos) meaning "tower, watchtower".
Possibly a combination of Per and got (from names like Ågot).

Possibly derived from Tupi piripiri, which refers to a type of reed. This is the name of the hero of José de Alencar's novel The Guarani (1857), a fictional member of the Goitacá people of Brazil. The Brazilian singer Pery Ribeiro (1937-2012) was born Peri Oliveira Martins.

Combination of Perry and Ann. It was brought to some public attention in 1959 by Perian Conerly, a Mississippi-born sports columnist for The New York Times and the wife of New York Giants quarterback Charlie Conerly; in late 1959, she appeared as a contestant on the American game show What's My Line?. In her 1963 book Backseat Quarterback, Conerly wrote: 'Confusion about the gender of my first name is understandable. The spelling does not indicate that it is pronounced Perry Ann, being a contraction of two family names.'
Latinized form of Periandros. Periander was a tyrant of Corinth (Greece) in the 7th century BC.
Russian and Ukrainian form of Periander.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Periander.
Derived from Greek περί (peri) "around, near, surrounding" combined with Greek ἀνδρός (andros) "of a man".
Italian, Spanish and Catalan form of Periboea.
Shortened form of the longer Egyptian name Seth-Peribsen.
From the given name Pericles combined with the patronymic suffix ίδας (idas) (see ides).

Derived from Ancient Greek περί (peri) meaning "around, about, exceedingly" and κλύμενος (klymenos) meaning "heard, famous", a participle of κλύω (klyo) "to hear, listen to". Also compare the Ancient Greek word περικλύμενον (periklymenon)# meaning "honeysuckle". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a Pylian prince who was given the power to shapeshift by his grandfather, Poseidon.
Georgian form of the Turkish name Feride.

Taken from the name of the gemstone, whose name is of uncertain origin and meaning. A current theory, however, derives it from Anglo-Norman pedoretés, ultimately from Greek paiderôs (via Latin paederos): pais "child" and erôs "love".As a given name, it has found occasional usage in the English-speaking world from the late 19th century onwards.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek περί (peri) meaning "around, exceedingly" and ἦρα (era) "service, gratification". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a king of Messene, as well as a Theban charioteer.
Variant of Perigune used in A Midsommer Night's Dream
From the Kurdish words perî, meaning "fairy" and gul meaning "flower".
The name of a daughter of Sinis and wife of Theseus in Greek mythology, also spelled as Perigouna, Perigone, and as Perigenia in A Midsummer Night's Dream.
Derived from Ancient Greek περί (peri) meaning "around, near, surrounding" as well as "exceedingly" combined with λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk".
Latinized form of Perilaos. This name was borne by a Greek tyrant of Argos (6th century BC) as well as by several characters in Greek mythology.
Variant of Perilaos using λεώς (leos), the Attic Greek form of Ancient Greek λαός (laos) meaning "people, folk". This is the name of several figures in Greek mythology.

One of the three performing sons of Sylvius in 'Campaspe', an Elizabethan era stage play, a prose comedy by John Lyly based on the story of the love triangle between Campaspe, a Theban captive, the artist Apelles, and Alexander the Great, who commissioned him to paint her portrait.
Means "very cunning" or "cunning all around", derived from Ancient Greek περί (peri) meaning "around, exceedingly" and μήδεα (medea) meaning "plan, cunning, art".

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek περί (peri) meaning "around, exceedingly" and μῆλον (melon) meaning "fruit", or euphemistically "cheeks, breasts". This was the name of a nymph in Greek mythology, a daughter of Hippodamas and lover of Achelous. When her father discovered her affair, he pushed her from a cliff into the ocean, where she was changed into the island of Perimele, one of the Echinades islands off western Greece.

Perimones was the third of four brothers whom Gareth encountered on his way to fight Sir Ironside at Castle Dangerous. The other brothers were Percard, Persant, and Pertolepe.Perimones was lord of the White Tower, “well matchecold all about, and double dyked,” where he was preparing to host a tournament when Gareth passed by and he fought the young knight in attempt to avenge his brother Percard. Perimones had at least fifty knights in his service; on being defeated he yielded them all, as well as himself, to Gareth’s command.He jousted in Lyonors’ tournament at Castle Dangerous and made a creditable showing, and later came to court about the time of Gareth’s wedding, obtained the favor of being made Gareth’s butler at the high feast of Michaelmas, and was made a member of the Round Table.Perimones was one of the knights in Guenevere’s guard at the stake and was killed when Lancelot rescued her.
Gascon diminutive of Pèr and Piedmontese diminutive of Pero.

Means "having good sense, wise, sagacious; very thoughtful, very careful" in Ancient Greek, derived from περί (peri) meaning "around, near, surrounding" or "beyond, exceedingly" combined with φρήν (phren) meaning "mind, heart, emotions". In Greek mythology, Periphron is the name of one of the suitors of Odysseus' wife Penelope. It was also a Homeric epithet often used to describe women, including Penelope herself.
Short form of Periandros and Periklis.
A character in "The Faerie Queene" by Edmund Spenser who lived with her two sisters, Elissa and Medina. Her hedonism stood in contrast to the asceticism of Elissa and the temperance of Medina.

From Greek περιστέρι (peristeri) meaning "dove, pigeon," from Ancient Greek περῐστέρῐον (peristérion), the diminutive of περιστερᾱ́ (peristerā́).This name is borne by Peristera "Betty" Baziana (1974-), the wife of the Greek prime minister Alexis Tsipras.

Means "exceedingly strong, mighty" in Ancient Greek, derived from περί (peri) meaning "around, exceedingly" and σθένος (sthenos) meaning "vigour, strength". This was the name of one of the fifty sons of King Aegyptus in Greek mythology, killed by his wife, Electra, on their wedding night.
Most likely a variant of Peretz.
One of the medieval Basque variants of Petra.Peritza has been recorded from the 1500s onwards.
From the English word for the color "periwinkle", from Middle English parwynke, referring to a "light blue and purple shade". It's also the name of a flower.
Kazakh and Kyrgyz form of Parizad.
A diminutive of Perkin and Perkins or a nickname. One bearer is Canadian hockey forward Percival Walter "Perk" Galbraith (1898-1961).

column3: Перка(Croatian Cyrillic, Serbian, Montenegrin, Macedonian, Bosnian Cyrillic)
column12: Originally a diminutive of Petra via the form Pera.
Means "mighty, strong" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रकाश (prakāśa).

Medieval English diminutive of Peter. (The surname Perkins is derived from this medieval diminutive.) A known bearer was Perkin Warbeck (ca. 1474-1499), a pretender to the English throne who was executed by hanging at age 24 or 25.
Transferred use of the surname Perkins.

Derived from Proto-Indo-European *perkwunos or *perkunos, which itself is ultimately derived from Proto-Indo-European *perkwus or *perkṷu meaning "oak tree" or "fir tree". Also compare Perun.In Baltic mythology, Perkūnas is the name of the god of thunder, rain, mountains, oak trees and the sky. His name has stayed the same in Lithuanian (where his name has even become synonymous with thunder), but it has changed slightly in the other Baltic languages over time: for example, in Latvian, his name is now Pērkons.
Derived from perlas, which in Lithuanian and Tagalog is the word for "pearl".In Lithuania, this name is strictly masculine, whereas in the Philippines, it appears to be strictly feminine.

A variant of Perceval, the knight most closely associated with the Quest for the Holy Grail. Early legends have him raised in the wilds of Wales, but others state he was the only surviving son of Evrawc, Earl of the North. There was a real Peredur, who was king of York between 560-580 AD.The work known as Perlesvaus (also The High Book of the Grail) is an anonymous Old French prose romance written in the early 13th century and presented as a continuation of Perceval, the Story of the Grail. Its central hero is Perceval, who is often referred to as Perlesvaus throughout.The Romance Perlesvaus etymologizes the name (there: Pellesvax) as meaning "He Who Has Lost The Vales", referring to the loss of land by his father, while also saying Perceval called himself Par-lui-fet (made by himself).A modern interpretation of the romance goes further, suggesting that after his failure at the Grail Castle, Perceval takes on the name Perlesvaus as a penitential or symbolic new identity. This is an interpretation of the text rather than an established historical fact.
Diminutive of Perle. In other words: you could say that this name is the French cognate of Perlita.
Transferred use of the surname Perley.
Directly taken from Breton perlezenn "pearl", this name is considered the Breton equivalent of Margaret.

Diminutive of Perla. In other words: you could say that this name is the Italian and Spanish cognate of Perline. Also compare Perlita.In the United States, the name has mostly been used in the southern states of the country. The name was probably introduced there by Spanish-speaking peoples that (over time) had migrated there from Latin America. But if not, then Perlina is very likely an English variant spelling of Pearlina, which itself is a variant form of Pearline, which in turn is an anglicization of the French given name Perline. Alternatively, in the southern United States, the name Perlina (or its spelling) might reflect the Appalachian pronunciation of the name Paulina, in which case Perlina could be considered to be an American English variant form of Paulina.
Means "quantity, amount, number" in Indonesian, ultimately derived from Sanskrit प्रमाण (pramāṇa).
From the ancient greek name Permanthea, derived from the greek word anthos meaning "flower, blossom".
Means "gem, jewel, precious stone" in Indonesian.

A Macedonian officer in 'Campaspe', an Elizabethan era stage play, a prose comedy by John Lyly based on the story of the love triangle between Campaspe, a Theban captive, the artist Apelles, and Alexander the Great, who commissioned him to paint her portrait.
Variant of Permelia, which is of unknown origin; possibly a variant of Pamela or a contraction of Pearl and Amelia.

Derived from Greek περνάω (pernáo) "to pass", this name was historically given to a girl with older sisters whose parents desperately hoped for a son. They "were literally praying for the curse of daughters to pass".
Ancient Egyptian masculine name meaning "Lord of his house".

This appears sporadically outside the U.S. Top 1000 and was found mainly in Southern States. My speculation is that it is an offshoot of Calpurnia, but I cannot verify if this is the source of the name.
Medieval Portuguese form of Peter and variant of Pero.
Aragonese, Ligurian and Piedmontese form of Peter as well as a medieval Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of this name.
A form of Pétronille (cf. Peronel, Perenelle). The virgin martyr Saint Petronilla is also known as Péroline in French.
Medieval Catalan feminine diminutive of Pere.
Catalan form and medieval Italian variant of Petronilla. The Italian novelist Boccaccio used this name in his work 'The Decameron' (1350).
Older form of Pierro used in the Canton of Vaud.
Derived from Latin perpetuus "perpetual, continuous, everlasting".
Masculine form of Perpetua. The 6th-century saint Perpetuus was a bishop of Tours in France.

This is the full first name of Peri Brown, a companion to the Fifth and Sixth Doctors in 'Doctor Who'. The character claims that her name means "she who lives in the hills", though the accuracy of this is unknown as she does not specify the name's language or origin.
a Latinized Swiss variant of Perrette
Medieval French feminine form of Pierre.
Variant of Perry. Also used as a diminutive of names that begin with Per-, e.g. Persephone.

Perria is a fairy-like mountain figure in Albanian mythology and folklore. The origin and meaning of her name are debated; theories include a derivation from Albanian përrua "brook" and a derivation from Old Albanian përruo, ultimately derived from Bulgarian порой (poroj) “torrent”.
Combination of Perri and Anne 1. Also see Perian.

Variant of Perry and Perri. It can also be used as a diminutive of names that begin with Per- and have the 'per' sound within the name and at the ending of the name. Examples include: Persephone, Persis, Juniper and Vesper.
Diminutive form of Pierre, Perre and Pier.
Recorded in French-speaking Switzerland between the 14th and 16th centuries.
Likely an alternative spelling of Perrin, influenced by the spelling of the name Perry.
Form of Perse used in several languages. In Serbia, it is also occasionally used as a short form of Persida.

Sir Persant earned his surname for his preference to “the colour of Inde”, dark blue, which he used for his arms, armor, and shield, the trappings of his horses, the livery of his male and female attendants, and his pavilion.A goodly knight and the lord of a fair city, he was the last of four brothers whom Gareth defeated on his way to fight Sir Ironside at Castle Dangerous; the other three were Percard, Perimones, and Pertolepe.On Gareth’s command, Persant, bringing a hundred knights, came with his surviving brothers to Arthur’s court at Pentecost, where they were pardoned for the war they had long held against the knights of the Round Table. Persant fought in Lyonors’ tournament at Castle Dangerous, and later came to court about the time of Gareth’s wedding and obtained the favor of being Gareth’s sewer-chief at the feast of Michaelmas. He was soon elected to the Round Table.

a variant of Persant, a goodly knight and the lord of a fair city, he was the last of four brothers whom Gareth defeated on his way to fight Sir Ironside at Castle Dangerous; the other three were Percard, Perimones, and Pertolepe.
Medieval Dutch variant form of Perche.
Meaning, "hostility and ill-treatment, especially because of race or political or religious beliefs."
Spanish and Portuguese form of Persephone.
From Egyptian pr-snt meaning "a sister comes forth", derived from pr "to come forth, emerge, escape" combined with snt "sister".
Italian and Spanish form of Perseus.
Shortened masculine form of Persephone, with pronunciation inspired by Joseph.
Variant of Persephone, possibly influenced by Stephanie in its spelling.
Older, archaic form of Persephone, which suggests pre-Hellenic origins.

Means "a Persian" in Ancient Greek, connected by folk etymology to πέρθω (pertho) meaning "to destroy". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including a Titan who fathered the goddess Hecate with Asteria, a king of Colchis who was a son of Helios and the Oceanid Perse, and a son of Perseus and Andromeda credited as the ancestor of the Persians.
Catalan, Portuguese and Romanian form of Perseus.

From the English word meaning "steadfastness in doing something despite difficulty or delay in achieving success", referring to persevering through the trials and tribulations that may come as a believer of Christ.

From Latin persevērāns meaning "enduring, persevering". This was the name of an 8th-century Spanish saint who journeyed to Poitiers (France) to found a convent, dying of exhaustion along the way while escaping pirates.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Perseus.
Medieval Dutch diminutive form of Perse.

Most likely used as a first name due to John Joseph Pershing, General of the Armies for the United States at the end of World War I. His paternal ancestors were of German descent, and the original spelling was likely Pfoersching. The name derives from pfersich, the German word meaning "peach", and was used as a metonymic occupational name meaning "grower or seller of peaches". Pfersich comes from persica, the Late Latin word for peach, originally malum persicum meaning "Persian apple".

From the name of the Middle Eastern country Persia, now referred to as Iran. Its name is derived from Avestan Parsa, the ancient tribal name of the people ruled by Cyrus the Great.As a given name, it has been occasionally found in the English-speaking world from the early 19th century onwards.
Derived from the word Persian meaning “From Persia”.
Serbian, Croatian, and Romanian form of Persis. This was the name of the wife of Alexander Karadordevic, Prince of Serbia and ancestor to the monarchs of Yugoslavia.

From the name of the Persimmon, a brightly colored fruit. The word persimmon is derived from Powhatan, an Algonquian language of the eastern United States, meaning "a dry fruit".As a given name, it has been occasionally found in the English-speaking world from the 19th century onwards.

"Persinette" is a 1698 French fairy-tale by novelist Charlotte-Rose de Caumont de La Force adapted from earlier 'Petrosinella' by Giambattista Basil and later adapted by the Grimms brothers to become 'Rapunzel'. The name was revived in the title of a child opera by the Austrian composer Albin Fries in 2019.

Possibly derived from Greek Περσίς (Persis) meaning "Persian woman" or περσέα (persea), the Greek name for a type of tree (species Mimusops kummel). This is the name of a character in the ancient Greek novel Aethiopica by Heliodorus of Emesa; Persinna is the queen of Ethiopia and the mother of the protagonist Chariclea.
Likely from the common Swedish surname Persson and/or the word person (German: Person), which is used as a gender neutral title by some nonbinary people.
Possibly a Romani corruption of Parascevas or place name Vesuvius.

Meaning uncertain, but likely derived from the English word pert.This is the name of a character from the novel Checkers: A Hard Luck Story (1896) written by the American author and playwright Henry Blossom (1866-1919). He later turned the novel into a play called Checkers (1903), which was successful on Broadway.A notable bearer from real life is the American actress Pert Kelton (1907-1968). She was named after the character at the suggestion of her aunt, who had seen Blossom's play and loved it.
From Persian پرتو (partow) meaning "ray of light".
From Persian پرتو (partow) meaning "ray of light" and نهال (nehal) meaning "sapling, shoot".
Bosnian and Croatian form of Pertinax.

Pertolepe was the second of four brothers whom Gareth encountered on his way to fight Sir Ironside at Castle Dangerous; the others were Percard, Perimones, and Persant. Pertolepe’s trappings were “all in green, both his horse and his harness.” On seeing Gareth in the black armor of his brother Percard, and learning that Gareth had slain Percard, the Green Knight rode unto a horn that was green, and it hung upon a thorn
Pertunda enabled sexual penetration. Pertunda is the female personification of the verb pertundere, "to penetrate", and seems to be a name for invoking a divine power specific to this function.
Derived from Serbo-Croatian perunika and Bulgarian and Macedonian перуника (perunika) "iris".
Vlach form or diminutive of Peruna.
Peruonto is an Italian literary fairy tale written by Giambattista Basile in his 1634 work, the Pentamerone.
Turkish form of Parviz and a variant spelling of Pərviz.
From name of holiday Первомая (Pervomaya) "First of May (International Worker's Day)".
Bosnian and Croatian form of Persephone.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Perseus.
Derived from פֶּסַח (Pesah), the Hebrew name for the holiday of passover itself, derives from the root פסח meaning "to skip, to pass". This name was typically given to boys born during passover.
Possibly derived from the modern Hebrew for Pesach, or Passover.
Variant of Pesha, recorded in medieval Frankfurt, Germany.

From Egyptian psš.t, derived from psš meaning "to divide, split, spread out" or "ritual instrument (for Opening of the Mouth ceremony)" combined with the suffix t. Peseshet was the earliest recorded female physician, titled the Lady Overseer of the Female Physicians in Fourth Dynasty ancient Egypt (ca. 2500 BC).
Related to Pesach. Alternately, a Yiddish diminutive of Batya.
It means bishop in albanian, also the city of Peshkopi comes from this name, it was a monastery around it.

Name of a holiday, the original Jewish version of Passover. It is commonly given to babies born on, or close to Pessach.The verb "pasàch" (Hebrew: פָּסַח) is first mentioned in the Torah account of the Exodus from Egypt (Exodus 12:23), and there is some debate about its exact meaning: the commonly-held assumption that it means "he passed over", in reference to God "passing over" the houses of the Israelites during the final plague of the Ten Plagues of Egypt, stems from the translation provided in the Septuagint (παρελευσεται in Exodus 12:23, and εσκεπασεν in Exodus 12:27). Judging from other instances of the verb, and instances of parallelism, a more faithful translation may be "he hovered over, guarding."
Diminutive of Pesse (compare Pessel) recorded in the border region between modern-day France and modern-day Germany in the 14th century.

From the Finnish fairy tale Pessi and Illusia by Yrjo Kokko, published in 1944.Pessi is a little hobgoblin boy whose name should be Pessimist like his father's but he was very small so his name had to be shortened. His family is proud of their practical and sensible attitude to life. Illusia is a little fairy girl whose father is Mr. Illusioni, a famous visionary living on a rainbow. The fairy Illusia and the goblin Pessi meet and the story begins. The book is a classic of Finnish children’s literature.
Possibly a Romani corruption of Persuvius.
Means "fourth" in Cornish. This is a modern Cornish name.
Diminutive of Paulina or Polina, often used as a given name.

Borne by Peta Nocona (d. 1864), a chief of the Comanche band Noconi, whose name allegedly means "he who leaves alone and returns" in Comanche. He led his tribe during the extensive Indian Wars in Texas from the 1830s to 1860. He was the son of the Comanche chief Iron Jacket and father of Chief Quanah Parker by Naduah (Cynthia Ann Parker). His band Noconis, or Wanderers, or travellers, were named after him. Nocona, Texas is also named after the Noconi leader.
Are constituent parts of the flower, located at its most protective whorl. They are normally membranous structures, broad, colorful and have many functions, among them the attraction of pollinators.
Meaning "moon coming up flower". This name was given to one baby girl in Alberta in 2023.
Anglicized form of Petko borne by Mr Petco Slabenoff, a Bulgarian passenger aboard the Titanic who died during the sinking of the ship in 1912.
Means "come to us with the sound of wings" in Cree.
Elaboration of Peter, feminized with the suffix -ina.
Medieval German pet form of Peter, as the Germanic element man has been used as a suffix for pet forms of both masculine and feminine names since the 7th century AD.
Tahitian and Old Hawaiian form of Peter. It appears in the Bible in Hawaiian.
Transferred use of the surname Peters.
Transferred use of the surname Peterson.
Petesis appears in historical records as a name associated with an archive of Memphite sealers-embalmers, specifically referring to a son of Chonouphis.
Dutch form of Pethuel, but less common than the main Dutch form (Petuël).

Apparently means "God's opening" or "persuasion of God" in Hebrew, derived from Hebrew pathah "to open, to allure, to persuade" combined with el "God". In the bible, this was the name of the father of the prophet Joel.
Variation of Petey. There is a typhoon in the 1950 Pacific typhoon season with this name.
The name of the Zimbabwian writer Petina Gappah.
Derived from Catalan petit "small", this name was used as a translation of Hebrew Katan.
Finnish form and Bulgarian variant transcription of Petya and Slovene diminutive of Petra (used as a given name in its own right).
Feminine form of Petko. Saint Paraskeva of the Balkans is known by this name in Serbia and Bulgaria.
Possibly a diminutive of names starting with Pe, such as Pèire or Pelegrina.
Sorbian form of Peter. Jan Pětr Jordan (German: Johann Peter Jordan), born 1818, was a Sorbian philosopher.

Latinized form of Greek Πετραία (Petraia) meaning "of a rock" as well as "rocky" and "living among the rocks", a derivative of πέτρα (petra). This was the name of an Oceanid according to Hesiod's Theogony, as well as an epithet of Scylla, who dwelt in or on a rock. Also compare the masculine Πετραῖος (Petraios), an epithet of the god Poseidon in Thessaly, as 'he who clave the rocks of Tempe, and drained Thessaly'.

Means "of a rock, rocky, living among rocks" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of a leader of the satyrs in Greek mythology, as well as an epithet of Poseidon in Thessaly, as 'he who clave the rocks of Tempe, and drained Thessaly'.

Modern Greek diminutive of Petros, as it contains the modern Greek diminutive suffix -άκης (-akis). This name is typically only used informally, meaning: it does not appear on birth certificates.A known bearer of this name was the Greek Cypriot student Petros "Petrakis" Giallouros (1938-1956), who was killed by British forces during a student demonstration in Famagusta during the EOKA struggle.

Albanian form of Petrakis. Unlike the original Greek name, the Albanian form is used as an official name on birth certificates.A notable bearer of this name was the Albanian writer Petraq Zoto (1937-2015).
Means "son of Peter" in Vlach and Serbian.

Full name of the character Tish from the early 2000s show The Weekenders. It was said to mean "girl with one nose", but the elements of the name could come from other names such as Petra (meaning of "stone") or Tish (from Letitia, meaning of "joy, happiness"). Invented To Sound Eastern European.
Feminine form of Petras. In other words, this name is the Lithuanian equivalent of Petra.
Elaborated form of Petra and Romanian variant of Petre.
Gallicized form of Petermann, a German diminutive of Peter. This name was found in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region up until the late 1600s.
Name of a 15th-century prince from Western Circassia. Possibly the Circassian version of the name Petros.

From the English word petrichor that denotes the earthy scent produced when rain falls on dry soil, which was coined by Australian mineralogist and biochemist Richard Grenfell Thomas in 1964 from Greek πέτρα (petra) meaning "rock" or πέτρος (petros) "stone" and ἰχώρ (ichor) "the juice, not blood, that flows in the veins of gods in Greek mythology".It was used as a given name for a girl in the Canadian province Alberta in 2016.
Feminine variant of Petri or an elaboration of Petra.
Croatian and Serbian form of Petromir.

A rare Greek given name, found mostly on the island Naxos of Cyclades where it probably originated. It is possibly a derivative form of the Latin name Petronilla, since Naxos and most of Cyclades were occupied, as the Duchy of Naxos, by the Republic of Venice from 1207 to 1579 A.D.
Croatian and Serbian form of Petroslav. Known bearers of this name were Serbian rulers Petrislav of Duklja and Petrislav of Rascia, who both lived in the 11th century AD.

This name started probably as a variant of Beatrice but was later understood as a feminine form to Peter/Petrus. During the Middle Ages this name was not uncommon in southern German-speaking areas, especially in noble families.Bearers include: Petrissa von Hotingen (*1160), granddaughter of Frederick I. von Staufen, Duke of SwabiaPetrissa von Zähringen (*before 1101)Petrissa von Weidenberg (*1340), abbess of Niedermünster AbbeyA modern-day bearer is German professional table tennis player Petrissa Solja (*1994)

This name is Christian in origin. The first element is derived from Petros (see Peter) and refers to Saint Peter, who was one of Jesus' twelve apostles and went on to become the first Pope of the Catholic Church. The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". The meaning of this name is thus roughly "peace to Peter".
Form of Petronella. Famous bearers include Petronėlė Gerlikienė (1905-1979).

Diminutive form of Petrona or Petronia, in a similar way as names like Antoinette and Nicolette. The name seems not very common throughout France, though it is reputed to be most often used in Brittany.
Croatian and Lithuanian form of Petronia.
Italian, Venetian and Galician form of Petronius.
Polish and Kashubian form of Petronius.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Petronius.
Bulgarian and Russian form of Petronia.

South Italian dialect word meaning "little parsley" derived from Latin petrosilium, from Greek πετροσέλινον (petroselinon) "rock-selery".This is the name of the main character in an early version of Rapunzel written by Giambattista Basile.

This name is Christian in origin. The first element is derived from Petros (see Peter) and refers to Saint Peter, who was one of Jesus' twelve apostles and went on to become the first Pope of the Catholic Church. The second element is derived from Slavic slav "glory". The meaning of this name is thus roughly "glorious Peter" or "glory to Peter".
Russian patronymic last name. Petrova is the name of one of the Fossil sisters in the book (and movie) 'Ballet Shoes' by Noel Streatfeild.
Formed from Petra and the Old Norse name suffix rún meaning "secret lore, rune".
Ukrainian form of Petronilla. It appears to have been most common among Poles living in Ukraine (see also Petronela.
Montenegrin, Croatian and Slovak diminutive of Petra and Petronela. This name is only used in Montenegro as a given name in its own right; in Croatia and Slovakia it is strictly used as a diminutive.
Diminutive of feminine given names that start with Petr- (such as Petrė and Petronėlė), since this name contains the feminine diminutive suffix -utė.
Diminutive of masculine given names that start with Petr- (such as Petras and Petronijus), since this name contains the masculine diminutive suffix -utis.
Lower Sorbian variant of Pětr (compare Pěc).
Medieval German diminutive of Peter, popular in the Rhineland region in Germany in the 1300s and 1400s.
A female English name. It is the first name of Real Housewife of Melbourne Pettifleur Berenger (1964-).
Possible variation or elaboration of Petula.
19th-century misinterpretation of Petur which was used in medieval Hungarian records as a written form of Pétör.
Khanty and Mansi form of Theodosia.
Petyr Baelish is a major character in the Song of Ice and Fire books by GRR Martin and the TV show Game of Thrones based upon the former. It is obviously an alternative spelling of real-world Peter.
Obsolete diminutive of Petra and Peter.
Latinized form of Peukestas. This was the name of a distinguished Macedonian officer in the service of Alexander the Great (4th century BC).
Latinized form of Peukolaos. This was the name of a Macedonian man who participated in Dimnus of Chalastra's conspiracy to assassinate Alexander the Great (4th century BC).

Derived from the Greek noun πεύκη (peuke) meaning "pine (tree)" combined with -τας (-tas), which is the Aeolic, Epic and Doric Greek form of the Attic Greek suffix -της (-tes). The suffix forms nouns that represent a state of being.

Derived from the Greek noun πεύκη (peuke) meaning "pine (tree)" combined with the Greek noun λαός (laos) meaning "(the) people". This was the name of one of the men who participated in Dimnos of Chalastra's conspiracy to assassinate Alexander the Great (4th century BC).Peukolaos was also the name of an Indo-Greek king from the 1st century BC. One source claims that the king's name ought to be interpreted as having the meaning of "the man from Pushkalavati". Pushkalavati was the historic capital of Gandhara, located in the Valley of Peshawar. In other words: this source basically indicates that the king's name is a hellenization of an Indian name. That is unlikely to be correct, despite the fact that the ethnicity of later Indo-Greek kings is sometimes not all that clear. After all: all other Indo-Greek kings bore names that are clearly of Greek origin. Why would king Peukolaos be the one exception to that rule?

Limburgish form of Paulus (see Paul). It has been in use since medieval times, as is evidenced by the existence of the patronymic surname Peulen, which is still primarily prevalent in the Limburgish language area.

Medieval Limburgish variant of Palm. It likely came about via its other variant Paum, as -au- is known to shift to -eu- in some parts of the Limburgish language area. The name Peul is a good example of this.

Medieval Limburgish short form of Paschalis and Paschasius. It was in use until at least the 18th century, and had become obsolete by the 20th century.Today, the name still survives in several patronymic surnames, most of which remain primarily prevalent in the Limburgish language area. Of these, the surname Peusens is the most common, both in Belgian Limburg and Dutch Limburg. The second place goes to Peusen in Dutch Limburg, and Peuskens in Belgian Limburg.
Means "clear up, reappearance of light" in Shipibo.
Variant of Pazanne. The name of an obscure French saint whose life and work are somewhat of a mystery. Nonetheless, she left her name in several place names throughout France.
Means "drinking cup, goblet" in Ottoman Turkish.
The pen name of Pierre Culliford, Belgian comic artist and writer, and creator of the Smurfs.
Mid 19th century from Latin American Spanish, from Nahuatl peyotl, meaning "glisten" or "glistening". Other sources translate the Nahuatl word as "Divine Messenger"
Occitan feminine form of Peyre as well as a Gascon feminine form of Pey.
From Persian پیوسته (peyvaste) meaning "connected, continuous; always, forever".
Alternate transcription of Persian پژمان (see Pejman).
Middle Breton variant of Pedr and Per.
Transferred use of the German surname Pfeiffer.
Pfiffi Buddenbrook is a figure in the novel "Buddenbrooks" by Thomas Mann.

Created by the translator Ute Eichler as the name for Princess Smartypants (by Babette Cole). The name contains the German word pfiffig "smart" and the German name element GUND "war" (see, e.g., Hildegund).
name used in a Filipino drama on radio in 1980's...
From Sino-Vietnamese 樸 (phác) meaning "sincere, modest" or 璞 (phác) meaning "uncut jade".
Derived from Thai เพชร (phetcha) meaning "diamond", ultimately from Sanskrit वज्र (vajra).
Greek form of Pedahel, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Alternate transcription of Thai พัดชา (see Phatcha).
Alternate transcription of Thai เผด็จ (see Phadet).

column3: เผด็จศักดิ์(Thai)
column12: From Thai เผด็จ (phadet) meaning "subdue, suppress, eliminate" or "absolute, complete" and ศักดิ์ (sak) meaning "power, honour".
Alternate transcription of Thai ผดุงเดช (see Phadungdet).
From Thai ผดุง (phadung) meaning "maintain, uphold, sustain" and เดช (det) meaning "power, might, authority".
From Thai ผดุง (phadung) meaning "maintain, uphold, sustain" and พงษ์ (phong) meaning "lineage, family".
Alternate transcription of Thai ผดุงพงษ์ (see Phadungphong).

column12: From Thai ผดุง (phadung) meaning "maintain, uphold, sustain" and ศักดิ์ (sak) meaning "power".

Latinized form of Phaiax. Bearers of this name include an architect and an orator, who both lived in the 5th century BC.In Greek mythology, Phaeax was a son of the sea god Poseidon, whom he had with the nymph Korkyra.
Latinized form of Phaidon. A notable bearer of this name was the Greek philosopher Phaedo of Elis (4th century BC).
Variant latinization of Phaidon, as well as a modern transcription. (Its proper latinized form is Phaedo.)
Variant of Phaedra used by Edmund Spenser in his epic poem 'The Faerie Queene' (1590), where it belongs to a water fairy who lures knights to her enchanted island.
A character in 'Curculio', also called The Weevil, a Latin comedic play for the early Roman theatre by Titus Maccius Plautus.
Latinized form of Phaidyme. This name was borne by a 6th-century BC Persian noblewoman, the daughter of Otanes, who would later go on to marry Darius I.

Latinized form of the Greek name Φαιναρέτη (Phainarete) meaning "she who brings virtue to light" or "one who shows virtue", derived from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to shine" as well as "to show, to appear" combined with ἀρετὴ (arete) meaning "virtue, excellence". This was the name of the mother of Socrates.
Means "dear, expensive" or "to love" in Lao.
Latinized form of Phainippos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 5th century BC.

Latinized form of Greek Φαῖνοψ (Phainops) meaning "bright-eyed, conspicuous", derived from φαεινός (phaeinos) "shining, radiant" and ὄψ (ops) "eye". This is the name of several characters in the Iliad of Homer.
The name of one of the Hyades, nymphs of rain, derived from Ancient Greek φαιός (phaios) meaning "grey, dusky, dull, ashy".

Means "beaming, radiant" in Ancient Greek, being a participle of the verb φαέθω (phaethô) "to shine" (see Phaethon). In Greek mythology this was the name of a daughter of the sun god Helios by the nymph Neaira. She and her sister Lampetia pastured the sacred herds of Helios on the mythical island of Thrinacia.
The name of an asteroid pertaining to the Main belt in the Solar System. It is named after the mythological character Phaethousa.
Greek form of Pagiel, as it first appeared in the Septuagint.
Means "army, troop, brigade" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit बहल (bahala).
From Sino-Vietnamese 湃 (phái) meaning "surge, powerful waves".

Means "dusky" or "grey" in Ancient Greek, from φαιός (phaios). This is the name of the Crommyonian Sow, a mythological pig slain by Theseus. Some versions of the story say that this was the name of the old woman who owned the sow, which was named after her. Plutarch reports that Phaia may have actually been a murderous female bandit slain by Theseus, and who had received the nickname of 'sow' due to her uncouth habits.

Derived from the Greek noun Φαίαξ (Phaiax) meaning "Phaeacian". A Phaeacian was an inhabitant of Phaeacia, a region in Greek mythology.The name of the region is written as Φαιακία (Phaiakia) in Greek. It might ultimately be derived from either the Greek adjective φαιός (phaios) meaning "grey" or the Greek noun φάος (phaos) meaning "light". The latter word is ultimately derived from the Greek verb φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to shine" as well as "to show, to appear". Also compare the related names Phaedra and Phaidon.
Alternate transcription of Thai ไพบูลย์ (see Phaibun).
Alternate transcription of Thai ไพบูลย์ (see Phaibun).
Alternate transcription of Thai ไพบูลย์ (see Phaibun).
Means "abundant, prosperous, plentiful" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वैपुल्य (vaipulya).

Derived from Greek φαίδιμος (phaidimos) meaning "shining, radiant, glistening". This was the name of several characters in Greek legend, including a king of Sidon mentioned in the 'Odyssey'. It was also borne by a 2nd-century BC Greek poet from Bisanthe (eastern Thrace).

Derived from Ancient Greek φαιδρός (phaidros) meaning "bright, beaming".Phaidon of Elis (better known as Phaedo) was a 4th-century BC philosopher and a friend and student of Socrates. He was present for the last hours of Socrates' life. Plato's book Phaidon (better known by its latinized form Phaedo) is named after Phaidon of Elis.
Hellenized form of an unidentified Old Persian name. According to Herodotus this was borne by the daughter of Otanes who in turn married Сambyses, False Smerdis (real name: Gaumata) and Darius.
Possibly from Lao ໄພ (phai) meaning "forest", "ripple", or "whisper" and ຄຳ (kham) meaning "gold".
Means "sapphire" in Thai, borrowed from the name of the Cambodian province of Pailin.
Possibly a Bengali form of Fahim.Phaim Bhuiyan (born 1995) is an Italian director, screenwriter and actor who won in 2020 the David di Donatello Awards.

Probably related to Phaenna, or perhaps from Greek φανης (phanes) meaning "appearing". A notable bearer was Saint Phaine of Ancyra, a 3rd-century Christian martyr. She was one of seven holy virgins, including Saint Tecusa, who were drowned in a lake under the emperor Diocletian.
Derived from the Greek verb φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to shine" as well as "to show, to appear" combined with the Greek noun ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".

Means "the shiner, the shining one" in Ancient Greek, referring to the planet Saturn, derived from φαίνω (phaino) "to shine, give light; cause to appear". This was the name of the personification of Saturn in Greek mythology, or occasionally of Jupiter.
Alternate transcription of Thai ไพโรจน์ (see Phairot).
Means "bright, shining, brilliant" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वैरोचन (vairocana).

Alternate transcription of Thai ไพฑูรย์ (see Phaithun).

MEANING - fruit, result, gain, a board, lath, plank, leaf. bench, a slab or tablet (for writing or painting on ; also = page, leaf), a slab at the base, any flat surface (often in comp. with parts of the body, applied to broad flat bones, the palm of the hand, the top or head of an arrow, a shield, bark (as a material for clothes), the pericarp of a lotus, a layer, the stand on which a monk keeps his turbanUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist, Hindu

Probably derived from Greek φάλαρον (phalaron), which was the name for a metal disc or boss that was worn as a military ornament on the breast. Phalaris was the name of a tyrant of Acragas (now Agrigento) in Sicily, who lived in the 6th century BC.
From a non-Sino-Vietnamese reading of Chinese 玻璃 (pha ly) meaning "lead glass, crystal".
From Φάλεκ (Phalek), a Hellenized form of Peleg. Allegedly the form used in the Septuagint is Φάλεγ (Phaleg).

Possibly derived from φάληρος (phaleros), the Ionic form of Ancient Greek φάλαρος (phalaros) meaning "having a patch of white or white spot". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including an Argonaut and eponymous founder of the ancient city Phaleron, a Lapith who fought against the centaurs (also called Phalereus), and a Trojan warrior.
From the name of the twelfth month of the Hindu calendar, itself from Sanskrit फल्गुन (phalguna) meaning "red". This is also an epithet of the hero Arjuna.
MEANING : reddish, red, spring season, small. It is feminine of Phalgu or FalguUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek φαλός (phalos) meaning "white, shining". This was the name of one of the fifty (or fifty-one) grandsons of Thespius fathered by Heracles in Greek mythology, his mother being Heliconis.
MEANING : : to obtain fruit or reward. Here फली means reward, fruit + भू means obtainingUsage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, BuddhistOther spell Falibhu, Falibhoo
Possibly means "with a white spot, dappled", from Greek φαλός (phalos) meaning "white".
Phallu was a son of Reuben according to Genesis 46:9, Exodus 6:14 and Numbers 26:5. He was one of the 70 souls to migrate to Egypt with Jacob.
Form of Paltiel used in the English, Greek and Latin Old Testament.
MEANING : a flower, bud Usage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
From Sino-Vietnamese 品 (phẩm) meaning "dye, rank, quality".
Means "bee" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit भ्रमर (bhramara)
From Sino-Vietnamese 判 (phán) meaning "to rule, to declare".
From Sino-Vietnamese 分 (phân) meaning "to divide, distinguish" or 雰 (phân) meaning "mist, fog".
Derived from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to shine, give light; to appear, show" and ἀγορά (agora) meaning "assembly, marketplace; speech".

Means "forest, jungle, grove" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वन (vana).

Means "to bring light, to make appear", from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to appear, make known; to shine, give light". This was the name of several historical figures, including Phanes of Halicarnassus, a councilman and mercenary who served the Egyptian pharaoh Amasis II. It was also the name of the primordial god of creation in the Orphic tradition.

Perhaps intended to be a feminine form of Phanes, probably influenced by the name Vanessa. In Greek mythology, Phanes was a primeval god of procreation whose name derived from Greek phainô "to bring light, make clear".
Means "young woman, girl" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वनिता (vanitā).
Means "girl, young woman, wife" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वनिता (vanitā).
Means "close friend, favoured person, confidant" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वल्लभ (vallabha).
Latinized form of Phanokles. This name was borne by an ancient Greek elegiac poet from the 4th century BC.
Derived from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to show, appear, reveal" or "to shine, give light" and δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people".
Derived from Ancient Greek φανός (phanos), which can mean "bright, shining, resplendent" as well as "torch, lantern" (compare phanes "appearing"), and κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".
Means "hill, mountain" (a poetic word) in Thai.
Probably derived from Ancient Greek φανός (phanos), which can mean "light, bright" as well as "torch, lantern" (compare phanes "appearing"), combined with μάχη (mache) meaning "battle".
Latinized form of Phanomachos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 3rd century BC.
Derived from Ancient Greek φανός (phanos), which can mean "bright, shining, resplendent" as well as "torch, lantern" (compare phanes "appearing"), and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".
Latinized form of Phanostratos. This name was borne by two eponymous archons of Athens, the earliest of which lived in the 4th century BC.

This name is best known for being the name of saint Phanourios (also known as Phanurius), a pre-congegration saint who is primarily venerated in the Greek Orthodox Church. Since nearly all relevant details about the saint's life have been lost - such as where (and when!) he lived and died - we cannot be certain if he was an ethnic Greek or a foreigner who had become at least partially hellenized. As such, his name (which is most likely a compound name) is either an authentic Greek name, or a hellenized foreign name.In the case of the former, the first element is almost certainly derived from Greek φανός (phanos) meaning "light" (adjective) as well as "torch, lantern" (noun). The second element is possibly derived from Greek οὖρος (ouros) meaning "watcher, guardian", which might give the name the meaning of "guardian with a torch". Also compare Ourania and Orion, which might possibly be etymologically related to varying degrees.In the case of the latter possibility, the name Phanourios might be a hellenization of the Arabic name Fannur (also written as Fanur), which is also strongly connected to the theme of light.

Means "rainy season, wet season" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वर्षा (varṣā). This is also the name for the three-month period during the rainy season (typically from July to October) during which Buddhist monks do not leave their temples in order to devote themselves to their studies.
From Thai พรรษา (phansa) meaning "rainy season, year" and วุฒิ (wut) meaning "knowledge, prosperity, growth".
Phantastes or Fantasy is the youth in the upper floors of the House of Temperance. He represents imagination and the vision of things to come.

Means "visible, appearing" or perhaps "shining one", derived from Ancient Greek φαίνω (phaino) meaning "to appear, show, reveal" as well as "to shine, give light". Phantes was one of the fifty sons of King Aegyptus in Greek mythology, and was killed by his wife, Theano, on their wedding night.

Derived from the Greek adjective φαντός (phantos) meaning "visible", which in turn is ultimately derived from the Greek verb φαντάζω (phantazo) meaning "to make visible".A notable bearer of this name was the Italo-Greek saint Phantinos (c. 927-1000), who is better known under the name Fantinus the Younger. He was born and raised in what is now the region of Calabria in the deep south of Italy. During his lifetime, Calabria was a Byzantine dominion, where the Greek culture and language was dominant. His parents were named Georgius and Vriena (also Beyena and Vryaini), while his three siblings were named Caterina, Cosmas and Lucas. All are names of Greek origin, so like most (if not all) Calabrians of the time, the saint and his family must have spoken Greek natively. Saint Phantinos later also travelled to Greece, where he ended up spending the remainder of his life.

Uncertain etymology. Possibly derived from an inflected form of Ancient Greek φημί (phemi) meaning "to say, speak, declare", or perhaps related to φάντωρ (phantor) meaning "one who displays". Phanto of Phlius was a Pythagorean philosopher.
From the English word "phantom" a synonym for "ghost", ultimately from Greek φάντασμα (phántasma) "phantom, ghost", "vision, dream", "fantasy".

Sapho and Phao is an Elizabethan era stage play, a comedy written by John Lyly. It’s known to have been performed at Court before Queen Elizabeth, probably on 3 March 1584.Possibly the name comes Greek Mythology. As in some of the myths, Phaon is an old ferryman of Lesbos who is rewarded by Aphrodite with renewed youth and beauty after he transports her from Mytilene to Chios

Probably derived from Ancient Greek φάω (phao) meaning "to shine, give light" (compare Phaethon). This was the name of an elderly boatman blessed with youth and beauty by Aphrodite in Greek mythology.
From Sino-Vietnamese 法 (pháp) meaning "rule, law, standard".

From Sino-Vietnamese 法螺 (pháp loa) meaning "conch shell of law", referring to Charonia tritonis, which are used as Buddhist trumpets. Pháp Loa (1284-1330), born Đồng Kiên Cương, was a Buddhist Thiên master.
Means "brother" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit भ्रातृ (bhrātṛ).
Alternate transcription of Thai ภราดร (see Pharadon).

From the English word pharaoh, the title given to the kings of Ancient Egypt. The term ultimately comes from Ancient Egyptian pr-ˤ3 meaning "palace, pharaoh", itself from pr "house" and ˤ3 "great, big".

The first element of this name is derived from xwarrah (also khwarrah), which is the Middle Persian form of Avestan 𐬓𐬀𐬭𐬆𐬥𐬀𐬵 (xᵛarənah) or (khvarenah). Known as فر (farr) or فره (farrah) in modern Persian, it literally denotes "glory" or "splendour", but in a figurative sense it refers to the Zoroastrian concept of divine right and favor granted to rulers and heroes by the god Ahura Mazda.The second element of this name is derived from Middle Persian mānag meaning "mind" - compare Avestan 𐬨𐬀𐬥𐬀𐬢𐬵 (manaŋh) or (manangh) meaning "mind, thought".Last but not least, Pharasmanes was the name of six kings of Iberia (now Georgia), the first of which lived in the 1st century AD. All of them are known as Parsman in modern Georgian.

Derived from the Adûnaic word pharaz, meaning "gold". In The Silmarillion, Ar-Pharazôn (King Pharazôn) was the name of the last king of Númenor and the husband and usurper of Miriel. Ar-Pharazôn brought Sauron to Númenor, who introduced the worship of Morgoth to Númenor. Later Sauron convinced Ar-Pharazôn to assail Valinor, which he did, and this action caused the Downfall of Númenor.
meaning "Gained, Earned"borne by several Parthian kings

A knight – whom Malory calls “a worshipful knight” – from Trebe in the service, as seneschal, of kings Ban of Benwick (Lancelot’s father) and Bors of Gaul. Pharien and Lionses (Leonce de Paerne) were the two “knights of worship” sent to greet the Britons. They accompanied their lieges to Britain to assist in Arthur’s wars against the rebellious kings and the Saxons at Bedegraine.King Bors banished Pharien after Pharien killed another knight to avenge his uncle’s death. Pharien took service with King Claudas, the enemy of Ban and Bors, but still retained his loyalty to Bors and his family.After Ban and Bors died during Claudas’s invasion of their lands, Pharien guided Bors’s widow to a monastery and then looked after her children, Bors and Lionel, whom he hid from Claudas. Claudas loved Pharien’s wife and made Pharien seneschal of Gannes for her sake.Claudas had an affair with Pharien’s wife and found out about the princes from her. After King Bors’ death, Pharien confiscated Bors’ two sons, Lionel (aged twenty-one months) and young Bors (aged nine months). Claudas agreed to take care of them and made Pharien heir to their lands until they were grown, making Pharien and his nephew Lambegue their tutors.In time, however, the people of Gannes (Bors’s former land) revolted and Pharien found himself in the uneasy situation of protecting King Claudas against his former allies and friends. This led to a temporary rift between Pharien and his nephew, Lambegue. After Seraide’s rescue of the two boys from Claudas’ court, Claudas threw Pharien and Lambegus into prison, but Lionses used a ruse to accomplish their rescue.Pharien and his family were brought to the French Lake. Pharien lived long enough to see Bors and Lionel placed in the care of the Lady of the Lake. His wife remained with Viviane, and his sons, Anguins and Tatains, went on to become gallant knights.
Uncertain etymology, possibly a variant of Paris 1. In Greek mythology, Pharis was the son of Hermes and the Danaid Phylodameia, and the eponymous founder of the ancient town Pharis in Laconia.

Primarily Southeastern in the United States, dating back to the 1840s and also used in the early 20th century.Pharisee (n) "from Aramaic (Semitic) perishayya, emphatic plural of perish 'separated, separatist,' corresponding to Hebrew parush, from parash 'he separated.' Extended meaning 'any self-righteous person, formalist, hypocrite, scrupulous or ostentatious observer of the outward forms of religion without regard to its inward spirit' is attested from 1580s" -etymonline.com

Feminine form of Pharnaces. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a Hyrian princess, daughter of King Megassares of Hyria, wife of King Sandocus of Celendreis, mother of Cinyras, king of Cyprus.
Latinized form of Farnaka via its hellenized form Pharnakes. This name was borne by several ancient Persians, one of them being the paternal uncle of Darius the Great.
Hellenized form of Farnaspa. This was the name of the father-in-law of Cyrus the Great (6th century BC).
Variant of Pharaoh. A notable bearer is Grammy Award winning American jazz saxophonist, Pharoah Sanders, born Farrell Sanders (b.1940).

This was the name of an ancient Greek poetess and priestess, said to be a daughter of Apollo in mythological traditions.

It was likely used as a baptismal name (or otherwise seen as a proper Christian name) for newborn girls with native Frisian names that look quite similar, such as Fenna and Fenneke.

From phoenix, the name of the immortal bird in Greek and Egyptian mythology. This is the name of a demon who appears in several works on demonology, including the 17th-century grimoire The Lesser Key of Solomon (author unknown) and the Pseudomonarchia Daemonum (1563) by Dutch physician Johann Weyer.

When she gave birth to a son, her father, Alcimedon, abandoned her and the infant on a mountainside to die; a jay flew to inform Heracles of their plight by mimicking the baby’s crying, and he rescued them both.

The island was flooded in 1970 and disappeared into the river, but its temple complex was moved to the island of Agilkia.Alternatively this may be a French variant of Philaeus or Phile.This name was used by French travel writers Alexandre and Sonia Poussin for their daughter born in 2004.

Originally a short form of a Greek name beginning with the element φίλος (philos) meaning "lover, friend". This was the name of an early Christian saint, a 3rd-century bishop of the Egyptian city of Thmuis. This name has been in rare use in the English-speaking world from as early as the late 17th century, used primarily by Catholics in honour of the saint. Jules Verne used it for the protagonist (Phileas Fogg, an Englishman) in his novel Around the World in 80 Days (1873).
Derived from Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and ἥβη (hebe) meaning "youth; vigour".

The use of Phileine as a feminine first name in The Netherlands is due to the 2003 film "Phileine Zegt Sorry" (English: "Phileine Says Sorry"). The film is based on a book written by Dutch author Ronald Giphart (b. 1965), which carries the same title and was published in 1996. Phileine is the first name of the book's main character, and the author derived the name from the Dutch adjective vilein, which means "mean, evil" in English and is etymologically related to the English noun villain. This is both fitting and deliberate, as it points to the unlikability of the main character.The name Phileine first started to get used in 2004, which is the year immediately following the release year of the book's film adaptation. The name was not in use before that, despite the book having been released in 1996 already. It was the film that finally popularised the name. According to the first names database of the Meertens Institute, the name was at its most popular in 2009, in which year 59 girls were given this name. However, according to the popularity statistics on this website, Phileine was at its most popular in 2011, i.e. more popular in 2011 than it was in 2009 (while the Meertens Institute states the reverse).It is easy to mistake the name Phileine as being a variant of Philine, which is derived from the Greek verb philein "to love". However, this is not the case, as Phileine as a first name in The Netherlands is completely inspired by the film (and thus indirectly, the book). And since the author derived it from Dutch vilein (as I explained before), that is really the only correct meaning for Phileine.
Possibly a variant of Philine, a contraction of Philomène, or a feminine form of Phil using the common name suffix lene.
Variant of Philomena, influenced by Wilhelmina.
Derived from Greek philia "love", specifically referring to any kind of platonic love. In the English-speaking world, this name has seen occasional usage from the 17th century onwards.

Derived from Philianus, which is the latinized form of Greek Philianos. It is ultimately derived from Greek philos "friend" or phileo "to love". Compare also Philon. A known bearer of this name is the American actor Ethan Embry, who carries Philian as a middle name.
Either a feminine form of Philian or an elaboration of Philia.

Perhaps based on Philadelphia or Fidelis. It was used by John Dryden in his opera 'King Arthur; or, the British Worthy' (1691), where it belongs to an air spirit in the service of Merlin who saves Arthur from the evil schemes of Osmond, a Saxon sorcerer, and Grimbald, an enemy earth spirit.

Philidore likely meaning "gift of love", from the Greek philos (φιλος) meaning "friend, lover" and doron (δωρον) meaning "gift".Philadore is also the name of the protagonist in Eliza Haywood's 1727 novel 'Philadore and Placentia'.
Feminine form of Philinos. In Germany it was brought to public attention when Johann Wolfgang von Goethe used it for a character in his novel Wilhelm Meister's Apprenticeship (1795-96).

Means "darling" in Greek, a term of affection derived from Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover". A famous bearer was Philinna of Larissa in Thessaly (4th century BC), the third wife of Philip II of Macedon and mother of Philip III Arrhidaeus. In theatre, the name occurs in Aristophanes' play The Clouds (423 BC).
Derived from Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "lover, friend".
Form of Philip used by Malayalam-speaking Syriac Christians in the Indian state of Kerala.

Means "son of Philippos" in Greek, derived from the name Philippos combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).Bearers of this name include a comic poet from the 4th century BC and a wealthy Athenian oligarch from the 3rd century BC.
Interlingua and Judeo-Catalan form of Philip.
King of England and father of Meliadice. He was succeeded by his son-in-law, Cleriadus.
Medieval Dutch form of Philippos (see Philip).This name is not to be confused with the patronymic surname Philips.
Latinized form of Philiskos. This name was borne by several ancient Greek philosophers and poets.
Derived from Ancient Greek φιλίσκος (philiskos) meaning "little friend", a diminutive form of φίλος (philos) "friend" using the diminutive suffix -ίσκος (-iskos).
From the biblical place name Philistia.
Means "son of Philistos" in Greek, derived from the name Philistos combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This was the name of a Greek tyrant of Oreus, who lived in the 4th century BC.

Derived from the Greek adjective φίλιστος (philistos) meaning "most beloved", which is a superlative of the Greek adjective φίλος (philos) meaning "beloved, dear".This name was borne by an Olympic victor from the 1st century BC.
Latinized form of Philistos. This was the name of a Greek historian from Syracuse in Sicily, who lived in the 5th century BC.

From Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "lover, friend" or φιλέω (phileo) meaning "to love" combined with the suffix -τας (-tas). This was the name of a Greek scholar, poet, and grammarian during the early Hellenistic period of ancient Greece.
Variant of Philemon. This form of the name appears to be used in southern Africa.
Diminutive form of Phillip, Phyllis and Philomena
Variant of Philip (masculine) as well as a vernacular form of Philipa (feminine) used in medieval times.
English variant of Philip and French variant of Philippe.
Transferred use of the surname Phillips.
Possibly a modern variation of Philiscus
Diminutive of Philippa, Phyllis and other names containing the element Phil-.
Likely a variant of Fillmore, influenced by Phil.

Derived from the Greek adjective φιλόχορος (philochoros) meaning "loving the choir or choral dance", which consists of the Greek noun φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" combined with the Greek noun χορός (choros) meaning "dance".
Latinized form of Philochoros. A known bearer of this name was Philochorus of Athens, a Greek historian from the 3rd century BC.

Latinized form of Greek Φιλόκλεια (Philokleia), a feminine form of Philokles. Sir Philip Sydney (1554-1586) used this name for a character, the younger sister of Pamela, in his pastoral romance The Countess of Pembroke's Arcadia.
Latinized form of Philokles. This name was borne by an Athenian tragic poet from the 5th century BC.
Means "friend of the people, popular", derived from Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and δῆμος (demos) meaning "the people."
Latinized form of Philodemos. This name was borne by a Greek philosopher and poet from the 1st century BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover; beloved" and δίκη (dike) meaning "law, judgement, justice". Compare the words φιλόδικος (philodikos) "litigious, argumentative, fond of lawsuits" and φιλοδίκαιος (philodikaios) "loving justice".
Dutch and Flemish form of Philogenes.

French form of Philogenes. Known bearers of this name include the French foreign minister Louis Philogène Brûlart de Sillery (1702-1770), the Belgian painter Charles-Philogène Tschaggeny (1815-1894) and the Belgian ornithologist Philogène Wytsman (1866-1925).
Derived from Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" combined with γενής (genes) meaning "born".
Latinized form of Φιλογόνιος (Philogonios), which is a variant of Philogonos.This was the name of a 4th-century bishop and saint of Antioch.

Derived from the Greek adjective φιλόγονος (philogonos) meaning "loving one's children", which consists of Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "beloved, dear" as well as "friend, lover" combined with the Greek noun γονή (gone) meaning "birth, offspring".
Means "friend of glory" or "glory of the friend", derived from Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) "friend, lover" combined with κλέος (kleos) "glory".
Means "loving the people", derived from Ancient Greek φιλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and λαος (laos) meaning "people, folk".
Latinized form of Philolaos. This name was borne by a Philolaus of Croton, a Greek philosopher from the 4th century BC.
Means "fond of words, talkative" in Ancient Greek, from φίλος (philos) "friend, lover" and λόγος (logos) "word, speech; reason, consideration, computation".
Latinized form of Philologos. A bearer of this name was Philologus of Sinope, a saint from the 1st century AD.

Means "lover of learning", derived from the Ancient Greek words φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover", and μαθ-/μανθάνειν (math-/manthanein) meaning "to learn".This was the name of one of the central characters in Daemonologie, a medieval compendium on witchcraft written by King James VI of Scotland and later England.

Means "pleasing to mortals" in Ancient Greek, from φίλος (philos) meaning "beloved, dear; friend, lover" and βροτός (brotos) meaning "mortal man, human being". Philombrotos of Sparta was a 6th-century BCE pankratist who won three crowns in pankration.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover; dear, beloved" and μήδεα (medea) meaning "plans, counsel, cunning" (compare Ganymede). Alternatively, could be a variant of Philomeides.

Means "smile-loving" in Ancient Greek, derived from φίλος (philos) meaning "lover, friend; beloved" and μειδιάω (meidiao) meaning "to smile". Compare Philommeides, an epithet of the goddess Aphrodite. Alternatively, could be a variant of Philomedes.
Masculine form of Philomele (see Philomela). A notable bearer of this name was the Greek general Philomelos of Phocis (4th century BC).
Latinized form of Philomelos. In Greek mythology, this was the name of a minor demi-god.
Latinized form of Philomenos. This was the name of two saints, namely Philomenus of Ancyra (3rd century AD) and Philomenus of Heraclea (century unknown).

An epithet of Aphrodite meaning "smile-loving" in Ancient Greek, derived from φίλος (philos) meaning "lover, friend; beloved" and μειδιάω (meidiao) meaning "to smile". The second element is often interpreted as the obscure related word μεῖδος (meidos) meaning "laughter".

Variant form of Philonilla, which is the name of a saint from the first century AD. The name Philonella is also used in reference to the saint (usually in sources that ultimately take their information from Latin texts rather than Greek texts), which has led people in at least the English-speaking world to use the two names interchangeably.

Latinized form of the Greek name Φιλονίκη (Philonike), derived from φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and νίκη (nike) meaning "victory" (related to the Greek noun φιλονικία (philonikia) meaning "love of victory, rivalry" and the Greek verb φιλονικέω (philonikeo) meaning "to be fond of victory, to engage in rivalry"). This is the name of the protagonist of the fairy tale La Tiranie des Fées Détruite (The Tyranny of the Fairies Destroyed) by Madame d'Auneuil; Philonice is a princess kidnapped and held captive by fairies.

Means "son of Philon" in Greek, derived from the name Philon combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).A notable bearer of this name was Philonides of Laodicea, an Epicurean philosopher and mathematician from the 2nd century BC.

This name is best known for being the name of saint Philonilla (also found written as Philonella), who lived in the first century AD. She was born into a Jewish family in Tarsus (located in what is now Turkey), which at the time was part of the Roman Empire, but had belonged to the Greeks not that long ago and as such was still heavily influenced by the Greek language and culture. Along with her sister Zenaida, saint Philonilla was a Christian physician who treated the sick for free, which made them the very first Holy Unmercenaries. This is what eventually caused them to become the first doctor-saints.With all of this in mind, the saint's name is most likely a feminization of the masculine Greek name Philon, which was created by adding the Latin feminine diminutive suffix -illa to it (see names like Drusilla and Lucilla). Because of this, the variant Philonella is also encountered, because -ella is also a Latin feminine diminutive suffix (see names like Marcella). All in all, this name is essentially a Greco-Roman name. It is unlikely to be a full Greek name, as -illa and -ella are not suffixes that are found in the Greek language or at least native to it.
Feminine form of Philon. In Greek mythology, Philonis (also called Chione or Leuconoe) was the mother of Philammon and Autolycus by Apollo and Hermes, respectively.

Derived from Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and νόος (noos) meaning "mind, thought". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a Lycian princess whose hand in marriage was won by Bellerophon when he slayed the Chimaera, as well as of a princess of Sparta who was granted immortality by the goddess Artemis. The latter’s name was also written as Φυλονόη (Phylonoe), in which case the first element could be φυλή (phyle) "tribe, clan".
Means "loving one’s grandfather" in Ancient Greek, derived from φίλος (philos) "friend, lover" combined with πάππος (pappos) "grandfather".

Means "father-loving, loving one’s father" in Ancient Greek, composed of φίλος (philos) "friend, lover; beloved" and πατήρ (pater) "father". This was a common royal epithet among Hellenistic monarchs.
Latinized form of Philopoimen. This was the name of a Greek general and statesman from the 2nd century BC.
Derived from the Greek noun φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" combined with the Greek noun ποιμήν (poimen) meaning "herdsman, shepherd" (see Poimen).
Means "diligent, industrious" in Ancient Greek, literally "loving labor", derived from φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and πόνος (ponos) meaning "labor, toil, work; suffering, pain".

Derived from Ancient Greek φιλόσοφος (philosophos) meaning "lover of wisdom, philosopher", composed of φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" combined with σοφός (sophos) meaning "skilled, clever, wise". Cognate to the English word philosopher.
Latinized form of Philosophos. This was the name of a 3rd-century martyr and saint from Alexandria.

Derived from Ancient Greek φιλόστοργος (philostorgos) meaning "loving tenderly, showing (familial) affection", composed of φίλος (philos) "friend, lover" and στέργω (stergo) "to love, show affection, be content".
Derived from Ancient Greek φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and στρατός (stratos) meaning "army."

Derived from Ancient Greek φιλωτέρα (philôtera) meaning "more beloved, dearer", the comparative form of φίλος (philos) "beloved, dear; friend, lover". This was borne by the younger sister of Arsinoe II and Ptolemy II.
Means "friendship, affection" in Ancient Greek (see philos). Philotes was the Greek goddess of friendship and affection, one of the children of Nyx. Her Roman equivalent is Amicitia.
French form of Philotheus (via its Latinized form Philotheos) and Philothea. While the masculine name has fallen out of use, the feminine name was revived in the late 2000s.
Medieval Greek form of Philothea. This name was notably borne by the Greek saint Philothei of Athens (1522-1589), whose birth name was Revoula Benizelou.

Derived from the Greek adjective φιλότιμος (philotimos) meaning "loving honour", which consists of the Greek noun φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" combined with the Greek verb τιμάω (timao) meaning "to honour, to esteem, to revere".
Latinized form of Philotimos. This name was borne by an eminent Greek physician from the 4th century BC.
In Roman legend, Philotis, also known as Tutula, was a slave whose plan resulted in an important victory of the Romans over the Latins in the late 4th century BC.

French diminutive of Philippe. In France, the name is strictly masculine and primarily used informally, i.e. it is not typically used on birth certificates.In the Netherlands, the name became popular in the 21st century, primarily as a feminine name (at least when used as an official name on birth certificates). This was probably a by-effect of the new but strong popularity of Phileine, plus some (indirect) influence from long-popular French feminine names like Milou.A known bearer of this name is the Dutch DJ Philou Louzolo (b. 1989). He was born in Zierikzee to a Congolese mother and a father who is half Nigerian and half Sierra Leonean.

From Ancient Greek φιλόξενος (philoxenos) meaning "loving strangers, hospitable", composed of φίλος (philos) meaning "friend, lover" and ξένος (xenos) meaning "foreign, strange" as well as "foreigner, guest".
Latinized form of Philoxenos. This name was borne by an Indo-Greek king from the 1st century BC.
Transferred use of the surname Philson.
Latinized form of Philoumena. In theatre, this is the name of a character from two different comic plays written by the Roman playwright Terence (2nd century AD), namely Andria and Hecyra.
Latinized form of Philoumenos. This name was borne by a Greek physician from the 4th century AD as well as by saint of the Orthodox Church.
Variant of Philyra.This name appears in Florence M. Kingsley's 1901 short story The Transfiguration of Miss Philura.

Means "lime tree, linden tree" in Greek. In Greek mythology Philyra was one of the 3,000 Oceanids, water nymph daughters of the Titans Oceanus and Tethys. She was loved by the Titan Cronus. 'When his wife Rhea came upon their rendezvous, he quickly transformed himself into a horse to escape detection. As a result, Philyra birthed a half-horse, half-man hybrid, the centaur Chiron. To ease her shame, Cronus transformed her into a lime-tree.'
Epic and Ionic Greek form of Philyra. In Greek mythology, Philyre or Philyra was an Oceanid nymph and mother of Chiron.

From Thai พิมพ์ (phim) meaning "print, type" and มาดา (mada) meaning "mother".
From Thai พิมพ์ (phim) meaning "type, print" and นารา (nara) which can mean "radius, length", "water" or "human, person".

From Thai พิมพ์ (phim) meaning "print, type" and พีร (phira) meaning "brave, warrior".

Means "to examine, to consider, to scrutinise" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit विनिश्चय (viniścaya).
Variant of Phineas. Also compare Finneas and Phinnaeus.

Derived from φίντατος (phintatos), the Doric form of Ancient Greek φίλτατος (philtatos) meaning "most beloved, precious", a superlative form of φίλος (philos) "friend, lover, beloved". This was the name of an ancient Greek vase painter.
From Thai พินทุ (phintu) meaning "drop, mark, circle" (of Sanskrit origin) and อร (on) meaning "maiden, damsel".

Possibly derived from a Doric variant of φίλτατος (philtatos) meaning "very dear, much loved, especially beloved", a superlative form of φίλος (philos) meaning "lover, friend". Phintys was allegedy a Pythagorean philosopher who lived around the 3rd century BCE, though the works attributed to her might have been a rhetorical exercise by later authors.

Taken from the name of the flower, whose name is derived from Greek phlox "flame". As a given name, it has been in occasional use in the English-speaking world from the late 19th century onwards.
