From Sino-Vietnamese 譜 (phổ) meaning "to compose or arrange a musical score" or 普 (phổ) meaning "universal, widespread, vast".

Means "frightener", ultimately derived from Ancient Greek φόβος (phobos) meaning "fear, terror, fright". In Greek mythology, Phobetor (called Ikelos "shaper" by other gods) was one of the Oneiros, gods and personifications of dreams and nightmares, varyingly called a son of Nyx, Hypnos, or Gaia.
Variant of Phúc via the Southern form Phước.
The earliest known use of the word "Phocian" is the Middle English period.
Latinized form of Phokides. A known bearer of this name was Phocides of Athens, the Olympic winner of either the stadion race or the wrestling contest in 364 BC.

Most likely derived from Greek φώκη (phoke), meaning "seal", referring to the animal. This name was borne by an Athenian politician who was also known as a subject of one of Plutarch's Parallel Lives.
Latinized form of the Greek name Φῶκος (Phokos), which is a variant form of Phokas (see Phocas). This name was borne by at least four characters in Greek mythology.
Latinized form of Phokylides. This was the name of a Greek gnomic poet from the 6th century BC.
Latinized form of Phoibidas. This was the name of a Spartan general from the 4th century BC.
Comedic male veriant of the name Phoebe from the popular American sitcom Friends.
Taken directly from the ancient Semitic thalassocratic civilization Phoenicia.

Latinized form of Greek Φοίνισσα (Phoinissa), the feminine form of Phoinix, as well as a proper noun meaning "Phoenicia" and a noun meaning "Phoenician woman". In Greek mythology Phoenissa was the daughter of Alphionis and thus can be considered a naiad. She bore to Zeus a beautiful son, Endymion.
Vietnamese form of Puxian, from Sino-Vietnamese 普賢 (phổ hiền). This is the Vietnamese name for the bodhisattva Samantabhadra.

Means "son of Phoibos" in Greek, derived from the name Phoibos combined with ίδας (idas), which is the Aeolic and Doric Greek form of the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This name was borne by a Spartan general from the 4th century BC. He is better known under the latinized form of his name, which is Phoebidas.
Means "son of Phokas" in Greek, derived from the name Phokas combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This name was borne by an Olympic victor from Athens (364 BC).
Means "son of Phokylos" in Greek, derived from the name Phokylos combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).

Meaning uncertain. The available possibilities for both the first and second element of this name indicate that the meaning of this name might be either "howling seal" or "forest of Phocis". And that is with the assumption that Phokylos is an authentic Greek given name, rather than a hellenization of a foreign name.In the case of the first possible meaning, the name is derived from the Greek noun φώκη (phoke) meaning "seal" (see Phocas) combined with the Greek verb ὑλάω (hylao) meaning "to bark, to bay, to howl".For the second possible meaning, the name would be derived from Φωκίς (Phokis) meaning "Phocis (region)" combined with the Greek noun ὕλη (hyle) meaning "forest, woodland".

Variant of Feuillen via Pholian, itself an older Gallicization of Foillan. This name is borne by Pholien Systermans, a Belgian swimmer who gained the Belgian 100m freestyle record in 2009.

Means "giving pasture or food, bounteous, nourishing", derived from Ancient Greek φέρβω (pherbo) meaning "to feed, nourish, pasture, graze" as well as "to enjoy, have". This was the name of many figures in Greek mythology.

Meaning uncertain. In Greek mythology, Phorkys was an old man ruling over the sea; later he was described as a god of the hidden dangers of the deep, a brother of Nereus, and was depicted as a kind of merman.

Derived from Ancient Greek φορμίον (phormion) meaning "small mat, small basket" as well as "straw covering", ultimately derived from φορμός (phormos) meaning "basket, wicker basket, mat", which itself is possibly related to φέρω (phero) meaning "to carry, to bear". This name was borne by an Athenian general and admiral from the 5th century BC.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek φέρω (phero) meaning "to carry, to bear" and ὦνος (onos) meaning "price". This was the name of a primordial king and culture-hero of ancient Argolis, a son of the river god Inachus credited with introducing the use of fire and laws to the Argolid.
From Thai พอ (pho) meaning "sufficient, adequate" and ฤทัย (ruethai) meaning "heart, mind".
Etymology unknown. This is the name of the Thai goddess of rice.

Means "bringing light, giving light" or "torch bearing" in Ancient Greek, derived from φῶς (phos) "light" and φέρω (phero) "to carry, to bear". In Greek mythology, this was the name of the personification of the morning star, sometimes called Eosphoros.

Derived from φωστῆρος (phosteros), which is the genitive singular of the Greek noun φωστήρ (phoster) meaning "that which gives light" as well as "splendour, radiance".This was the name of a Byzantine hermit saint from the 6th or 7th century AD.
Latinized form of Phosterios. This was the name of a Byzantine hermit saint from the 6th or 7th century AD.

Derived from Ancient Greek φωστήρ (phoster) meaning "that which gives light, illuminator" as well as "radiance, brilliance". In Greek mythology, this was the name of one of the Alcyonides (daughters of Alcyoneus) also called Phthonia or Chthonia. When Herakles slew their father, they cast themselves into the sea and were transformed by Amphitrite into kingfishers.
Means "phrases, words, speech" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वचन (vacana).

From the name of a teaching practiced in Buddhism as a devotional tool to achieve spiritual liberation, ultimately from Sanskrit बोध्यङ्ग (bodhyaṅga). It is also refers to the name of protective chants that monks recite to gravely ill people.
French form of Φωτεινός (Photeinos) and Φωτίνος (Photinos) via their latinized form Photinus.

Latinized form of Φωτεινός (Photeinos) and Photinos. This name was borne by a Christian heresiarch and bishop of Sirmium from the 4th century AD and by Photinus of Thessalonica, a 5th-century deacon of the Eastern Orthodox Church.
Derived from Ancient Greek φωτίζω (photizo) meaning "to shine, to give light", which is ultimately derived from φῶς (phos) meaning "light".Also compare the related names Photine and Photios.
Latinized form of Photios. Saint Photius the Great was a famous Patriarch of Constantinople.
Comes from the elementary particle that transmits light. From the Ancient Greek phos.

column12: From Thai ไพรวัน (phraiwan) meaning "forest, woods" or from ไพร (phrai) meaning "forest, jungle" and วัลย์ (wan) meaning "climbing plant, creeper, vine".

column3: พระแม่ธรณี(Thai)
column12: Thai chthonic earth goddess. Her name is derived from พระ (phra), an honorific title, แม่ (mae) meaning "mother" and the Pali word dhāraṇī meaning "ground, earth".

column3: พร่างเพ็ชร(Thai)
column12: Etymology uncertain, however the first name element may be from พร่าง (phrang) meaning "sparkling, glittering".
Hellenized form of Old Persian Fravartiš. Phraortes (c. 665-633 BC) was the son of Deioces, and the second king of the Median Empire.
From Greek φρίττω (phrittō) meaning "to tremble". This is the name of the divine spirit of horror in Greek mythology.
From Thai พร้อม (phrom) meaning "with, together" and พร (phon) meaning "blessing".

Derived from Ancient Greek noun φρόνις (phronis) meaning "prudence, wisdom", itself from φρονέω (phroneo) meaning "to think, to be minded", ultimately derived from φρήν (phren) "mind, heart, emotions". In Greek mythology, this was the name of a Triccan prince who journeyed to the Amazons with Heracles.
Latinized form of Phronios. This is the name of a character in Greek mythology.
Diminutive of Sophronia, the name of the youngest child in Margaret Sydney's "Five Little Peppers"

Derived from Ancient Greek φροντίς (phrontis) meaning "thought, care, attention", itself from φρονέω (phroneo) meaning "to think, to be minded", ultimately derived from φρήν (phren) "mind, heart, emotions". Phrontis is the name of several characters, both male and female, in Greek mythology. The inflection Φροντίς seems to be exclusively feminine, while Φρόντις could be either masculine or feminine.

Greek form of the Latin cognomen Fronto.Phronton was the name of a Greek author and rhetorician from the 2nd century AD, who (as it should be noted) is often confused with the 2nd-century Roman grammarian and rhetorician Marcus Cornelius Fronto (see Fronto).
Truncated form of Euphrosine. Mélidore et Phrosine (1794) is an opera by the French composer Étienne Méhul. It is considered an important example of early Romantic opera.
Means "Jupiter (planet)" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit बृहस्पति (bṛhaspati). It is also the formal Thai name for the weekday Thursday.
Means "tree, plant, flora" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit वृक्ष (vṛkṣa). This is also the Thai name for a deciduous tree native to the Indian subcontinent and Myanmar (species Albizia lebbeck).
Means "prosperity, wealth, abundance" in Thai, ultimately from Sanksrit वृद्धि (vṛddhi).

Ancient Greek nickname meaning "toad", literally "the brown animal". Phryne was a 4th-century BC hetaira or courtesan, famed for her beauty, whose stage name - like those of many hetairai - was based on a physical feature; she was called that either because of a dark complexion (*phrynos being cognate with brown) or because of a "snub nose" (phrynē "a kind of toad"). This stage name was borne by other hetairai also.It is also the name of the detective in Australian author Kerry Greenwood's Phryne Fisher mystery series, beginning in 1989.
Variant of Phryne used by Shakespeare in his play Timon of Athens (first performed between 1607 and 1608).
Derived from Ancient Greek φρῦνος (phrynos) meaning "toad" (compare Phryne).
Latinized form of Phrynichos. This name was borne by two Greek poets from the 5th century BC; one was a tragic poet, while the other was a comic poet.

Perhaps derived from the Greek place name Φθία (Phthia); compare Φθῖος (Phthios) meaning "a Phthian, inhabitant of Phthia". In Greek mythology, the city of Phthia in Thessaly was the home of Achilles. It could be related to Ancient Greek φθίω (phthio) meaning "to decay, to wane, to dwindle". This was the name of a 4th-century BC Greek queen, daughter of Menon of Pharsalus, the Thessalian hipparch, and wife of King Aeacides of Epirus with whom she had his successor, son Pyrrhus, and two daughters named Deidamia and Troias.
Simply from the English word meaning "wasting, consumption", ultimately from Greek φθίσις (phthisis). A Phthisis Smith was born in England in 1915.

From Greek φθόνος (phthonos) meaning "ill-will, malice, envy, jealousy, grudge". In Greek mythology, Phthonos (also called Zelos) was the daimon or spirit of envy and jealousy; he was particularly associated with the jealous passions of love.
From Sino-Vietnamese 輔 (phụ) meaning "to assist" or 㷆 (phụ) meaning "flourishing".
From Sino-Vietnamese 甫 (phủ) meaning "courtesy name", "great", or "to begin".
From Thai พวง (phuang) meaning "bunch, cluster, string" and พร (phon) meaning "blessing".
From Sino-Vietnamese 復 (phục) meaning "to restore, to recover".
From Sino-Vietnamese 芙蓉 (phù dung) meaning "cotton rose (Hibiscus mutabilis)" or "lotus (Nelumbo nucifera)", also used to refer to a beautiful woman.
From Thai ภู (phu) meaning "mountain" and ฟ้า (fa) meaning "sky, heaven".

Means "good reputation", from Sino-Vietnamese 芳 (phương) meaning "fragrant" and 名 (danh) meaning "name, fame".
From Sino-Vietnamese 芳 (phương) meaning "fragrant, flower" and 蓉 (dung) meaning "hibiscus" referring to a kind of orchid, Dendrobium devonianum.
From Sino-Vietnamese 鳳凰 (phượng hoàng) meaning "fenghuang, phoenix".
From Sino-Vietnamese 芳 (phương) meaning "fragrant" and 桂 (quế) meaning "cinnamon", referring to someone with filial piety.
From Sino-Vietnamese 芳 (phương) meaning "fragrant" and 草 (thảo) meaning "grass". This is a literary term that also refers to a person's beauty and virtue.
From Sino-Vietnamese 鳳尾 (phượng vĩ) meaning "phoenix tail", referring to the royal poinciana flower.
Alternate transcription of Thai ภูผา (see Phupha).
Derived from Biblical Hebrew פֹּארָה (pō'râ) "branch, foliage, bough". Phurah was a servant of Gideon in Judges 7. Gideon takes Phurah with him to spy on the Midianites before battle.
From Tibetan ཕུར་བ (phur-ba) referring to a ceremonial three-sided dagger used in Tibetan Buddhist rituals.
From Tibetan ཕུར་བུ (phur-bu) meaning "Jupiter (the planet)" or "Thursday".

Alternate transcription of Thai ภูริพัฒน์ (see Phuriphat).
From Thai ภูริ (phuri) meaning "wisdom, intellect" and พัฒน์ (phat) meaning "prosperity, progress, development".

column12: From Thai พุทธิ (phutthi) meaning "prosperity, abundance" and พงศ์/พงษ์ (phong) meaning "lineage, family".

Phuvah was a son of Issachar according to Genesis 46:13 and Numbers 26:23. He was one of the 70 souls to migrate to Egypt with Jacob.

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ภูวนาถ/ภูวนาท (see Phuwanat).

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ภูวนาถ/ภูวนาท (see Phuwanat).

column12: Means "king" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit भुव (bhuva) meaning "earth" and नाथ (nātha) meaning "master, lord".

Means "white" or "covered, broad, distinct" in Burmese.
Name of a fictional, possibly historical woman in Greek history.
Diminutive of Phylip, Philippa and other names that begin with Phil.

Means "guard, sentry, guardian" in Ancient Greek, a variant of φύλαξ (phylax). In Greek mythology, Phylacus was the eponymous founder of the ancient city Phylace in Thessaly. It was also the name of a Trojan soldier, and of a hero whose ghost frightened Gaulish troops at Delphi.
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek φυλάσσω (phylasso) meaning "to watch, guard, protect" as well as "to ambush, lie in wait" and "to maintain, preserve".
Variant of Felicia. Also compare Phylicia.
Possibly a feminine form of Phyleus. This was the name of one of the fifty daughters of Thespius in Greek mythology.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek φυλή (phyle) meaning "tribe, clan, race, people". However, compare Phyllis and also Greek φυλάσσω (phylassō) meaning "to keep watch, to guard". In Greek mythology, Phyleus was a son of King Augeas of Elis. He was exiled for supporting Heracles over Augeas in a dispute over payment, and was thus given the throne after Heracles killed his father and brothers.
Blend of Phyllis and Felicia. Famous bearer is Phylicia Rashad, actress.
Variant of Phyllis mainly used in Kenya and the United States.
Variant of Felicity influenced by Phyllis.

The name of one of the Nereids listed by the Latin author Hyginus, possibly derived from Ancient Greek φύλλον (phyllon) "leaf, foliage" combined with either δοχή (dokhé) "receptacle, container", from δέχομαι (dekhomai) "to accept, receive, welcome", or δοκή (doké) "vision, fancy; appearance", from δοκέω (dokeo) "to think, imagine, suppose".
From Greek φύλλον (phyllon) "leaf", perhaps intended to be a masculine form of Phyllis. This name was used by Dutch model Doutzen Kroes for her son born 2011.
Means "tamer of tribes", derived from Ancient Greek φυλή (phyle) meaning "tribe, clan" and δαμάζω (damazo) meaning "to tame, subdue". This was the name of a Trojan soldier in Greek mythology.
Feminine form of Phylodamas. Phylodameia was a daughter of King Danaus in Greek mythology, and mother of Pharis by the god Hermes.
Derived from Greek φυλή (phyle) meaning "tribe, clan" and μάχη (mache) meaning "battle".
Alternate transcription of Burmese ဖြိုး (see Phyo).

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek φύσκη (physke) meaning "intestine, sausage, blood pudding; blister, weal on the hand" or the related φύσκων (physkon) meaning "pot-belly, paunch". Physcoa was a heroine of Greek mythology, one of the original Sixteen Women chosen as an envoy between cities to organise the Heraean Games. She was the mother of Narcaeus by Dionysus.

The name of an obsuce Irish saint. According to legend, Piala and her brother Fingar were children of an Irish king. They were converted by Saint Patrick, driven into exile by their father, and landed first in Brittany, where they were well received, before moving on to Cornwall where they died at the hand of Tewdrick, king of Dumnonia. They were supposedly martyred at Hayle (Cornwall) c.455.
Altered form of Piamoun, which likely derives from the name of the Ancient Egyptian deity Amoun. This was the name of an Orthodox saint who lived in Egypt in the 4th century.
May derive from Ancient Egyptian element ankh, meaning "life, truth". Name borne by a Nubian queen who lived in the 6th century BCE.

column3: 比亜乃, 比亜音(Japanese Kanji)|ぴあ乃, etc.(Kanji/Hiragana)
column12: From Japanese 比 (pi) meaning "the Philippines", 亜 (a) meaning "sub-, second, Asia" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle. Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.Usage of this name is influenced by the English word piano.

Piast was a legendary Polish monarch, protoplast of the Piast dynasty. The name itself might have been an alternative of piastun, which meant "the one who takes care of the prince's house and family", derived from piastować - "to take care of"

Uncertain etymology, perhaps related to Ancient Greek πιέζω (piezo) meaning "to press, squeeze, oppress, distress", or to πίων (pion) meaning "fat, rich, wealthy, fertile". Piasus was a king of Thessaly or Anatolia in Greek mythology. He raped his daughter, Larissa, and she drowned him in a cask of wine in revenge.
From Latin piatus meaning "cleansed". Saint Piat or Piaton was a 3rd-century missionary and martyr.

From the name of a village in Idaho, which supposedly derives from a Native American word meaning "silver water". A known bearer is Picabo Street (1971-), an American Olympic skier who was born and raised in nearby Triumph, Idaho.
Transferred use of the surname Picasso, likely given after the Spanish painter Pablo Picasso.

Feminine form of Piccardo. Piccarda Donati was a 13th-century Florentine (Italian) noblewoman who appears as a character in Dante's Paradise. Another notable bearer was Piccarda Bueri (1368-1433), an Italian noblewoman whose son Cosimo de' Medici founded the Medici dynasty.
Medieval Italian name, probably meaning "from the French region of Picardy".
From the Italian word piccola, meaning "small, little".
From the name of the musical instrument, meaning "small" in Italian. This was the name of one of the characters in the anime franchise Dragon Ball made by Akira Toriyama.
Alternate transcription of Thai พิชัย (see Phichai).
Alternate transcription of Thai พิชฌามลณ์ (see Pitchamon).
Alternate transcription of Thai พิเชฐ (see Phichet).
Alternate transcription of Thai พิชิต (see Phichit).
Derived from the surname Pickering. This is the middle name of Bo Burnham.
Transferred use of the surname Pickney.
A character in the novel, "The Pilgrim's Progress" whose name is modeled on Puritanical nomenclature.

From Modern Greek πικρός (pikrós) "bitter" and χολή (cholí) "gall, bile". This is the name of a fictional character in the novel Pentalogy Gargantua and Pantagruel characterized as a 'stereotypical bad king'. François Rabelais gave him the name to allude to his dark and acerbic moods possibly.
From the Roman cognomen Pictor, which is derived from Latin pictor "painter." Quintus Fabius Pictor was a Roman historian from the 3rd century BC.

Derived from Latin picus, meaning "woodpecker". In Roman mythology, Picumnus was a minor god of fertility, agriculture, matrimony, infants and children, as well as a personification of the woodpecker. He was the brother of Pilumnus.

Picus was the founder of the first Latin tribe and settlement, Laurentum, located a few miles to the Southeast of the site of the later city of Rome. According to Festus he got his name as a consequence of the fact that he used to rely on a woodpecker for the purpose of divination.
From Uygur پىدا meaning "self-sacrifice", from Arabic فِدَاء (fidāʔ).
Variant transcription of Fidan, used by Azerbaijani population living in Georgia (country)
Diminutive of Peter. See also Peacock.
Means "she of Piten". This was a Hurrian epithet for the goddess Shalash, referring to her cult center in Piten (also written as Bitin).
From the word pidgeon. It has been used extensively as a nickname and also rarely as an official name.

Archaic form of pigeon, a bird, inherited from Middle English pygeoun, borrowed from Old French pyjon, inherited from Late Latin pīpiōnem “chirping bird”, derived from Latin pīpiāre “chirp”. Pidgeon Pagonis (1986- ) is an American intersex activist, writer, artist, and consultant.
Variation of Pidge. This was the nickname of American baseball player Pidgey Morgan (1853-1910).

Etymology uncertain. Possibly derives from the Semitic element pdr ("to scatter/spread"). Another possible origin is the element bqr ("lightning"). A Hurrian origin for her name has also been speculated, specifically from the element pedari ("bull"). Name borne by a Ugaritic goddess described as a daughter of Baal. It's theorised that she was a tutelary deity for the kingdom of Ugarit.
Alternate transcription of Thai พิษณุ (see Phitsanu).
French form of Pius and Pia.
This is either a medieval Polish vernacular form of Bella, being derived from piekna "beautiful", or a medieval Polish contraction of Petronela. This name is now obsolete in Poland.
Derived from Portuguese and Galician piedade "piety; pity, compassion".
Romansh form of Peter, traditionally found in the Surselva region.

Means "written stone" in Spanish, taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora de Piedraescrita meaning "Our Lady of the Written Stone". She is the patron saint of the municipality of Campanario, located in the Spanish province of Badajoz.According to folk legend, around the 15th century, a shepherd found a carved image of a female figure under a tombstone. When the shepherd found the figure in which he believed he saw the Virgin Mary, and after the supposed apparition or vision of the Virgin, he decided to take it to the town. The next day the figure disappeared from the town, appearing under the tombstone. The locals then decided to build a hermitage in the same place.

Means "white stones" in Spanish (the second word only used as a Latinism or in a poetic/literary sense, in place of blanca), taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de Piedras Albas and Nuestra Señora de Piedras Albas, meaning "The Virgin of White Stones" and "Our Lady of White Stones" respectively.She is the patroness of El Almendro in the Andalusian province of Huelva.
Singular (slightly more common) form of Piedrasantas.

Means "holy stones" in Spanish, taken from the titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen de Piedrasantas and Nuestra Señora de Piedrasantas, meaning "The Virgin of Holy Stones" and "Our Lady of Holy Stones" respectively.She is the patroness of Pedroche in the Andalusian province of Córdoba.
Possibly a combination of Pietro and Pedro.
The name of a child character in 1982 Franco-Hungarian animated science fiction film "Les Maîtres du Temps", directed by René Laloux.
Transferred use of the surname Pieper.

in the case of of actress Pier Angeli, born Anna Maria Pierangeli, it was a stage name based on her surname. The name peaked in popularity in 1957, during the middle of Angeli's career, when it was given to 35 baby girls.
Cremish Lombard feminine form of Piéro.
Full first name of Pierce Hawthorne, a character played by Chevy Chase on the sitcom Community (2009-15). Possibly a combination of Pierce and Reginald.
A variant of Piers, a Middle English form of Peter. Peter is derived from the Greek petros, meaning "stone" or "rock".
Combination of the names Piero or Pier and Giuseppe. This was the name of Italian medievalist Piergiuseppe Scardigli (1933-2008).
This was the name of one of the multiple wives of King Danaus of Libya.
Combination of Pietro and Massimiliano. A famous bearer of this name is the Italian rugby union player Piermassimiliano Dotto (1970-2012).
Transferred use of the surname Pierpont.
A feminine form of Pierre formed in countries where French is NOT spoken.
Local diminutive of Pierre found in the Bourgogne-Franche-Comté region up until the late 1600s.
The name of a genus of flowering plants, and when used as a name probably a feminine form of Pierre or Piero. This makes it a variant of Pierina, Perrine and Pierrette.
Transferred use of the surname Pierson.

Probably derived from Ancient Greek πιαρός (piaros) meaning "fat thick; (of soil) fertile, rich, fruitful". In Greek mythology, this was the name of the king of Emathia and eponym of the region of Piera, famed for having nine daughters named after the nine muses. This was also the name of a lover of the muse Clio and father of Hyacinth in some accounts.
Traditionally given to the first born child - the name literally means "erupting from an anthill", from pie "erupt from a place", and sie meaning "anthill".
A variant of Beata and a diminutive of Pietari.
Means "piety, compassion; duty" in Latin. This name belonged to the goddess of duty and personification of piety in Roman mythology.
Variant form of Pietertje. This form is not as common as Pietertje in The Netherlands.

When borne by a female person, this name is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Pieter) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix tje to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix.

Diminutive of Piet, as it contains the Afrikaans diminutive suffix -ie.This name is occasionally also used on women. An example of a female bearer is the South African field hockey player Pietie Coetzee (b. 1978).

When borne by a female person, this name is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Piet) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix -je to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix. Also compare Peetje.In Dutch children's literature, this is the name of the eponymous (male) character of the book series Pietje Bell written by the Dutch author Chris van Abkoude (1880-1960). Three films based on the books have since been released; in respectively 1964, 2002 and 2003.
Maltese and Sicilian form of Peter.
Derived from the Lithuanian noun pieva meaning "meadow, grassland".
This name is belongs to two notable characters.It is the nickname of "Piggy" in William Goulding's novel Lord of the flies.It is also the name of Miss Piggy, from Jim Henson's Muppets.

Derived from Greek πηγή (pêgê) "a spring, fountain; fount, source", possibly taken from the Greek title of the Virgin Mary, Ζωοδόχος Πηγή (Zôodochos Pêgê), meaning "life-giving spring" (or πηγή ζωής (pêgê zôês) "fountain of life" or "source of life"). In some cases it may be a short form of Chrysopigi.
Possibly from pig. This was the name of Pigma Dengar, a character in Star Fox who betrayed James McCloud and Peppy Hare in Venom and then battled the Star Fox team as a member of Team Star Wolf.
Feminine form of Pigmenius. In the Spanish-speaking world (especially in Mexico), this name is also encountered as a short form or variant of Epigmenia.
Italian and Spanish form of Pigmenius. In the Spanish-speaking world (especially in Mexico), this name is also encountered as a short form or variant of Epigmenio.

This name is best known for being the name of the 4th-century saint Pigmenius of Rome, who was martyred during the reign of the Roman emperor Julian the Apostate (died in 363 AD). Some sources suggest that he may possibly be the same person as saint Epigmenius of Rome (early 4th century AD).The meaning and origin of his name is unknown. It might perhaps be of Greek origin, in which case it probably consists of the Greek noun πυγμή (pygme) meaning "fist" combined with the Greek noun μένος (menos) meaning "power, strength, spirit", thus giving the name the meaning of "powerful fist". Alternatively, the name ultimately comes from a hellenization of a foreign name, just like e.g. Pygmalion (variantly transcribed as Pigmalion).And last but not least: since the saint is sometimes referred to as Pigmentius, it is also possible that his name is of Latin origin, in which case it is derived from the Latin noun pigmentum meaning "colour, pigment, paint".
The meaning of this name is still unknown to me at this time. This name was borne by a Coptic saint from the 5th century AD.
Means "blowhole, gills" in Maori. Also Maori form of Fisher.
Possibly derived from Nahuatl pihui "to increase, multiply" and yollotl "heart, life".
Possibly derived from the Estonian word "piibeleht" meaning "lily of the valley".
From Japanese 姫 (pi) meaning "princess" combined with 苺 (chi) meaning "strawberry". Other kanji combinations are possible.Usage of this name is, most likely, influenced by the word peach.
Hawaiian unisex name meaning "the life ascends".

Means "rising sky" or "to ascend to heaven," from piʻi meaning "climb, ascend, advance, mount, rise" and lani meaning "sky, heaven, heavenly, spiritual, royal, exalted, noble, aristocratic."One (male) bearer of this name is Piʻilani (ca. 1577-?) who ruled as the 15th Mōʻī of Maui.
Diminutive of Pirkko and other names beginning Pi-.Famous bearer is Pirkko "Piitu" Uski (b. 1967), a Finnish actress.
Derived from the definite masculine article ⲡⲓ- (pi-) combined with ϫⲓⲙⲓ (čimi) "finding, thing found".
West Frisian form of Pieter and Pietertje (also Pieterke), which started out as a hypocorism (via baby talk).
Means "fast, ascend" in Maori and "peach" in Hawaiian.
Vow to it. Promise. Name of a Zimbabwean journalist Pikirayi Deketeke.
Pikiru is the deity of the night in Inca Mythology. His name has an unknown meaning.
From Japanese 飛 (pi) meaning "to fly" combined with 鼓 (ko) meaning "drum". Other combinations of kanji characters can also form this name.

a Slavic surname and the feminine form of the Russian name Pikov. It translates literally to "of spades" (referring to the spade suit in a deck of cards). In Eastern European culture, it is famously associated with Alexander Pushkin's 1834 classic novella The Queen of Spades (Russian: Pikovaya Dama).

Georgian form of Fikriyya. Also compare the Georgian noun ფიქრი (pikri) meaning "thought", which is also of Arabic origin.A known bearer of this name is the Georgian politician Pikria Chikhradze (b. 1966).

English form of the Roman cognomen Pilatus, which meant "armed with a javelin" from Latin pila "javelin". This was most famously borne by Pontius Pilate, the prefect of the Roman province of Judaea ca. AD 26-36 who allegedly tried, judged, and sentenced Jesus during his term of office. It came into use as an English name in the 18th century.
Of uncertain Hebrew etymology. In the Bible, Pildash was the sixth son of Nahor and Milcah (Genesis 22:22).
Italian and Spanish form of Pylaeus.
Taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Maria Santissima del Pilerio whose name is derived from the Calabrian dialect word pileri (pilastro in Standard Italian) "pillar" (compare Spanish Pilar).
Possibly from Calabrian pilíeri, meaning "pillar", referring to Our Lady of the Pillar, one of the titles given to Mary, or from Ancient Greek πυλωρός ("gatekeeper, guardian").

Medieval German form of both Biligrim and Peregrinus (see Peregrine), as these names were conflated with each other in the Middle Ages. Also compare the Old High German word piligrim meaning "pilgrim".In the Anglophone world, Pilgrim is found as a given name from the 16th century onwards. It was first used by the Puritans, in reference to someone undertaking a religious pilgrimage. Later on, however, the use of the name for religious reasons ceased. Instead, people began to use it in reference to the surname Pilgrim.

Either from the surname Pilot, which is derived from Pilate, or directly from the vocabulary word pilot, which is derived from either Greek πηδον (pedon) "steering oar" or πλωτης (plotes) "sailor". This name is borne by Pilot Inspektor Lee (2003-), son of American actor Jason Lee.

Means "young prince" in Nahuatl, from Nahuatl piltzintli, a diminutive form of pilli "child, youth" and teuctli "lord". In Aztec mythology, Piltzintecuhtli was a god of the rising sun, healing, and visions, associated with Tonatiuh.

Meaning, "staker." The god who grants the pestle necessary for making flour from grain. He ensured children grew properly and stayed healthy. Ancient Romans made an extra bed after the birth of a child in order to ensure the help of Pilumnus. He also taught humanity how to grind grain. He was also sometimes identified as the husband of Danaë, and therefore the father of Danaus and the ancestor of Turnus.
From Greenlandic pilu "leaf", and -nnguaq, a diminutive or endearing suffix.

Compound Hebrew name meaning "serpent's mouth"; from Hebrew words peh פֶּה "mouth" and nakhash נָחָשׁ "serpent" with the Hebrew feminine grammatical ending of the letter Hay ה. Hebrew consonant shin שׁ (sometimes pronounced sin) changed to the consonant samek ס to clarify name pronunciation.

Anglicized form of Pindaros. This was the name of a Greek lyric poet from Thebes (died around 438 AD).

Meaning uncertain. This name might possibly be derived from Πίνδος (Pindos), which is the ancient Greek name for Mount Pindus in northern Greece.Pindaros was the name of a Greek lyric poet from Thebes (died around 438 AD). In the Anglosphere, he is best known under the name Pindar.
Latinized form of Pindaros. This name was borne by a Greek tyrant of Ephesus from the 6th century BC.

This was the name of several Egyptian people including an Ancient Egyptian High Priest of Amun at Thebes in Ancient Egypt from 1070 to 1032 BC and the de facto ruler of the country's south from 1054 BC.

Meaning unknown. Bret Harte, author of the short story The Outcasts of Poker Flat (1869) used this name for the fifteen-year old runaway lover Piney Woods. However, presumably it is applied for the fact that Piney had been left alone, pining and yearning for her lover.

This was the name of the most important goddess in Elamite religion. It is uncertain what the meaning of her name was in the Elamite language. Pinikir started out as the mother-goddess (in which capacity she was also the goddess of love and fertility), making her rank above all Elamite gods - even the male ones. This indicates a reverence of that what is feminine, which is reflective of both Elamite religion and Elamite society: women were held in high regard and Elamite royal families' system of succession was always through the female line (although a ruler was always male and was called "the son of a sister"). The goddess Pinikir was mostly worshipped in Susa, the capital city of Elam, where there was a temple dedicated to her. She was married to the god Humban, and over time, her husband became the most important god in the Elamite religion, making her become second to him. The explanations as to why that happened differ: for example, some sources state that it was because she got married in the first place, others state that it was because Humban divorced her and remarried with the goddess Kiririsha. However, it should be noted that some sources state that Kiririsha may have been an epithet of Pinikir (thus making Pinikir and Kiririsha one and the same person), while other sources view them as separate goddesses whose cults eventually merged (by about 1800 BC). This Pinikir vs. Kiririsha matter is a bit of a murky area, in part caused by the fact that little is known about the Elamite religion as well as the fact that the Elamite language is not yet fully understood by modern linguists.

A known bearer was Pinito del Oro (1931-2017), born María Cristina del Pino Segura Gómez, a Spanish circus performer and novelist from the Canary Islands.
A nickname from the color pink, or a diminutive of names such as Patrick or Patricia.
The full name of the 'My little pony' character Pinkie Pie.

Derived from Dutch pink meaning "pinkie" (as in, the little finger) combined with Lotje. Also compare the Dutch verb pinkelen meaning "to shine" as well as "to twinkle, to sparkle, to flicker".In Dutch literature, this is the name of the wife of Pinkeltje Witbaard (his surname translates to Whitebeard in English), a white-bearded gnome who is the main character of the popular children's book series Pinkeltje written by Dick Laan (1894-1973).

Derived from Dutch pink meaning "pinkie" (as in, the little finger) combined with the Dutch suffix -el and the Dutch diminutive suffix -tje. Also compare the Dutch verb pinkelen meaning "to shine" as well as "to twinkle, to sparkle, to flicker".In Dutch literature, this is the name of Pinkeltje Witbaard (his surname translates to Whitebeard in English), the main character of the popular children's book series Pinkeltje written by Dick Laan (1894-1973). He is a white-bearded gnome who was named so because he is the size of a human's pinky finger. As such, he is known as Fingerling in the anglophone world.
Possibly a variant of Pinkie or Pinky. A known bearer is Pinki Virani (1959-), an Indian writer and social activist.
Diminutive of Pink. Borne by a character of My Little Pony: Friendship is Magic.

Variant of Pink. Sometimes used for someone with a pink complexion.

Means "pine tree" in Spanish. It is taken from the title of the Virgin Mary Nuestra Señora del Pino, meaning "Our Lady of the Pine". This is an epithet of the Virgin Mary in her role as the patroness of the island of Gran Canaria, Spain.
From the Shipibo pino meaning "hummingbird" and the genitive suffix -n.

column12: From Chinese 品 (pǐn) meaning "article, product; to sample, to savour" combined with 青 (qīng) meaning "blue, green, young", 清 (qīng) meaning "clear, pure, clean" or 庆 (qìng) meaning "congratulate, celebrate, celebration". Other hanzi combinations are possible.

Variant of Shoshoni name Pina Quanah meaning "sweet-swelling", from pihnaa "sugar, honey, sweet" and -kwana(h) "to smell (of)". This was the original name of 19th-century Shoshone leader Chief Washakie.
Diminutive of Pina ultimately a short form of Giuseppa, Giuseppina or Filippa.

Diminutive of Pino, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.In addition to that, this name is also used as a short form of Crispinuccio and other pet forms that end in -pinuccio.Known bearers of this name include the Italian actor Pinuccio Ardia (1914-1994) and the Italian sculptor Giuseppe "Pinuccio" Sciola (1942-2016).

The name Pinus is associated with the Pompilius family, suggesting that this individual was a member of the gens Pomponia, an old Roman family, which relates to the Roman king Numa Pompilius (second king of Rome).
From the Chinese 频 (pín) meaning "frequently, again and again" and 怡 (yí) meaning "happy, joyful, harmony, joy".

The earliest known bearer of this name is the Egyptian saint Pitirim of Porphyry (4th century AD), who is primarily venerated in the Eastern Orthodox Church. The meaning and origin of his name are uncertain. It is not even clear whether Pitirim is the original form of his name; it may well be a later form that arose in medieval Russia, for the name has been most prevalent there.Should that indeed happen to be the case, then it must be said that the form of the name is actually rather peculiar. You see, Russian names that originate from saints primarily come from Greek sources, as is typical of Eastern Orthodox Christianity. The standard Greek form of the name is Pityroun, which would normally have been rendered into Russian as Питирун (Pitirun), as the language usually remains quite faithful to the original Greek form of names. Not in this case, however.Perhaps Pitirim is actually based on a different Greek form of the name, namely the variant Πιτυροῦμ (Pityroum). Another possibility is Πιτηροῦμ (Piteroum), since this name becomes Pitiroum in (early) modern Greek. But even with these variants, the Russian adaptation is not as faithful as it should have been: -ροῦμ (-roum) should have become -рум (-rum) instead of -рим (-rim), which is visually and phonetically quite different. However, it is worth noting that this type of deviation is not unique to these names: comparable examples include the noun Рим (Rim) meaning "Rome" and the adjective римский (rimskiy) meaning "Roman".Another Greek variant of the name is Πιτυρίων (Pityrion). Some sources also mention Pithyrion, which must be an alternate transcription of the aforementioned name, since the corresponding Greek spelling Πιθυρίων does not appear to have been recorded in historical sources. With that said, Pityrion is too different to have been the basis for Pitirim; it would almost certainly have become Питирион (Pitirion) in Russian, as Greek -ίων (-ion) has always been preserved in Russian as -ион (-ion). There have been no exceptions to this rule, at least to my knowledge.Instead, Pityrion is notable for a different reason: it is very reminiscent of the obscure Greek name Πιτύρων (Pityron), which is most likely derived from Greek πίτυρον (pityron) meaning "husks of corn, bran". In turn, the word is ultimately derived from Greek πίτυρα (pityra) meaning "bran". Due to this close resemblance, some people have come to associate Pityrion (and by extension Pitirim) with that origin and meaning. However, the name is not necessarily of Greek origin: it can easily be a hellenization of a Coptic name, since saint Pitirim was born and raised in Egypt. The previously mentioned Greek forms of Piteroum, Pityroum and Pityroun certainly do point in that direction, as no plausible Greek etymology exists for them.However, even a Coptic origin is not necessarily guaranteed, as Egyptian society was not homogeneous at the time. As a result, it is possible that Pitirim (and by extension its hellenizations) is actually of Nubian or even Semitic origin. For example, compare the ancient Hebrew word פיתרונ (pytrwn) or פיתרוו (pitaron) meaning "interpretation (of dreams)".All in all, it is very difficult to determine the linguistic origin of this name - at least at this point in time. Perhaps in the future it will be possible to do so, especially once it becomes clear how the saint's name is written in the Coptic language. After all, he should also be venerated in the Coptic Orthodox Church, which means that the Copts must have their own name for him.Lastly, notable Russian bearers of this name include the Russian-American sociologist Pitirim Sorokin (1889-1968) and Pitirim of Krutitskiy († 1673), the 9th Patriarch of Moscow and All Russia.
