Form of Platon with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.
Russian feminine form of Platon. This is the name of a character in Ivan Turgenev's novella: 'Klara Milich' (1883).
Plator (? –169 BC) the Illyrian was brother to King Gentius, the last Illyrian king of the Ardiaean State.
Transferred use of the surname Platt.
Late Latin and Italian feminine diminutive of Plautus.
Roman nomen that derives from Plautus. Among others, this name belonged to Aulus Plautius, a politician and general and the husband of Pomponia Graecina.

Roman cognomen possibly meaning either "flat-footed" or "flat-eared" in Latin.Ancient Roman bearers include the playwright Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC); and the politician Gaius Rubellius Plautus (33–62 AD), who was executed by Emperor Nero due to their political rivalry.

From Serbian плав (plav) meaning "blue" but it is used to denote a "blonde haired" person such as in this case. This is because the word had an ancient meaning of "shining, bright" from which the sense of "blonde haired" comes from and later it came about to mean "blue".
In the case of American singer Plavka Coleridge (née Lonich) the name was derived from a Croatian worn meaning "blondie". It is not used as a name in Croatia.
Unknown meaning. This is the name of American football player Plaxico Burress, who was named after his uncle.

Derived from the English word, which is derived from Anglo-Norman plaisant "delightful" and ultimately from Latin placens "pleasing; agreeable".As a given name, Pleasant has been in occasional use in the English-speaking world from the 16th century onwards. It was generally used as a masculine name among the English Romani community.
From the English word pleasrue meaning "A state of being pleased or contented; gratification." This name is most common in African countries like Nigeria, Zimbabwe and Uganda.
Variant as well as the French form of Plectrud. Plectrude lived in the 8th century AD and was the wife of Pepin of Herstal.
Derived from the Old English elements pleġa "playing, game" and beorht "bright".
Derived from the Old English elements pleġa "playing, game" and here "army".
Derived from the Old English elements pleġa "playing, game" and mund "protection". This was the name of a 9th and 10th Century Anglo-Saxon Archbishop of Canterbury.
Derived from the Old English elements pleġa "playing, game" and ræd "advice, counsel, wisdom".
From the Greek word Πλειάδες "pleiades", which were the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione and companions to Artemis.

Name of a star cluster, likely meaning "to sail", from the ancient Greek 'plein'. Also used in Greek mythology, the Pleiades were the seven daughters of Pleione and Atlas, thus meaning "daughters of Pleione".
Derived from the Greek adjective πλεῖστος (pleistos) meaning "most, greatest, largest" combined with Greek ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man".

The first element of this name is derived from Greek πλεῖστος (pleistos) "most, greatest, largest". The second element is either derived from Greek ἀρχός (archos) "master" or from Greek ἀρχή (arche) "origin, source".

Variant form of Plistarchus, which is the main latinized form of Pleistarchos, as Greek names containing -ei- are usually latinized to -i- (some examples of this are the names Dinocrates, Euclides, Pisistratus and Pithagoras).This name was borne by a king of Sparta (Greece) from the 5th century BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek πλεῖστος (pleistos) "most, greatest, largest" combined with σθένος (sthenos) "vigour, strength." In Greek mythology, this is the name of several different people descended from Tantalus.
Derived from Greek πλεῖστος (pleistos) meaning "most, greatest, largest" and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord, king".This name was borne by a king of Sparta from the 5th century BC.
Derived from Latin plena "full, plump, satisfying"

Name invented by Gavriil Romanovich Derzhavin (1743 - 1816), one of the most highly esteemed Russian poet. It is derived from Russian verb пленить (plenit') meaning "to captivate", "to charm". He called by this name his first wife in poetic works. Her real name was Yekaterina Yakovlevna Bastidon, and she was known for her beauty.
Simply from the English word plenty.
Variant of Plasch, traditionally found in the Upper Engadine region.
Borne by Palestinian journalist Plestia Alaqad (2001-), whose father named her after one of the first tribes that lived in Palestine.

In Limburgish, Pleunie is a diminutive form of Pleun (a pet form of Apollonia) and is thus strictly used on females. It is different in Dutch, however, where Pleunie used on a female is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Pleun) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix ie to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix.

Medieval short form of Apollonius, which is still in use today (albeit rarely). In more recent times, the name has also been used as a short form of Apollonia for women, but very rarely so, especially when compared to the more traditional feminine forms Pleunie and Pleuntje.
Dutch diminutive of Apollonia. Also compare the related name Pleuntje.

When borne by a female person, this name is a good example of how one can turn a very masculine name (Pleun) into a feminine name by simply adding the diminutive suffix je to the original name. But when borne by a male person, this name is simply a pet form because of the diminutive suffix.

Means "striking horses, driving horses" in Ancient Greek, derived from πλήσσω (plesso) meaning "to strike, smite" and ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse". This was the name of several princes in Greek mythology, including two of the fifty sons of King Aegyptus, both killed by their wife, Amphicomone and Pyrantis respectively, on their wedding night.

Of debated origin and meaning. Some scholars try to link this name to Breton bleiz "she-wolf", while others see a connection with Breton plezh "plat; braid"; the second part of the name is a diminutive suffix.Either way, from the early 1600s onwards, when every given name "had to" be linked with a Catholic saint, Plezou was used as a feminine quasi-equivalent of Saint Blaise.
From late Middle English from French, from plier ‘to bend’.
Contraction of Paulien, Paulina and Pauline.A notable bearer of this name is the Dutch actress and comedian Plien van Bennekom (b. 1971).
Catalan and Occitan form of Pliny.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Pliny.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Plinius (see Pliny).
Abbreviation of партия Ленина и народная трудовая армия (partiya Lenina i narodnaya trudovaya armiya) "party of Lenin and the people's working army (i.e. Communist Party and proletariat).

Anglicized form of Pleistarchos via its latinized form Plistarchus. Also compare the similar-looking name Plutarch.This name was borne by a king of Sparta (5th century BC) and by a nephew of king Cassander of Macedon (4th century BC).
Italian and Spanish form of Pleistarchus.
Alternate transcription of Thai พลอย (see Phloi).
Dutch diminutive of Apollonia. Also see the related name Pleunie.
Dutch diminutive of Apollonia via its short form Plonia.
Short form of Apollonia (feminine) and Apollonius (masculine). Also see the related name Pleun.This name is rare for both genders, but it is more often seen on women than on men.
Dutch diminutive of Apollonia. Also see the related name Pleunke.
Dutch diminutive of Apollonia. Also see the related name Pleuntje.
This was the name of a Greek philosopher and the inventor of Neoplatonism.

Used in the eastern region of Macedonia, Greece. It comes from the ancient Greek word πλουμίον (ploumíon) or the Latin word pluma, which means "painted or embroidered decorative design, flower, ornament". It is used on women and means "ploumous, decorated, the woman who is beautiful as if she wore jewelleries, the woman whose beauty compares to an ornament".
From Greek πλούσιος (plousios) meaning "rich, wealthy, noble", a derivative of πλοῦτος (ploutos) "wealth".
Derived from Ancient Greek πλοῦτος (ploutos) meaning "wealth, riches". In Greek mythology, Plouto was the name of an Oceanid and of the mother of Tantalus.
Alternate transcription of Thai พลอย (see Phloi).
From Thai พลอย (phloi) meaning "gem; precious stone" and ชมพู (chomphu) meaning "rose apple".
From พลอย (phloi) meaning "gem, precious stone" and นิศา (nisa) meaning "night".

From Middle English ploume, from Old English plume "plum, plum tree," from an early Germanic borrowing (Middle Dutch prume, Dutch pruim, Old High German pfluma, pfruma, German Pflaume) from Vulgar Latin *pruna, from Latin prunum "plum," from Greek prounon, a later form of proumnon, a word of unknown origin, which is probably, like the tree itself, of Anatolian origin.
From the name of the flowering plant that is also known as frangipani.
Transferred use of the surname Plummer.

Means "the flower of women", deriving from the Anglo-Norman element flur ("flower, blossom"), and the Irish element na mban ("of the women"). Name borne by the daughter of Oisín and Niamh in the Fenian Cycle of Irish mythology.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Plutarch.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Plutarch.

Probably an invented name, used primarily in the Southern United States in the 19th century. Plutina Cox is the heroine of Waldron Baily's novel 'The Heart of the Blue Ridge' (1915), set in Wilkes County, North Carolina.
Either derived directly from the place name (see Plymouth) or transferred from the surname which is derived from the place name.
Possibly from the Armenian փունջ (punj) meaning "bunch".
Diminutive of names beginning with P like Philip, etc.

Named for the human settlement in Muskiz, Greater Bilbao, Biscay, Northern coastal Spain. Primarily Basque/Spanish. Pobeña. localidad de España. The word translated to English means "Poor" as in destitute.
Contraction of поколение борцов и строителей коммунизма (pokoleniye bortsov i stroiteley kommunizma) "generation of fighters and builders of communism".

The name of a Shoshone chief which is the namesake of the city of Pocatello, Idaho. The meaning of the name has been long disputed: it was proposed to mean "he does not follow the road" from Shoshoni po "road," ka "not," and tello "to follow", but it was ultimately proven to not be Shoshoni at all, and the chief referred to himself as Tondzaosha, meaning "buffalo robe".

Derived from Spanish poco "little" and yo "I (nominative form of the first person singular pronoun)". Pocoyo, a 4-year-old boy, is the title character of a computer animated children's television show that debuted in 2005.
A character from The Borrowers, a book by Mary Norton, from the ordinary vocabulary word pod.

An epithet of the harpy Aello derived from Ancient Greek ποδάρκης (podarkes) meaning "succouring with the feet, running to the rescue; swift-footed", composed of πούς (pous) (genitive ποδός) meaning "foot" and ἀρκέω (arkeo) meaning "to defend, assist, succour" as well as "to be enough, suffice" (compare Arke 1). Podarce was also the name of one of the fifty daughters of King Danaus, killing her husband, Oeneus, on their wedding night.

Derived from Ancient Greek ποδάρκης (podarkes) meaning "succouring with the feet, running to the rescue; swift-footed", composed of πούς (pous) (genitive ποδός) meaning "foot" and ἀρκέω (arkeo) meaning "to defend, assist, succour" as well as "to be enough, suffice".

Means "swift-footed, foot-speedy", sometimes interpreted as "white-footed", derived from Ancient Greek πούς (pous) (genitive ποδός) meaning "foot" and ἀργός (argos) meaning "shining, white, bright" and figuratively "swift". Podarge was a harpy in Greek mythology, possibly another name for Aello.

Podo is a character from Andrew Peterson's Wingfeather Saga, the grandfather of the main characters. His name may be related to the Scandinavian place-name PODO. He hides dark secrets, but loves his family to the end.
Podrick Payne, frequently called Pod, is the squire of Tyrion Lannister (from the "Song of Ice and Fire" series of books by George R. R. Martin).

Transferred use of the surname Poe.-------------------------------------Poe Dameron is a fictional character from the movie Star Wars. Poe Dameron is played by actor Oscar Isaac and is named partially after JJ Abrams assistant Morgan Dameron. Abrams did it so Morgan whould be happy that he named a character partially after her. Abrams got Poe from his daughters Polar bear who was named Poe (short for "polar bear").
Meaning unknown. The surname (and later given name) Paxton derives from this name.
Older spelling of Puji influenced by Dutch orthography.
Old English name of unknown meaning. It relates to the name Peyton.
Means "pearl of love"; a combination of Tahitian poe "pearl" and here "love".
Means "brilliant pearl"; a combination of poe "pearl" and iva, a diminutive of iva iva meaning "brilliant".
From French poème or Latin poema, from Greek poēma, early variant of poiēma ‘fiction, poem,’ from poiein ‘create.’ See also Poema.

Latinized form of the Greek given name Ποίμανδρος (Poimandros), which is derived from Ancient Greek ποιμήν (poimen) meaning "herdsman, shepherd" (see Poimen) combined with ἀνδρός (andros) meaning "of a man". As such, one could say that the name basically means "shepherd of men".This name is not to be confused with Ποιμάνδρης (Poimandres), which is a name used as the title for the first chapter of the medieval literary work Corpus Hermeticum. That name is most likely a hellenization of the Egyptian theophoric name P-eime n-Re meaning "intelligence of Re" or "knowledge of Re", since it cannot be a genuine Greek given name because it doesn't follow the grammatical rules that all genuine Greek names do.In Greek mythology, Poemander was the founder of the city of Tanagra.
Polynesian origin name, meaning "pearl of the garden".

Latinized form of Poimen. This name was borne by Poemen the Great, a saint from Egypt who lived in the 4th century AD. However, since the saint originated from Egypt, one should take into account the possibility that his name is the hellenized form of a Coptic name or word.

Latinized form of Ποιμενία (Poimenia), which is the feminine form of Poimenios and perhaps also Poimen. Their latinized forms are Poemenius and Poemen respectively.This name was most notably borne by a wealthy but pious 4th-century Roman noblewoman, who financed the construction of a church named Imbomon (now called Chapel of the Ascension) on the Mount of Olives in Jerusalem.

Latinized form of Poimenios. This name was borne by a 4th-century Roman governor of Corycus in Asia Minor (now Turkey) and by a usurper who led a revolt at Augusta Treverorum (now Trier in Germany) in the same century.In Greek mythology, Poemenius was one of the fourteen satyrs that led the satyr troops of Dionysos in his war against the Indians.

column3: ぽえむ(Japanese Hiragana)|詩, 詩夢, 保笑夢, 保絵夢, 星影夢, 歩恵夢, 歩笑, 帆絵夢, 穂笑, 母恵夢, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 詩 (poemu, poe) meaning "poetry, poem", 保 (po) meaning "protect, guarantee, keep, preserve, sustain, support", 星 (po) meaning "star", 歩 (po) meaning "walk", 帆 (po) meaning "sail", 穂 (po) meaning "grain" or 母 (po) meaning "mother", 笑 (e) meaning "laugh", 絵 (e) meaning "picture, drawing, painting, sketch", 影 (e) meaning "shadow, silhouette, phantom" or 恵 (e) meaning "favor, blessing, grace, kindness" combined with 夢 (mu) meaning "dream" or 笑 (emu) meaning "laugh". Other kanji or kanji combinations can form this name as well.Usage of this name is, most likely, influenced by the word poem.
From poe "pearl" and ori "dance, move", a synonym of poeupa meaning "dancing pearl" in Tahitian.
Means "heavenly pearl" or "divine pearl"; a combination of Tahitian poe meaning "pearl" and rani, which is derived from Tuamotuan rangi meaning "heaven".
Means "black pearl"; a combination of Tahitian poe meaning "pearl" and rava meaning "black".
Older spelling of Purnomo influenced by Dutch orthography.
Older spelling of Purwoko influenced by Dutch orthography.
Originally a variant of Posy, this name was sometimes associated with poetry, from Old French poesie, ultimately from Greek poesis "composition, poetry," from poein "to make or compose"
As an East Frisian name, Poet is a short form of names containing the element boto "messenger", for example Boeterich.This name was in use as a strictly masculine name during the 1700s and 1800s.
Name of a minor character in C.S. Lewis', 'The Last Battle'.
Transferred use of the surname Pognon.
Transferred use of the surname Pogue. In the 2006 horror film 'The Covenant', Taylor Kitsch portrays one of the main protagonists, Pogue Perry.
Hokkien and Teochew romanization of Bao.
Probably derived from Greek ποιέω (poieo) meaning "to make, create, compose; to pretend". This was the name of one of the Argonauts, considered the greatest archer of the group.

Possibly means "God is here", derived from Hebrew פה (po) meaning "here" combined with אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God". This is the name of an angel belonging to the order of the Principalities. He is one of the 72 angels bearing the explicit name of God (the Shem HaMephorash), as interpreted by some Christian Kabbalists.
Genitive form of Pól, usually found in the medieval compound name Maél Póil meaning "devotee of Paul (the apostle)".
Derived from Ancient Greek ποιμήν (poimen) meaning "herdsman, shepherd".

Derived from Ancient Greek ποιμένιος (poimenios) meaning "pastoral, of the shepherd" as well as "rural, simple", itself from ποιμήν (poimen) meaning "herdsman, shepherd" (see Poimen). In Greek mythology, Poimenios was a leader of the satyrs in Dionysos’s campaign against India.

This was the name of a character in the made-for-TV cartoon version of 'Felix the Cat', introduced to the show in 1959. From an English surname which was originally a nickname from Old French poing destre meaning "right fist"; the surname is particularly associated with Huguenot refugees who fled from France to England, and from there to the U.S. state of Virginia.
From the flower Euphorbia pulcherrima, which was named for an American Minister to Mexico, Joel Roberts Poinsett, who discovered the flower in 1828.
Character in the Ainu epic Kotan Utunnai. In the story, he discovers that he is of Ainu heritage and reunites with his people.
Of unknown meaning.It is used by the Mossi in Burkina Faso.
Shorter form (or variant form) of Opokosław.
Variant of På and, to a lesser extent, short form of Lèyopôl.
Short form of Apòla and Apòloniô.
Derived from the Kurdish polat meaning "steel".
From the surname Pollard, from the name Pòl or polle meaning "head"; or from the English word polar meaning "end of an axis" relating to the North and South Pole.

Derived from Latin stella polaris, meaning "pole star". This is the proper Latin name of the brightest star in the constellation Ursa Minor, commonly called the North Star or Pole Star. It is borne by a character (real name Lorna Dane) in Marvel's X-Men line of comics, created in 1968.
Derived from po'lat meaning "steel" or "invincable" and gul meaning "rose, flower".
From Uzbek po‘lat meaning "steel" combined with Persian جان (jān) meaning "soul, life".
Alternate transcription of Thai พลวัฒน์ (see Phonlawat).

Polish short form of Leopold.Poldek Pfefferberg, a holocaust survivor, inspired the Australian writer Thomas Keneally to write the novel Schindler's Ark, which in turn was the basis for Steven Spielberg's film Schindler's List.
Diminutive of Leopolda, used as a given name in its own right.
Derived from Ancient Greek πολέμαρχος (polemarchos) meaning "polemarch, warlord, chieftain", composed of πόλεμος (polemos) meaning "war, battle" and ἀρχός (archos) meaning "leader, ruler".
Latinized form of Polemarchos. This name was borne by an Athenian philosopher from the 5th century BC.
Derived from Greek πόλεμος (polemos) meaning "warlike, hostile".
From Polish pole "field" and mir "peace" roughly translating to "fields of peace, peaceful fields".
Derived from Greek πόλεμος (polemos) meaning "war, battle" and the possessive suffix -ων (-on).
Tagalog diminutive of Paula, Paulina and other similar names.
Contraction of помни Ленина, Сталина (pomni Lenina, Stalina) "remember Lenin and Stalin".
Hungarian borrowing of Paulette, reflecting the French pronunciation.

The name of a sorceress in the Belgeriad series of books by David and Leigh Eddings.Her name consists of Gara, the name of the village where her father was born, preceded by Pol, the element which the god Aldur prefixes to the original names of his female apprentices.
The name of Hawaiian snow goddess and enemy of Pele. Her name is derived from poli meaning "bosom" and 'ahu meaning "garment, clothed".
Galician, Italian and Spanish form of Polybius.
Romanian and Provençal form of Polycarp.
Spanish feminine form of Polycarp. This was borne by Colombian revolutionary Policarpa Salavarrieta (1795-1817), known as "La Pola".
French form of Pulcinella, a character from the Italian commedia dell'arte. This can also refer to the little clown dolls that run out from under Mother Ginger's skirt in The Nutcracker.
Bosnian and Croatian form of Pollux.
Polish and Hungarian form of Polydorus.
Spanish, Italian and Portuguese form of Polydorus.
Romanian form of Polyeuktos via the Latinization Polyeuctus.
Italian Portuguese and Spanish form of Polyeuctus (see Polyeuktos).
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Polyphemus.
Originally a diminutive of Apollónia, Paula and Polixéna, occasionally used as a given name in its own right.
Polish, Serbo-Croatian, Slovene and Lithuanian form of Polyxena.

The first element of this name is derived from Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "many, much". The second element is derived from either Italian nesso meaning "connection, link, nexus" or from Greek νῆσος (nesos) meaning "island". In case the latter applies, then it must be said that this name is neither derived from nor inspired by Polynesia, the group of islands in the Pacific Ocean. This is because the name Polinesso comes from Ludovico Ariosto's epic poem Orlando furioso from 1516, while the name Polynesia was first used for the group of islands in 1756.Polinesso also appears in George Frideric Handel's opera seria Ariodante (1735), which was based on canto V of Ariosto's epic poem.
Louisiana French truncated form of Hypolite and Walloon truncated form of Hipolite.
Derived from the Greek noun πολίτης (polites) meaning "citizen, freeman".In Greek mythology, prince Polites of Troy was one of the many children of king Priam of Troy.
Anglicized form of Politianus.In literature, this is the name of the eponymous character of the unfinished play Politian (1835) written by Edgar Allan Poe (1809-1849).
Hellenized form of Politianus. This name was borne by a Greek Patriarch of Alexandria from the 9th century AD.
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Greek personal name Polites.
Italian form of Polyeuctus (see Polyeuktos). Masculine form of Poliuta.
Italian form of Politianus. A notable bearer of this name was the Italian classical scholar and poet Poliziano (1454-1494).
Transferred use of the surname Polk.
Alternate transcription of Thai พลวัฒน์ (see Phonlawat).
A blend of Polly and Colleen.

Probably derived from the historical territory Polesia including the cities Brest (Poland) and Pinsk (Belarus).This unique name was borne as a second given name by Ferdinand Pollexius Heinrich von Leinigen-Westerburg-Neuleiningen (* 13. January 1720; † 3. February 1789)

This name is one of the two Italian forms of Thumbelina (the other is Mignolina). It is derived from Italian pollice meaning "thumb" combined with the Italian feminine diminutive suffix -ina. Also compare the similar-looking name Polissena.
Name borne by Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (80–70 BC–after c. 15 BC) a Roman architect and engineer during the 1st century BC, known for his multi-volume work entitled 'De architectura'.

Italian form of Pollio. This name was used by Vincenzo Bellini and Felice Romani for the main masculine character in the opera 'Norma' (1831), based on Alexandre Soumet's play 'Norma, ou L'infanticide'.
This name likely roots from Paolo or Paulo, and Polo is a variant of both. It can be used in association with the sport also, but very rarely is.
Derived from the Slavic element pulku "people, host, army". Is noticed in birch bark letter num.155 from Veliky Novgorod.
Medieval Lithuanian variant of Pelagija, recorded in the 15th century.
Spanish truncated form of Apolonia and Venetian form of Apollonia.
Means "rise, appearance (of the moon)" in Batak.

The name of a supernatural creature in Eastern European mythology, known in English as "Lady Midday" or the "Noon Witch". Her name is probably derived from the proto-Slavic *polъ meaning "half" and dьnь meaning "day", therefore "midday", and the related terms in the various Slavic languages. Alternatively, her name may share an etymological root with the Serbo-Croatian poludjeti meaning "to go crazy".
Means "midnight", used in Russian fairy tale “Zorka, Vechorka, and Polunochka” by Aleksandr Afanasyev.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Pollux.

Uzbek form of Palvan, which is a medieval Persian contraction of the Persian name Pahlavan (see Pahlavon).In Uzbek, polvon is also a word that can mean "strong, heroic, brave" (adjective) and "strong man, wrestler" (noun). It is derived from the same root as the aforementioned Persian name Pahlavan, so ultimately, there is no etymological difference between the two.

The first element of this name is derived from either the name Polvon or the Uzbek word polvon meaning "strong, heroic, brave" as well as "strong man, wrestler". Both are ultimately derived from the same root, namely the Persian noun پهلوان (pahlavan) meaning "hero, paladin, champion". The second element of this name consists of the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".

Latinized form of Polyainos. A notable bearer of this name was the Greek mathematician Polyaenus of Lampsacus (3rd century BC), who was a friend of the famous Greek philosopher Epicurus. Polyaenus was also the name of a Macedonian author and rhetorician from the 2nd century AD.

Derived from the Greek adjective πολύαινος (polyainos) meaning "much-praised". It consists of the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek noun αἴνη (aine) meaning "praise, fame" (see Aeneas).
Derived from Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "much, many" and ἄναξ (anax) meaning "master, lord, king".In Greek mythology, Polyanax is the name of a king of Melos.
Derived from Ancient Greek πολύανδρος (polyandros) meaning "with many men, full of men" as well as "populous", composed of πολύς (polys) "much, many" and ἀνδρός (andros) "of a man".

Derived from the Greek noun πολυάνωρ (polyanor) meaning "with many men", which consists of the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek noun ἀνήρ (aner) meaning "man".Also compare the Greek name Polyandros, which is closely related and essentially means the same.

Saint Polyanus was a 3rd century African Bishop and companion of Saint Nemesianus. They were seized in the persecution under Valerian, scourged and otherwise tortured, finally condemned to servitude in the mines (A.D. 260).
Means "many lives", derived from Greek πολυς (polys) "much" combined with Greek βιος (bios) "life."
Latinized form of Polybios. This name was borne by a Greek historian from the 2nd century BC.
Means "having many oxen, worth much cattle; the rich one", derived from Ancient Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "many, much" and βοῦς (bous) meaning "ox, cow".

Derived from Ancient Greek πολυκαής (polykaes) meaning "much-burning", composed of πολύς (polys) "many, much" and καίω (kaio) "to kindle, set on fire, burn". In Greek mythology, Polycaon was the husband of Messene, who convinced him to conquer the territory of Messenia and name it after her.

Derived from Ancient Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "much, many" and κέκασμαι (kekasmai) meaning "to surpass, excel, shine" (pluperfect κέκαστο (kekasto)). This name belonged to several characters in Greek mythology, including the youngest daughter of Nestor in Homer's Odyssey.

Derived from the Greek adjective πολυχαρής (polychares) meaning "feeling much joy" as well as "graceful". It consists of the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with either the Greek noun χαρά (chara) meaning "joy, delight, happiness" or the Greek noun χάρις (charis) meaning "grace, kindness" (see Chares).Known bearers of this name include a tyrant of Athens (5th century BC) and the Olympic victor Polychares of Messenia (8th century BC).

Derived from the Greek noun πολυχρονία (polychronia) meaning "length of time". However, one could also regard this name as the feminine form of Polychronios.This was the name of the mother of Saint George, who lived in the 3rd century AD. She was a saint herself, or at least she appears to be viewed as such in the Greek Orthodox Church.
Latinized form of Polychronios. This name was borne by several bishops and saints from the Byzantine Empire.
Latinized form of Polykles. This name was borne by several ancient Greeks, of which at least two were Olympic victors.
Latinized form of Greek Πολυκράτεια (Polykrateia), a feminine form of Polykrates.

Derived from Ancient Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "many, much" and δαμάζω (damazo) meaning "to tame, subdue". Polydamas was a lieutenant of Troy in the Trojan War, often recommending a more cautious battle strategy.
Latinized form of Polydektes. In Greek mythology, Polydectes was the king of the island of Seriphos.
Doric Greek form of Polydektes. This was the name of a Spartan king from the 9th century BC, but he is usually known as Polydectes, which is the latinized form of the aforementioned Polydektes.

Derived from the Greek noun πολυδέκτης (polydektes) meaning "all-receiver". It consists of the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek noun δέκτης (dektes) meaning "receiver, beggar".
Dutch form of Polydoros via its latinized form Polydorus. A known bearer of this name was Polydoor Lippens (1810-1889), a Belgian engineer and inventor.

English and French form of Polydoros via its latinized form Polydorus.Known bearers of this name include the Italian humanist scholar and historian Polydore Vergil (c. 1470-1555), the English saint Polydore Plasden (1563-1591), the Belgian-English businessman and politician Polydore de Keyser (1832-1898) and the Belgian rower and Olympic medalist Polydore Veirman (1881-1951).

Derived from Greek πολύευκτος (polyeuktos) meaning "much desired, much wished for", which was composed of Greek πολυς (polys) "much" and εὐκτός (euktos) "desired, wished for, prayed for". This was the name of a 3rd-century martyr from Melitene. It was also borne by a 10th-century patriarch of Constantinople.
Means "well-known, renowned" in Ancient Greek, composed of πολύς (polys) "much, many" and γνωτός (gnotos) "known" (older and more correct form of γνωστός (gnostos)).

Latinized form of Greek Πολύγνωτος (Polygnotos) meaning "well-known, renowned", composed of πολύς (polys) "much, many" and γνωτός (gnotos) "known" (older and more correct form of γνωστός (gnostos)). This name was borne by an ancient Greek vase painter of the mid-5th century BC.

From the Greek adjective πολύκλειτος (polykleitos) meaning "far-famed, of great renown", itself from πολύς (polys) "much, many" and κλειτός (kleitos) "famous, renowned, splendid". A notable bearer was Polykleitos of Argos, a 5th-century BC Greek sculptor.
Derived from the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek noun κλέος (kleos) meaning "glory".

From Ancient Greek πολυμάθεια (polymatheia), πολυμαθία (polymathia) meaning "much learning, erudition", from πολύς (polys) "much" and μαθ- (math-), the root of the verb μανθάνω (manthano) "to learn, know, seek". In Greek mythology, Polymatheia was one of the three Muses recognized at Sicyon, as remarked by Plutarch. He compares her to Polymnia, to whom he ascribes precedence over accumulation and preservation of knowledge.
Derived from πολύς (polús) “much” and μηδομαι (medomai) "to think, to plan".
Derived from Ancient Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "many, much" and μέδων (medon) meaning "ruler". This was the name of a son of King Priam in Greek mythology.

Latinized form of Greek Πολυνείκης (Polyneikês) meaning "quarrelsome, much-wrangling", derived from πολύς (polys) "much, many" and νεῖκος (neikos) "quarrel, strife, fight". In Greek mythology, Polynices was the son of Oedipus and Jocasta, brother of Eteocles, and husband of Argea. When it was revealed that Oedipus killed his father and married his mother and was subsequently expelled from Thebes, Polynices and Eteocles were left to rule together. However, they were cursed by Oedipus and as such the brothers did not rule together peacefully and ended up killing each other in battle for control of Thebes.

Derived from the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek verb πείθω (peitho) meaning "to persuade, to convince" as well as "to obey, to yield to" and "to believe, to trust (in)".This name was borne by an Olympic victor from 484 BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "much, many" and σπέρχω (sperkho) meaning "to set in rapid motion, rush, hurry". This was the name of a Macedonian Greek general who served both Philip II and Alexander the Great and then played an active role in the ensuing battles for control between Alexander's generals.

This is the name of an Oceanid in Greek mythology, the mother of the goddess Hippeia Athena ("Athena of horses") by Poseidon. The name is theorised to derived from Ancient Greek πολύφρων (polyphron) "thoughtful, ingenious, inventive", comparing it to the name of Athena’s usual mother in mythology, Metis ("wisdom, cunning"). However, there is no evidence to back up this theory.

Means "much-thinking, ingenious, inventive" in Ancient Greek, derived from πολύς (polys) meaning "many, much" and φρήν (phren) meaning "mind, intellect, heart, emotions".This name was borne by Polyphron of Pherae, an ancient Greek tyrant from the 4th century BC.
Means "one who makes much", derived from Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "much, many" and ποιέω (poieo) meaning "to make, create, compose; to pretend".
Derived from Ancient Greek πολύς (polys) meaning "much, many" combined with στρατός (stratos) meaning "army".
Latinized form of Polystratos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 3rd century BC.

Derived from the Greek adjective πολύτιμος (polytimos) meaning "much-revered", which consists of the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek verb τιμάω (timao) meaning "to honour, to esteem, to revere".
Modern Greek feminine form of Polybios.

Aeolic and Doric Greek form of Polyxenides, because it contains ίδας (idas), which is the Aeolic and Doric Greek form of the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).This was the name of a Rhodian general and admiral from the 3rd century BC.
Means "son of Polyxenos" in Greek, derived from the name Polyxenos combined with the patronymic suffix ἴδης (ides).
Masculine form of Polyxene (see Polyxena). A notable bearer of this name was the Indo-Greek king Polyxenos Epiphanes Soter, who reigned around 100 BC.
Latinized form of Polyxenos. In Greek mythology, this was the name of one of the suitors of Helen of Troy.

Etymology uncertain, derived from πολύς (polys) meaning "many, much" and perhaps an unknown second element. Possibly a shortened form of Polyxena. This was the name of many figures in Greek mythology, including an Oceanid, a Naiad of the river Nile who married King Aegyptus, one of the Hyades nymphs, a Lemnian seer, and a Maenad.

Doric Greek form of Polyzelos, because it contains ζᾶλος (zalos), which is the Doric Greek form of ζῆλος (zelos) meaning "emulation, zealous imitation" as well as "jealousy" (see Zelos). Also compare the Greek noun ζάλη (zale) meaning "squall, storm, driving rain".This name was borne by a tyrant of Gela in Sicily (5th century BC). He is better known under the latinized form of his name, which is Polyzalus.
Latinized form of Polyzalos. This was the name of a tyrant of Gela in Sicily, who lived in the 5th century BC.

Derived from the Greek adjective πολύζηλος (polyzelos) meaning "full of emulation, much admired". It consists of the Greek adjective πολύς (polys) meaning "many" as well as "much" combined with the Greek noun ζῆλος (zelos) meaning "emulation, zealous imitation" as well as "jealousy" (see Zelos).
Latinized form of Polyzelos. Known bearers of this name include an eponymous archon of Athens (4th century BC) and a Greek comic playwright (flourished around 400 BC).
Contraction of помни ленинские заветы (pomni leninskiye zavety) "remember Lenin's testaments".
Variant transcription of Bom and Beom.A famous bearer is Pom Klementieff (1986-), a half-Korean French actress.

This name is best known for being the name of the sister of Saint Memmius (3rd century AD). She was a virgin and monial in Châlons-sur-Marne, a city that is nowadays located in France and known under the name Châlons-en-Champagne. She was once venerated as a saint herself, but is no longer recognised as one by the Catholic Church. Her feastday used to be on June 27th.Like her brother Memmius, Poma was a Roman citizen, meaning that she was born and raised in the Roman Empire. At some point (possibly around the same time as her brother), she was sent to Gaul (most of which is nowadays known as France), in order to convert the Gauls to Christianity. Little else is known about her life. Given her Roman descent, her name is most likely derived from Latin pomus or pomum, both of which are nouns that can mean "fruit" as well as "fruit tree". Also compare Pomona.
From the word meaning "good fortune, blessing, profit, prosperity."
Derived from poma i ka lani meaning "apple of the sky" or from pō mai ka lani meaning "darkness from heaven; nightfall" in Hawaiian.
Ortographically correct form of Pomare in Tahitian.

Variant form of Pomelline. This name is best known for being one of the middle names of Charlotte Casiraghi (b. 1986), who is the daughter of Princess Caroline of Hanover (formerly of Monaco). She was given this middle name in honour of her ancestor Pomellina Fregoso (c. 1387-1468), a Genovese noblewoman who was the wife of Jean I of Monaco (c. 1382-1454). Her name had been gallicized to Pomelline in Monaco, as it was (and still is) predominantly a French-speaking country.

Diminutive of either Poma or Pomona, which are both given names that are ultimately derived from Latin pomus or pomum, both of which are nouns that can mean "fruit" as well as "fruit tree".In some cases, the name Pomellina can also be a direct derivation of the word pomella, which means "apple" in some Italian dialects. In other Italian dialects, the same word means "grapefruit", as a variation on pomello, which is the usual word for the fruit. And finally, in the Venetian language (which is often mistakenly believed to be an Italian dialect), the word pomella means "red berry (of thorny bushes)".As you can see, all etymological explanations for the name ultimately refer to some type of fruit. As such, we can conclude that the aforementioned Latin pomus and/or pomum are ultimately at the very root of each of the explanations, because Italian (as do its dialects) and Venetian are ultimately descended from the Latin language.The name Pomellina was mainly used in the Republic of Genoa during the Late Middle Ages. A known bearer of this name was Pomellina Fregoso (c. 1387-1468), a Genovese noblewoman who was the wife of Jean I of Monaco (c. 1382-1454), who himself was ultimately of Genovese descent as well. Her name was gallicized to Pomelline in Monaco, as it was (and still is) predominantly a French-speaking country.
Transferred use of the surname Pomeroy.

Meaning unknown. This name was borne by the 17th-century Georgian noblewoman and poetess Pominisa Beridze, who was from the village of Dzimiti in the Georgian region of Guria. She is also known under the name ვომინიჯა (Vominija), because that is how she is mentioned in the documents of the Italian missionary Teramo Castelli (1597-1659), who lived in Georgia from 1632 to 1654.

Modern form of Pomelline via its variant form Pomeline. The spelling of this form of the name was influenced by the French word pomme meaning "apple", which the name (and its variant form) has always shared a certain resemblance with and thus often led people to associate it with apples (to some degree).
Derived from Old Czech word pomníti meaning "memorable". It is the Czech name for the flower forget-me-not.
Derived from Church Slavic pomineti or pominiti meaning "to think" (which corresponds with Russian помнить (pomnit) meaning "to think") combined with the Slavic element slava meaning "glory".

This was what explorer, Captain William Clark, of Lewis and Clark fame, nicknamed the son of Sacagawea. The child's real name was Jean Baptiste Charbonneau. Many sources say that Pomp was a Shoshone name given to him by Sacagawea, meaning anything from 'first born', 'first son', 'leader', 'unborn', and 'little son', yet none of the Shoshone words for those meanings match anything like Pomp. It's likely the name was given by Clark and not Sacagawea and that it is not a Shoshone name. The origin of the nickname, whether it's derived from the English word "pomp", or is a diminutive of a name containing the element -pomp-, is unknown.Pompeys Pillar on the Yellowstone River in Montana and the community of Charbonneau, Oregon are named after him.
French masculine and feminine form of Pompeius (see Pompey). This was the name of a female Breton saint, also known as Aspasie, Pompaïa or, in Breton, Coupaïa/Koupaïa.
Croatian and Serbian form of Pompey.
The name of an asteroid, named after the Roman town of Pompeii, which was destroyed due to a volcanic eruption.
Catalan and Portuguese form of Pompey.
Derived from the Late Latin adjective pomposus meaning "stately, dignified, pompous". Saint Pomposa was a 9th-century martyr, a nun who was beheaded by Moors in Córdoba, Spain.
The first element of this name is related to the Polish verb pomścić "to avenge, to wreak". The second element is derived from Slavic bor "battle" or borit "to fight".
Means "watch out for this one" in Ponca. This is the Ponca name of Native American artist Paladine H. Roye.
Alternate transcription of Thai พรชัย (see Phonchai).
The name of a character (a dog) in Disney's 101 Dalmatians.

From Thai ปอง (pong) meaning "desire, intend" and พล (phon) meaning "force, strength, power".

Derived from Ancient Greek πόνος (ponos) meaning "labor, work, toil, exercise; pain, suffering (as a result of labor)". In Greek mythology, Ponos was the personification of toil and a son of Eris, the goddess of strife.
Leader of a band of Native American fugitives in California who called themselves Los Insurgentes and who rebelled against Mexican rule and the mission system in California.

Pontiac or Obwaandi'eyaag was an Odawa war chief known for his role in the war named for him, from 1763 to 1766 leading Native Americans in an armed struggle against the British in the Great Lakes region due to, among other reasons, dissatisfaction with British policies.Pontiac was also the name of a car manufacturer, in his name.

Son of Pontos, from the Greek suffix -idas, meaning "son of". Alternatively, this name could be in reference to the Italian commune of Pontida. While most commonly used as a surname, there have been instances in which it has been used as a first name.
Alternate transcription of Thai พรทิพย์ (see Porntip).

The word "pony" comes from the Old French word "poulenet", meaning a young horse. It evolved into English by the 16th century, referring to small horses or certain breeds. Over time, it became a popular term for pets, nicknames, and pop culture references.
Means "one who loves bamboo" in Nepal.

The names come from the Japanese onomatopoeic word ぽにょ-ぽにょ (ponyo-ponyo), which refers to something squishy and soft. In the animated movie by Hayao Miyazaki, the titular character Ponyo is a goldfish who becomes human.

Poojya is a girl name which has the meaning of very pure, respectful, sacred. It is also one of the names of goddess Saraswati.

Popiel is a legendary ruler of the 9th century who is said to have ruled over the Polans or Goplanes. However, there is no historical evidence of his existence to date.At the beginning of the 12th century, an anonymous author, Gallus Anonymus, wrote numerous legends about the events of Popiel's reign. He is said to have been the last representative of the Popielid dynasty, which preceded the Piast dynasty.
Feminine form of Popillius. Popillia was one of the Vestal Virgins.
Late Greek form of Publius. In other words, you could say that this name is a late Greek variant of Poublios.

Short form of Popocatepetl, which means "smoking mountain" in Nahuatl from popoca "it smokes" and tepetl "mountain". This is the name of a hero in Mexican legend and Aztec mythology, the lover of Princess Ixtli. His wife-to-be died of grief when she mistakenly believed he had been killed in war, and Popo returned to her and carried her up to a hill, where they became the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Ixtaccihuatl (the latter of which resembles a woman sleeping on her back).

Name of a shape-shifting shetani (evil spirit) in Zanzibar mythology. It is derived from Swahili elements popo (bat) and bawa (wing), therefore literally meaning "bat-wing" or "winged bat". The spirit may manifestate itself by physical and/or sexual assault, which typically includes anal sodomising. Incubus-like visits of Popobawa would then repeat every night unless the victim confessed the assault to anyone else.
Means "to smoke, to emit smoke" in Nahuatl.

column12: Means "smoking mountain" in Nahuatl, derived from popoca "it smokes" and tepetl "mountain". This is the name of an active volcano in Mexico, named after a warrior from Aztec mythology said to be kneeling beside the body of his lover, Iztaccihuatl, a twin volcano to the north.
Variant of Popoca. Alternately, could mean "smoking water", derived from Nahuatl popoca "to smoke" and atl "water".
Feminine form of Poppaeus. Poppaea Sabina was the second wife of Nero.

Means "provision, resource, contrivance" in Ancient Greek, more literally "means of passage, opening, way" as well as "bridge, ford, ferry" and "journey". In Greek mythology, Poros was the personification of resourcefulness and expediency.

Means "energetic sky, red dawn" in Māori from porou "eager" and rangi "sky". Porourangi is the ancestor of the Ngāti Porou tribe. The character Porourangi, played by actor Cliff Curtis, is the father of Paikea in Witi Ihimaera's "Whale Rider".

The name of a main character in J. K. Rowling's series 'Fantastic Beasts and Where to Find Them.'Derived from porpentine, an archaic form of the word porcupine used by Shakespeare in his play 'Hamlet.'

Feminine form of Porphyrios (see Porfirio). The name was given to the female character in Robert Browning's dramatic monologue "Porphyria's lover", where she is strangled over her 'lover's' obsession with her.

Derived from Greek πορφυρα (porphyra) meaning "purple dye" as well as "purple-fish". Also compare the Greek noun πορφυρίς (porphyris) meaning "purple garment, purple cloak" and the Greek given name Porphyrios (see Porfirio). In Greek mythology, Porphyrion was one of the Gigantes (Giants).
Anglicized form of Porphyrios (see Porfirio). This name was borne by a Neoplatonic philosopher from the 3rd century AD.
Meaning uncertain; it might possibly be a variant of Porpire.
Meaning unknown. This was another name for the goddess Prorsa. It is also the name for Gamma Virginis, a binary star system in the constellation of Virgo.
Variant of Porsche, the spelling probably influenced by that of Portia.

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek πέρθω (pertho) meaning "to destroy". In Greek mythology, Porthaon (also written Parthaon or Portheus) was the name of several characters, including a Caledonian king and son of either Agenor or Ares.
This was the name of one of the 3 Musketeers, from the well-known novel by Alexandre Dumas.

Roman cognomen which was derived from Portius. Also note that there are instances where this name is a misspelling of Porcianus. The name Portianus was borne by an obscure (Catholic) saint from the 6th century AD.
French form of Portianus. This name was borne by Portien Colombel de Bois-Aulard (1730-1805), a French politician.
Derived from Latin portus "port, harbour". Also note that there are instances where this name is a variant of Porcius.

Meaning, "land surrounding the water" and used in reference to the place of Portland, Oregon which itself is named after Portland, Maine, which is thusly named after the Isle of Portland, England. This name was borne by comedienne, actress, and dancer, Portland Hoffa.
Derived from Latin porta, meaning "gate, door" or portus, meaning "harbor". This was the name of a Roman god of keys, doors, livestock and ports. Its Greek counterpart was Palaemon.
Transferred use of the surname Portwood.
Greenlandic name meaning 'a bag (made of seal skin) for blubber'.
Means "horse of Poseidon", derived from the name of the Greek sea god Poseidon combined with the Greek noun ἵππος (hippos) meaning "horse".
Means "gift of Poseidon" from the name of the god Poseidon combined with Greek δῶρον (doron) meaning "gift".
Bosnian, Croatian and Polish form of Poseidon.
A variant of the nicknames for Josephine, Posy and Posie. Alternately, a transferred use of the surname Posey.
From the English word posh, assigned as a nickname 'Posh Spice' to the Spice Girl Victoria Beckham by the magazine 'Top of the Pops'.
Derived from poshsha, an endearing term for a girl or woman, and gul meaning "rose, flower".
Derived from poshsha, an endearing term for a girl or woman, and oy meaning "moon".
Elaboration of Posie probably inspired by Rodica or Florica.
Latinized form of Poseidippos. This name was borne by two Greek poets from the 3rd century BC, namely Posidippus of Pella and Posidippus of Cassandreia.
Feminine form of Posidonius. Posidonia is also a genus of marine plants found in the seas of the Mediterranean and around the south coast of Australia.
From Toba Batak pos meaning "fixed, firm, happy, trusting" and the suffix -ma indicating emphasis.
Extremely rare variant of Posy/Posie or transferred use of surname Possi
Rare variant of Posy or a transferred use of a rare surname, Possy.

Feminization of Posthumus. (Cf. Postuma.) This was used as a second or third name to indicate the child's father had died before her birth, e.g. Gulielma Maria Posthuma Springett (1644-1694), the wife of William Penn, founder of Pennsylvania.

Used as a second or third name to indicate the child of a deceased parent. ex. Thomas Posthumus son of Thomas. This has also been seen on its own, unlike the feminine variation. ex. Posthumus, son of Thomas.
Georgian form of Phosterios via its modern Greek transcription Fostirios.

From the Russian word "постник" (postnik), which means "one who fasts" or "faster." Postnik Yakovlev the architect was a Russian architect in the 16th century traditionally credited with designing the Saint Basil's Cathedral in Moscow.

Postumia was a priestess of the virginal earth deity Vesta, goddess of the hearthfire. Livy briefly mentions that in 420 BCE she was accused of the crime of incestum and went on trial for the loss of her virginity.
Of unknown origin. This name was borne by a man named Rufius Caecina Postumianus.

Derived from Latin post meaning "backwards, behind; after" and the verb vertere "to turn (oneself), to turn about, to direct one's way". Postverta or Postvorta was a Roman goddess presiding over childbirth who was prayed to when a baby was being birthed feet first (instead of head first, as is normal), originally a surname of Carmenta. See also Prorsa.
Used as a nom de guerre by Cambodian communist dictator Pol Pot (1925-1998; born Saloth Sâr), in which case it is derived from French politique potentielle, meaning "potential politics".
Altered form of Tapiomis, possibly influenced by Greek ποταμός (potamos) meaning "river, stream".

Latinized form of Potamon. Bearers of this name include the rhetorician Potamo of Mytilene (died around 15 AD) and the philosopher Potamo of Alexandria (lived in either the 1st century BC or the 2nd century AD).
Derived from Ancient Greek ποταμός (potamos) meaning "river, stream". Potamon was a son of King Aegyptus in Greek mythology, and was killed by his wife, Glaucippe, on their wedding night.
Possibly a Romani form of Potamon.
Ukrainian and Russian folk form of Patapios.
Means "night door; enduring night" in Māori. Pōtatau Te Wherowhero (d. 1860) was a Māori chief of the Waikato tribes, who reigned as the Māori King from 1858 until his death.

Variant of Potentia.According to "'Ancient Magnificence': St Andrews in the Middle Ages", this name belonged to one of the three consecrated virgins, along with Saint Triduana, who accompanied Saint Regulus to Scotland with the bones of Saint Andrew.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Potentiana. This was the name of a Spanish saint from the late 16th century.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Potentianus. A notable bearer of this name was the Filipino musician Potenciano Gregorio (1880-1939).
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin adjective potens meaning "able, strong, powerful, potent".
English form of Potentianus. This name was borne by a 4th-century saint from Roman Gaul.
Feminine form of Potentianus. This is the name by which saint Pudentiana (2nd century AD) is sometimes known.

Extended form of Potentius. This name is not to be confused with the similar-looking name Pontianus.This name was most notably borne by a 4th-century saint from Roman Gaul, who is better known under the name Potentian.
French and German form of Potentinus.

Roman cognomen which was derived from Potens and/or Potentius.This is the name of an obscure 4th-century saint from Aquitaine, who was martyred together with his sons Felicius (also recorded as Felix) and Simplicius in what is now Karden in Germany.

Either derived from the Latin noun potentia meaning "power, might, force" or from the Latin adjective potens meaning "able, strong, powerful, potent" (see Potens).This name was borne by a Roman tribune who was killed at the Battle of Adrianople in 378 AD. He was the son of the Roman general Ursicinus.
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin noun potestas meaning "power, ability".
Means "longed for, desired, full of longing" in Ancient Greek, derived from πόθος (pothos) meaning "longing, yearning, regret".
French form of Potheinos via its latinized form Pothinus.This name is not to be confused with the similar-looking name Photin.

Latinized form of Potheinos.Pothinus was the name of a eunuch who served as regent for pharaoh Ptolemy XIII Theos Philopator (1st century BC) and of a Greek saint who lived and died in Roman Gaul (2nd century AD).
Pōtiki means "child, pet" in Māori, a synonym of tamariki meaning "young, children" in Māori. Pōtikī means "Portuguese" in Māori, referring to someone from Portugal.
Goddess who enables a child to drink.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Potheinos via its latinized form Pothinus.

From Egyptian p-di-p-r' meaning "he whom Ra gave", composed of the definite article p- "the one" combined with di "whom he gave" and r', the name of the supreme god Ra. In the Old Testament, Potiphar is a wealthy Egyptian who purchases Joseph as a slave.
Bulgarian, French, Russian and Serbian form of Potitus.
Roman nomen gentile of which the etymological origin is most likely the same as that of the Roman cognomen Potitus.
Italian form of Potitus. A notable bearer of this name is the Italian former tennis player Potito "Poto" Starace (b. 1981).

Roman cognomen which was most likely derived from Latin potitus, which is the perfect participle of the verb potior meaning "to acquire, to obtain". Also compare the Latin adjective potior, which is the comparative of the adjective potis meaning "able, capable" (also see Potens). Alternatively, this cognomen was derived from the Latin verb potito meaning "to drink often".This name was borne by several ancient Romans, such as the consul Lucius Valerius Potitus (5th century BC). It was also the name of a boy saint from the 2nd century AD, who was born into an affluent pagan family from Serdica in Roman Thracia (now Sofia in Bulgaria). As such, in his case, the name is possibly a latinization of his original Thracian name.
The name of Grace Kennedy given to her by her twin sister Virginia (Cabengo) in their own private language.The story of Poto and Cabengo was popularised through a 1980 documentary film.
Derived from the Georgian noun ფოთოლი (potoli) meaning "leaf".
Diminutive of names that end in p, such as Josèp and Halip.
Swedish children's book heroine Pippi Longstocking is known as Potpot Habangmedyas in Tagalog.
From Maranao potri' meaning "princess", ultimately from Sanskrit पुत्री (putrī).
Derived from the Georgian noun ფოცხვერი (potskhveri) meaning "lynx" (as in, the feline).
Transferred use of the surname Potter.
Nuorese diminutive of the Italian compound name Maria Antonia.
Old French poi "little" + Old French biau, belle "beautiful".
Means "born on the riverside" in Ijaw.
Modern Greek form of Pulcheria. 'It is not a very common name, but relatively popular in the northern regions of the Greek mainland and also among the people who come from Pontus.'
Alternate transcription of Malayalam പൗലോസ് (see Paulose).
Alternate transcription of Persian پونه (see Pouneh).
Meaning uncertain, possibly from Persian پور (pur) meaning "son" and رنگ (rang) meaning "colour".
Possibly derived from Avestan pouruyô meaning "first, foremost". Alternately it may be from Sanskrit पुर्य (purya) meaning "being in a stronghold or fortress".
Alternate transcription of Persian پوریا (see Pouria).
Probably means "the one who is noticed by many people, the charming one" in Avestan. This was the name of Zarathustra's younger daughter.
Modern Greek spelling of Poublios, which is the ancient Greek form of Publius.
Means "runner, seeker, searcher, explorer" in Persian.
Feminine form of Povilas. Also compare Paulė.
Variant of Pouline. Famous bearer is Povline Lütken (6 May 1893 - 30 December 1977), Danish writer.
Variant of Pavsikakiy. Also compare Pavsekakiy.
Transferred use of the surname Powell.
From the English word power meaning "a source or means of supplying energy" or transferred use of the surname Power 1 or Power 2.
From Middle English pouerful, powarfull, equivalent to power +‎ -ful.
Transferred use of the surname Powers.

The name of the Native American confederation of tribes in Virginia, which English colonists mistook for the name of Chief Wahunsenacawh, the paramount chief of Tsenacommacah, an alliance of Algonquian-speaking Virginia Indians in the Tidewater region of Virginia at the time English settlers landed at Jamestown in 1607. The name Powhatan is the name of the village or town that Wahunsunacawh came from. Chief Powhatan, as he came to be known, is best known as the father of Pocahontas.
Alternate transcription of Persian پویا (see Pouya).

From Sanskrit प्रभु (prabhu) meaning "mighty, powerful, master, lord" combined with जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".

From Sanskrit प्रभु (prabhu) meaning "mighty, powerful, master, lord" combined with मित्र (mitra) meaning "friend".
From Sanskrit प्रभु (prabhu) meaning "mighty, powerful, master, lord" and नीति (nīti) meaning "guidance, moral conduct, behaviour".
From Sanskrit प्रभु (prabhu) meaning "mighty, powerful, master, lord" combined with Arabic نور (nūr) meaning "light".
From Sanskrit प्रभु (prabhu) meaning "mighty, powerful, master, lord" combined with प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".
From Javanese prabawa meaning "power, majesty, splendour", ultimately from Sanskrit प्रभाव (prabhāva). It is borne by current Indonesian president Prabowo Subianto (1951-).
Means "people, citizens, populace" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रजा (prajā).
From Thai ประ (bprà), a meaningless article, and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Means "clear, manifest, evident" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रत्यक्ष (pratyakṣa).

column3: ประจักษ์ชัย(Thai)
column12: From Thai ประจักษ์ (prachak) meaning "clear, manifest, evident" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Alternate transcription of Thai ปรัชญา (see Pratchaya).
Alternate transcription of Hindi/Marathi प्राची (see Prachi).
Means "be close to, approach, adjoin" in Thai.
Alternate transcription of Thai ปรัชญา (see Pratya).
Meaning unknown. It is used in reference to the Italian luxury brand Prada, which is named after its founder Mario Prada.
Pradakshina is called parikrma means to take a round of statue of god, holy Placea or place worth to pay respect.
Alternate transcription of Thai ปรัชญา (see Pratchaya).
From the surname, Pradel, which is derived from the Italian word prato, "feild, meadow".
Alternate transcription of Thai ประเดิม (see Pradoem).

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ประเดิมชัย (see Pradoemchai).
From Sanskrit प्रदीप्त (pradīpta) meaning "kindled, illuminated, blazing, burning, shining".
Meaning "of light" or "illuminating" in Bengali. Feminine form of Pradip or Pradeep. Derived from Sanskrit प्रदीप (pradipa) meaning "light" or "lantern".
Alternate transcription of Bengali প্রদীপ্ত (see Pradipta).
Means "to establish, to create, to invent" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रतिष्ठ (pratiṣṭha).

Means "meadow" in Spanish, taken from the Spanish titles of the Virgin Mary, La Virgen del Prado and Nuestra Señora del Prado, meaning "The Virgin of the Meadow" and "Our Lady of the Meadow."She is venerated at the Basílica de Nuestra Señora del Prado in Talavera in the province of Toledo, the Ciudad Real Cathedral and the Ermita de Nuestra Señora del Prado in the province of Cáceres.

column3: ประเดิมชัย(Thai)
column12: From Thai ประเดิม (pradoem) meaning "begin, start, initiate" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
Plural form of Prado, most often used in the province of Toledo in Spain.

From Sanskrit प्रद्युम्न (pradyumna) meaning "pre-eminently mighty one, pleasant, intellect". This is the name of the eldest son of the Hindu deities Krishna and his consort Rukmini and is widely considered to be the reincarnation of Kamadeva, the god of love.
Derived from Latin praejacio ("to throw"). This is the name of a saint (625-676).
From Thai แพรก (praek) and วัน (wan).
Alternate transcription of Thai แพรว (see Phraeo).
Alternate transcription of Thai แพรวพรรณ (see Phraeophan).
From Latin praepes "swift; lucky" and digna "worthy". This is the name of a Roman martyr from the 3rd century AD.

Derived from Latin praetextus "fringed, bordered, edged", which is ultimately derived from the Latin verb praetexere "to weave, to border, to fringe". The modern English word pretext derives from the same root. This name was borne by a saint from the 6th century AD.
From Thai แพรว (praew) meaning "gleaming, glistening, shining" and ไพลิน (pai-lin) meaning "sapphire".
From Sanskrit प्रफुल्ल (praphulla) meaning "blossoming, blooming, expanded, open, smiling".
From Sanskrit प्रगति (pragati). The name means progress, development, and advancement.

Derived from Greek πράγματος (pragmatos) "to gather evidence", which itself is ultimately derived from Greek πρᾶγμα (pragma) "deed, action". Also compare Greek πράσσειν (prassein) meaning "to do". This was the name of a Frankish saint, as well as the name of Roman orator from the 5th century AD.
Italian form of Pragmatius and variant of Prammazio.
From Sanskrit प्रज्ञा (prajñā) meaning "wisdom, knowledge, judgment".
Another name of the Hindu Goddess Saraswati, it means "intellectual" or "the most intelligent".

No History, this Name has two words of Indian Ancient Language "Sanskrit" words are "Pragya" which means "ENLIGHTED CONSCIOUSNESS” and "Asmi" which means "I AM"so taken together "Pragyasmi" means "I am Enlightened Consciousness".
Used in Ghana, West Africa among Akan peoples. Shortened form of the name of the river spirit Bohsum-Prah. Usually used together with Nana: Nana-Prah.
Meaning "Person with a Lot of Qualities".
Variant of Praeiecta or Praejecta, the feminine form of Praejectus.

From the English word for a flat treeless grassland, taken from French prairie "meadow". This was used by Thomas Pynchon for a character in his novel 'Vineland' (1990). In modern times it is mostly feminine.

From the English phrase praise God, referring to giving God glory. A known bearer was Praise-God Barebone (or Barbon; c. 1598-1679), an English preacher and Fifth Monarchist after whom Barebone's Parliament of 1653 was named. He was the father of the economist Nicholas Barbon.
The name comes from the the phrase Praise the Lord. Some of the letters from the pharse are removed to turn it into a name.

Means "night-blooming jasmine" (scientific name Nyctanthes arbor-tristis) in Marathi.

Means "lord of creatures" from Sanskrit प्रजा (prajā) meaning "creature, animal, mankind" and पति (pati) meaning "husband, lord". This is the name of a Vedic Hindu god of creation, later identified with Brahma.
The name means to be coming from different expectations and be on top.
Alternate transcription of Kannada ಪ್ರಜ್ವಲ್ (see Prajwal).
Means "brilliant, lustrous, burning brightly" in Kannada, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रज्वाला (prajvālā) meaning "flame, light".

From Javanese prakasa meaning "clear, obvious, well-known, famous", ultimately from Sanskrit प्रकाश (prakāśa).
Prakriti means nature in Sanskrit, it's also an alternative name for ma Durga from Hindu religion.

The English and French word praline refers to "a sweet chocolate confectionery filled with nuts/nut paste". Named after the Comte du Plessis-Praslin (1598-1675), whose cook invented it in the 17th century.
Means "to measure, to estimate, to approximate" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रमाण (pramāṇa).
Means "to be full of wisdom and knowledge" in Indonesian.

From Javanese pramèsthi meaning "supreme god", ultimately from Sanskrit परमेष्ठि (parameṣṭhi) referring to the Hindu god Brahma. In Javanese Hindu tradition this is an epithet of Batara Guru.
Means "enervation, exhaustion, fatigue" in Sanskrit. This is the name of a wife of Arjuna in some versions of the Mahabharata.
Italian form of Pragmatius and variant of Pragmazio.

Meaning "One Who Is Conscious and Aware".
Means "he with the qualities of a leader" in Gujarati and Marathi.
Name of Lord Vishnu and Lord Brahma.
Tamil and Malayalam form of Pranati.
From Sanskrit प्रणति (praṇati) meaning "bow, salutation, reverence, courtesy".
From Sanskrit प्रणय (praṇaya) meaning "love, guidance, leader".
From the English word prancer. This is the name of one of Santa's reindeers, first attested in the 1823 poem “A Visit from St. Nicholas”.
Malayalam form of Francis used in central Kerala
Short form of Pranciška. In other words, you could say that this name is the feminine equivalent of Pranas.

The name Prasath is of Indian origin, often derived from Sanskrit, and means “blessing,” “grace,” or “gift.” It is commonly used in South Indian cultures as a given name or part of a name.

One who win expert army and Never lose any war in his life.PRASENJEET was an Aikṣvāka dynasty ruler of Kosala. Sāvatthī was his capital. He succeeded his father Sanjaya Mahākosala. He was a prominent Upāsaka of Gautama Buddha, who built many Buddhist monasteries and a lover of Nandini.
From Javanese prasêtya meaning "to promise, to take a vow (to be loyal or faithful)".

Means "lamp, light, candle" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रदीप (pradīpa).
Means "to enhance, to enrich" in Thai.
Sanskrit and Hindu origins with links to Lord Ganesha. Prathula means "Lord of the beast", "Abundant", and "plentiful".
From Thai ปทุม (pathum) meaning "lotus".

From Sanskrit प्रत्याशा (pratyāśā) meaning "expectation, hope, future prospects".

Derived from the Proto-Slavic word *pravьda meaning "truth; justice" in many Slavic languages.

From Sanskrit प्रवेश (praveśa) meaning "entrance, access, approach".
From Sanskrit प्रवीर (pravīra) meaning "hero, warrior, excellent, distinguished".

Variant of Pravlen including Stalin's name.

Pravuil is an archangel briefly mentioned in the Second Book of Enoch as God's scribe and recordkeeper. In Enoch II, God commands Pravuil to bring Enoch writing materials so he could document his journey through the heavens.

The first element of this name is derived from Polish prawda "truth, verity", which is derived from Old Church Slavonic pravida "truth" (which in turn is probably derived from Proto-Slavic pravъ "straight, right"). Also compare Croatian pravi "true" and Czech pravda "truth". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, this name's meaning is something along the lines of "peace is truth".
Alternate transcription of Thai ประเวศ (see Prawet).
Means "heroic, brave" in Indonesian, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रवीर (pravīra).

column3: ประวิทย์, ประวิตร(Thai)
column12: From Thai ประวิตร (prawit) meaning "pure, clean", ultimately from Sanskrit पवित्र (pavitra).

The first element of this name is derived from Polish prawy "right, upright, righteous", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic pravъ "straight, right". Also compare Croatian prav and Czech pravý, both of which mean "right, straight". The second element of this name is derived from Slavic mir "peace". As such, this name's meaning is something along the lines of "righteous peace".

The first element of this name is derived from Polish prawy "right, upright, righteous", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic pravъ "straight, right". Also compare Croatian prav and Czech pravý, both of which mean "right, straight". The second element of this name is derived from Polish myśl "thought", which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic mysliti "to think". As such, this name's meaning is something along the lines of "righteous thought".
From Javanese prawata meaning "mountain, hill", ultimately from Sanskrit पर्वत (parvata).

Derived from Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (praxis) meaning "action, exercise, work" and ἀγορά (agora), which can mean "assembly, marketplace" as well as "speech, public speaking". A known bearer of this name was Praxagoras of Kos, an ancient Greek physician from the 4th century BC.

Latinized form of Πράξανδρος (Praxandros), a name derived from Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (praxis) "action, exercise" combined with ἀνδρός (andros) "of a man". In Greek mythology, Praxander was one of the founders of the city of Keryneia (now Kyrenia) in Cyprus.
Form of Praxedes found in England from the 16th century.
Latin form of Praxedes. This name was used by Joseph Victor von Scheffel for a character in his historical novel 'Ekkehard' (1857).
Derived from Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (praxis) meaning "action, exercise" combined with βουλή (boule) meaning "counsel, advice" as well as "will, determination".
Latinized form of Praxiboulos. This name was borne by an eponymous archon of Athens, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Possibly a derivative of Praxis. Praxilla of Sicyon was a Greek lyric poet of the 5th century BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (praxis) meaning "action, exercise, work" combined with φανής (phanes) meaning "appearing". This name was borne by a Peripatetic philosopher, who lived in the 4th century BC.

Derived from Ancient Greek πρᾶξις (praxis) meaning "action, exercise" and θεά (thea) meaning "goddess". Alternatively, the second element could derive from θέα (thea) meaning "sight, view". This was the name of several figures in Greek mythology, including one of the fifty daughters of King Thespius, mother of Nephus by Heracles, and of a naiad nymph of Athens.
Likely an invented name made to sound like other popular names like Braxton or Jaxton.
Meaning "Very Likable" or "Someone that Everyone Loves".
Means "save, preserve" in Thai, ultimately from Sanskrit प्रयत्न (prayatna).
Middle English from Old French preiere, based on Latin precarius ‘obtained by entreaty,’ from prex, prec- prayer.’
From Javanese prayitna meaning "careful, cautious, thoughtful, prudent".
Combination of the English word pray and the popular element lee.
Combination of the word pray and the given name Lynn.
From Javanese prayoga meaning "good, proper, advisable, acceptable", ultimately derived from Sanskrit प्रयोग (prayoga).
From the Thai name for a flowering evergreen plant native to Southeast Asia (species Aglaia odorata), ultimately from Sanskrit प्रियङ्गु (priyaṅgu).
Alternate transcription of Thai ประยูร (see Prayun).

Contraction of Russian пролетариат (proletariat) "proletariat" and Tatar азатлыгы (azatlıgı) "freedom of proletariat".
Contraction of праздник советской власти (prazdnik sovetskoy vlasti) "holiday of Soviet power", influenced by Russian свет (svet) "light, world".

Derived from Portuguese prazeres, the plural form of prazer "pleasure", this name is used in reference to the title of the Virgin Mary Nossa Senhora dos Prazeres ("Our Lady of Pleasures"). This title refers to the seven pleasures of the Virgin Mary's life.
Transferred use of the surname Preacher. This name can also be given in direct reference to the English word preacher. A known bearer of the name is American comedian Preacher Lawson (1991-).
Derived from the Slavic elements prebi and slav "glory".
Name of a medieval Russian princess.
Feminine form of Précieux, cognate to English Precious.
Derived from Middle French precieuse, the feminine form of the adjective precieux "precious (of great value)" (via Old French precius, ultimately from Latin pretiōsus, from pretium "worth; value").
Means "precious" in Spanish, Portuguese and other languages of the Iberian peninsula, from Latin pretiōsa "precious, of great value".
Derived from Spanish preciosísima meaning "most precious".
A girl on Tiktok tells the story of her first name. It's his progenitor called Marvel, who named her Précis-De-Marvel.
Likely a short form of Predestinación.
Means "predestination" in Spanish, likely after the predestination of the Virgin Mary to be the mother of Jesus by choice of God.

The first element of this archaic name is derived from the Serbo-Croatian adjective pred "in front of, before" (the latter can also be used to refer to an earlier point in time), which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic perdъ "in front of, against". Also compare modern Russian pered and Polish przed, both of which mean "before, in front of". The second element of this name is either derived from Slavic mir "peace" or Slavic mer "great, famous".

Lithuanized Prussian name, meaning "The one, who is near household". Composed of Prussian prep. prei- "near, close to, by", a root -but- "to be", which was taken either from a word Buttan "household, home" or Būton "to be", and the ending -a, that indicates feminine gender.

Derived from the Latin verb premo meaning "to press into, to press upon", referring to the insistent sex act. Although the verb usually describes the masculine role, Augustine calls Prema dea Mater, a mother goddess. She was also mentioned by Tertullian in Ad Nationes.

From Hindi प्रेम (prem) meaning "love" and दीप (dīp) meaning "lamp, light", thus "lamp of love".

From Sanskrit preman "love" (cf. Prema) and latā "creeper" - the name of a small plant, used as a symbol of love. This is borne by Premlata Agarwal (1963-), the first Indian female mountaineer to complete the Seven Summits, the seven highest continental peaks in the world.
From Thai เปรม (prem) meaning "content, happy, delighted" and วดี (wadi) meaning "possessing, having".

Prende is the goddess of love, beauty and fertility in the Albanian pagan mythology, who is thought to have been worshiped by the Illyrians in antiquity. She is the wife of the thunder and sky god Perëndi.
East Prussian German form of Franziskus.

The origin of Prerak is the Sanskrit language. The name means one who encourages others.

A notable fictional bearer of this name is Preshea Villentia, née Buss from Gail Carriger’s Finishing School book series. A notable bearer of a variant of this name is gospel singer Preashea Hilliard.
Presian I of Bulgaria was the Khan of Bulgaria from 836–852. He ruled during an extensive expansion in Macedonia.
Either from the English word president or transferred use of the surname President.

Priarius was a king of the Alemmanic Lentienses sub-tribe in the 4th century. He was killed in 378, in the Battle of Argentovaria against the Western Roman Empire.

Medieval Slavic form of Przybymir. Also take note that some sources each list a different meaning for the first element. Some say it means "pierced" or "breaking" (in the sense of destroying something), while others say it means "more, much more, multiple" (in the sense of abundance). Yet another source states it means "against" and a single source states that it means "to help". The last one seems most unlikely, but all the others have an outward resemblance (more or less) to the Polish word that means "to arrive, to come", so that might explain the confusion.

Medieval Slavic form of Przybysław. Also take note that some sources each list a different meaning for the first element. Some say it means "pierced" or "breaking" (in the sense of destroying something), while others say it means "more, much more, multiple" (in the sense of abundance). Yet another source states it means "against" and a single source states that it means "to help". Derived from Vulgar Latin prīmavēra "spring". The descendant word primavera is used in Asturian, Catalan, Galician, Italian, Portuguese (and Old Portuguese), Sicilian, and Spanish.

Italian and Spanish form of Primianus. A bearer of this name was the Argentinian jurist and politician Primiano Acuña Vieyra (1852-1934).

Roman cognomen which was derived from Primus (see also Primanus). A bearer of this name was Marcus Ulpius Primianus, a Roman prefect from the 2nd century AD. This name was also borne by Primianus of Larino, a saint from the 4th century AD.

Derived from Latin prīmigenia, the feminine form of the adjective prīmigenius "original, primitive; firstborn", ultimately derived from primus "first" and genus "birth, origin", this was an epithet of the Goddess Fortuna. Primigenia was an Alban vestal of Bovillae, mentioned by Symmachus in two of his letters.

Diminutive of Primula (traditional) and Primrose (modern).A known bearer of this name was Primula "Primmie" Rollo (1918-1946), the first wife of the English actor David Niven (1910-1983). She died in a tragic freak accident at age 28, which made the news at the time. She left behind her husband and two young sons (aged 3 years and 6 months, respectively).
Medieval Italian diminutive of Primo, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
