From Chinese 似 (sì) meaning "to look like, to be similar to, to resemble" combined with 道 (dào) meaning "path, road, way". Other hanzi combinations are possible.
Derivation of Sanskrit word "Siddha" meaning "enlightened, accomplished, fulfilled"

Either an elaboration of Sidda using the popular name suffix lee, or a variant of Sidalie or Cidalise. This name was used by American author Rebecca Wells for a character in her novels Little Altars Everywhere (1992) and Divine Secrets of the Ya-Ya Sisterhood (1996), which are set in Louisiana.

The name Siddhanth (also spelled Siddhant) is of Sanskrit origin, predominantly found in Indian culture. It derives from the Sanskrit words 'siddha,' meaning 'accomplished' or 'achieved,' and 'anta,' meaning 'end' or 'conclusion. Represents principles and righteousness. Also means Lord Krishna in Hinduism. Siddhanth is currently #9185 in the popularity of the name rankings.
From Sanskrit सिद्धिद (siddhida) meaning "giving success, conferring felicity".
Possibly a diminutive of any name starting with Sid.
Alternate transcription of Arabic صديق (see Siddiq), as well as a Bengali and Indonesian variant.
Truthful, honest, veracious. It is one of the names of Fatimah ,the daughter of Prophet Muhammad.
Alternate transcription of Urdu صدیق (see Siddiq).
Means "truthfullness of Allah" from Arabic صدّيق (ṣiddīq) meaning "honest, truthful" combined with الله (Allah).

Means "pomegranate" in Ancient Greek. This was the name of several people in Greek mythology, including a woman who killed herself and was transformed into a pomegranate tree to escape her own father, the wife of Orion who was condemned to the Underworld by Hera for rivalling her beauty, and several legendary eponyms of various ancient towns and cities of the same name.
Turkish name of unknown origin and meaning.

The second middle name of Exa Dark Sideræl Musk (2021-), daughter of Elon Musk and Claire "Grimes" Boucher. According to Grimes, it is a spelling variation of the English word sidereal "of or pertaining to the stars", in order to be more 'Elven'. The word itself is ultimately derived from Latin sidus meaning "star, constellation".

Transferred used of the surname Sideris or the reduced and altered form of the personal name Isidoros (see Isadore), altered by folk etymology as if derived from sidero ‘iron’ (classical Greek sideron), and hence regarded as an omen name: ‘may the child grow up to be as strong as iron’.
Derived from Greek σίδηρος (sideros) meaning "iron". In Greek legend Sidero was the abusive stepmother of Tyro, finally murdered by Tyro's adult son Pelias atop an altar to the goddess Hera.
The meaning of this name is still unknown to me at this time. A bearer of this name was Sidhom Bishay, a 19th-century Coptic saint.

Sidimund was a 5th-century Ostrogothic warrior. Under the Ostrogothic king Valamir, Sidimund had been plundering Epirus. He was a member of the Amali dynasty and a close relative of Aidoingus, the comes domesticorum. Sidimund later served in the Eastern Roman army with great distinction and acquired extensive land holdings in the area near Durrazo. He was considered a friend of the Romans and was held in great esteem. In 479, Sidimund helped his relative Theodoric the Great settle in Epirus, despite the opposition of another fellow Goth, Gento.
Alternate transcription of Arabic صدّيق (see Siddiq), as well as an Indonesian variant.

Romanian form of a Crimean Tatar name probably from Arabic صَادِق (ṣādiq) meaning "true, truthful, veracious" or صَدِيق (ṣadīq) meaning "friend". A known bearer was Sîdîyîk Ibrahim H. Mîrzî (1909-1959), a Romanian imam and activist of Crimean Tatar heritage.
Finnish, Norwegian and Swedish form of Tzidqiyyahu (see Zedekiah).
He was the brother in Disney's Brother Bear. The oldest brother was killed and was the brother to Kenai.
Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Sidonius.
Croatian and Slovene form of Sidonia.
Italian and Spanish form of Sidonius.
Bulgarian, Russian and Ukrainian form of Sidonius.
Bulgarian, Russian, and Ukrainian form of Sidonia. In Ukraine, it is used mostly in Chernivtsi oblast.
Variant or short form of Isidor.
Campidanese and Sassarese form of Isidore.
Means "order, sequence" in Hebrew. It refers to a weekly reading portion of the Torah, so the whole Torah is completed every year. This name is typical of North African Jewry.
From the Arabic سِدْرَة (sidre(t)) meaning "ceder, date palm".
Possibly a variant of Sitric (see Sithric).
Variant of Sisse, the Danish form of Sissa.
Possibly derived from the Old English elements sidu meaning "modesty, custom, manner" and mæġden meaning "virgin, unmarried young woman".

Attested as an epithet for several Hurrian goddesses, as well as the Mesopotamian goddess Ishtar. It is possibly derived from the Hurrian word šiduri, meaning "young woman". Another proposed origin is from the Akkadian šī-dūrī ("she is my protection"). A character bearing this name also appears in the Epic of Gilgamesh, however it is accepted that she is unrelated to Ishtar.

Anglicized form of Sadfyl which itself is considered a Cornish calque of Old English sidu "morality, good conduct; purity; modesty" as well as "ritual, religious practice, rite" and Old English full "full, filled, complete, entire" and hence understood as "the virtuous one". Saint Sidwell was a virgin saint from the English county of Devon. The Catalogus Sanctorum Pausantium in Anglia describes her as a native of Exeter who was beheaded by reapers, who were incited so to do by her stepmother. She is said to have been buried outside the city, where the sick could be healed at her grave. Saint Sidwell is the patron saint of Exeter.
Name of the founder of Sidyma, a town in Lycia according to Greek myth.
Contracted form of Germanic names beginning with the element sigu "victory".
Dutch for Siegbrand.Sig means victoryBrand - flaming sword
The name's origin is in the Dutch province of Friesland.
Name of an Polish Count Palatine in the eleventh Century and alleged lover of the Polish Duchess Judith

From siecie-"to understand, to perceive" combined with ciech- "enjoy". As well as this, its initial element can also be interpreted as wsze- "universe, all", so this name can mean "he who enjoys the universe".
From the Slavic elements siecie- " to understand , remember , guess , feel, perceive " combined with sława - "glory". Therefore, this name means "to perceive/understand glory".
Possibly a variant of Saida or Sayyida. A known bearer is American singer and songwriter Siedah Garrett (1960-), born Deborah Christine Garrett.
The name is a combination of the Germanic name elements sigu "victory" and bald "bold". The name can also be read as the sentence Sieg bald! "Win soon!".
Derived from the Germanic name elements sigi "victory" and boto "lord, ruler".
Rare form of Sieglinde. Used by German actress Lil Dagover, whose full name was Marie Antonia Siegelinde Martha Seubert.

The name is formed from the German name elements Sieg "victory" and Minne "courtly love".It is the name of the mermaid Rauch Else in the Wolfdietrich epic after being transformed to a beautiful women.
Variant of Sieghard. The name was borne by the Austrian actor Sieghardt Rupp (1931–2015).
Abbreviated, more modern form of Sigenot. In popular culture, this name is borne by a character from "Die Rose vom Liebesgarten", an opera by German composer Hans Pfitzner (1869-1949).
Variant of Sigrun used by Richard Wagner as name for a valkyria.
An early 20th century coinage from the Germanic name element sigu "victory" and the biblical name Ruth 1.
" A girl who is as high as a mountain "
From Sino-Vietnamese 覘 (siêm) meaning "to fathom, look, investigate".
Low German pet form of Siegmar.
Means "rejoicing with family" from Proto-Slavic *sěmьja meaning "family" combined with rad meaning "to rejoice".

From the proto-Slavic elements sěmьja meaning "family, kin, retinue, staff" or "property" and sław meaning "glory". The meaning can be interpreted as "one who brings glory to his kin". The feminine version Sěmislava was popular in South-Slavic countries.This name is also found rendered as Siemosław.
Derived from Slavic siem "family" combined with Polish myśl "thought" (which is ultimately derived from Proto-Slavic mysliti "to think").
Short form of Francina, Josina, Klasina and other names with a similar ending.
Name: SienahMeaning:1: To dance with joy in love.2: Reddish orange brown ColorOrigin: Hebrew and Italian
Welsh form of Jenkin, a Middle English diminutive of John.

This name is originally from the Arabic name Said. Among West Africa's Manding people, mainly in Northern Cote d'Ivoire in places like Kong, Dabakala, Satama Sokura and Sokoro. A variant of the name in Burkina Faso, Mali, Guinea where the same Mande people with differing dialects live, Seydou. The Manding actual name for Said is "Bakounandi" (the lucky one). It may be given to a baby girl, and yet has to be written "Makounandi", the prefix "Ba" being form males and "Ma" for females.
Combination of the names Sienna and Rose.
A variant of Sienna or possibly inspired by also combining Vienne
From Sino-Korean(Hanja) 時(shi) meaning "Excellent", "Great", "Good" and 嫣(eon) meaning "Beautiful, Pretty, Charming" or 彦(eon) meaning "Talented, Good, Noble".
From Sino-Korean (Korean Hanja) 時(shi), 彦(eon) meaning "Exellent", "Best", "Great" or 詩(shi), 嫣(eon) meaning "Beautiful", "Elegant", "pretty".
Contracted form of Germanic names beginning with the element sigu "victory".
Taken directly from the country Sierra Leone.
From Egyptian zꜣ-ꜣst meaning "son of Isis".
From Sino-Vietnamese 超 (siêu) meaning "to exceed, surpass, super".

column3: 시은(Korean Hangul)|時銀, 詩恩, 始恩, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 時 (si) meaning "time, season", 詩 (si) meaning "poem, verse", or 始 (si) meaning "beginning, start" combined with 銀 (eun) meaning "silver" or 恩 (eun) meaning "favour, grace". Other hanja character combinations are possible.
From Sino-Vietnamese 超人 (siêu nhân) meaning "superhuman", composed of 超 (siêu) meaning "super" and 人 (nhân) meaning "human".
From Sino-Vietnamese 超越 (siêu việt) meaning "transcendental," composed of 超 (siêu) meaning "to exceed, surpass" and 越 (việt) meaning "to surpass".
Romansh form of Eusebius, traditionally found in the Surselva region.

column3: 秀, 晓, 修, 寿, 诗, 守, 绍, etc.(Chinese)
column12: Hokkien romanization of Xiu, Xiao, Shou, Shi or Shao.
Means "torch; ray of light" in Amazigh.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سيف الدين (see Sayf ad-Din), chiefly used in Northern Africa.
Danish variant of Siv via Old Norse Sif.
Variant of Sigfrido. In an ecclesiastical context, this name is used to refer to Siffredus of Carpentras.
Medieval South German form of Siegfried.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 芙 (fú) meaning "hibiscus".
Means 'God's violet' in Hebrew.Related to Sigal and Sigalit
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" and bant "band, bond".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" and bjǫrg "help, salvation".
Derived from the Germanic name elements sigr "victory" and bjǫrn "bear".
From the Old (West) Norse name Sigbjörg which was composed of the elements sigr "victory" and björg "protection, help".
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and bjǫrn "bear".
Danish and Norwegian form of Sigbjörn.
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" and boto "messenger".
Combination of Sig (from Signe, Sigrid, or other names beginning with the Old Norse element sigr "victory") and Britt. It might also be used as a Dutch feminine form of Siegbert.
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and djarfr "bold, brave, daring, courageous".
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and dís "goddess; woman, lady"
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Means "bright victory", derived from Old English sige "victory" and beorht "bright". Cognate of Sigibert and variant Sigeberht.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Sigebert.
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old Norse brand "sword."

The first element of this name is derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert). The second element is derived from Gothic bairgan (bergan in Old High German) "to keep, to save, to preserve", or from Old High German burg "fortress."
Derived from Old English sige meaning "victory" and flæd, possibly meaning "beauty".
Derived from Proto-Germanic Sigifriþuz, using the Old English elements sige "victory" and friþ "peace". Cognate to German Siegfried.
Derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and gar "spear". Cognate to Old Norse Siggæirr.
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Gothic hardus (hart in Old High German) "brave, hardy."
Derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and heard "hard, firm, brave, hardy".. Old English cognate of Sigihard.
Derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and helm "helmet, protection".
Derived from Germanic Sigimar, using the Old English elements sige "victory" and mære "famous". Cognate to German Siegmar.
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with man "man."
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old High German mâri "famous."
Derived from Germanic Sigimundaz, using the Old English elements sige "victory" and mund "protection". Cognate to Old Norse Sigmundr and Germanic Sigismund.

The first element of this name is derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert). The second element is derived from Gothic nand "bravery" (or from Gothic nanthjan "to venture, to risk, to dare").

Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old High German not "need, necessity." The second element might also have been derived from hnôd, which comes from Old High German hnôtôn "to crush."
Derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and noð "boldness, daring".
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old High German rât "counsel."
Derived from Old English sige "victory" and ræd "counsel". This name was borne by a King of Essex, as well as a King of Kent.

The name of the last king of Essex before being defeated and reduced to duke by his Mercian overlords, in response he ceded his former title to King Egbert of Wessex and possibly pledged vassalage to Egbert soon after. He reigned as King of Essex from 798 to 812 before said Mercian overlords reduced his title.

Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler." Sigeric was the name of a 5th-century king of the Visigoths.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Sigeric.
Croatian, Dutch and Norwegian form of Sigeric.
Dutch and West Frisian form of Sigehard.
Old English name composed of the elements sige "victory" and stan "stone" (making it a cognate of Sigsteinn).
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Gothic valdan "to reign."
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old High German wart "guard."
Derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and weald "powerful, mighty" or "authority, leader". Cognate to Germanic Sigiwald and Old Norse Sigvaldr.
Means "friend of victory", derived from Old English sige "victory" and wine "friend". Cognate of Sigwin.
Derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and wulf "wolf". Cognate to Old Norse Sighulfr.
Old Swedish and younger form of Sigfastr.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and fastr "firm, strong".
Derived from sigr ("victory") and faðir ("father"). This is a by-name for Odin.
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and finnr "Sámi, person from Finland".
Modern form of Sigfrøðr. This was the name of an 8th century Danish king.
Faroese younger form of Sigfríðr and Icelandic variant of Sigfríður.
Old English form of Sigrid and feminine form of Sigefrið, derived from the Old English elements sige "victory" and friþ, ultimately from Old Norse Sigfríðr.
Old Norse combination of sigr "victory" and fríðr "beautiful", originally "beloved".
Variant of Sigríður, as well as the Faroese form of Sigfrøðr.
Icelandic and Faroese younger form of Sigfúss.
Old Norse combination of sigr "victory" and fúss "willing, eager".
Short form of names beginning with the element Sig-, such as Sigrid or Signe.
Derived from Old Norse sigr meaning "victory" and geirr meaning "spear".
Derived from the Germanic name elements sigr "victory" and garðr "enclosure", "protection".
Derived from sigr ("victory") and gautr ("Goth, Geat, one from Gautland"). This is a kenning for Odin.
Icelandic younger feminine form of Siggarðr.
Old Norse diminutive of Sigurðr and other names beginning with the element sigr "victory".
Derived from the Germanic name elements sigr "victory" and gunnr "battle, fight".
Diminutive of names containing the name element Sig.
Old Swedish form of Sigfríðr and Sigfrøðr.
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Sigmundr.
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Signý.
Old Danish and Old Swedish form of Sigtryggr.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and ulfr "wolf".
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and hvatr "quick, active, brave, manly".
Modern Icelandic and Faroese form of Sighvatr.

The first element of this name is derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert). The second element is derived from Proto-Germanic beran or bernu "bear" (bero and bern in Old High German).
Hispanic Latin American variant of Siegfried
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" combined with hari "army."
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with Old High German helm "helmet, protection".
Means "blackbird" in Potawatomi. This was the name of a chief of the Milwaukee Potawatomi.
Short form of Sigismundas and/or Sigitas and perhaps also of other masculine given names that contain the Germanic element sigu meaning "victory", such as Sigurdas.
Derived from Gothic sigis "victory" combined with Old High German beraht "bright".
Lithuanian form of Sigismund, which is an older form of Sigmund. Also compare Zigmantas and Žygimantas.
Lithuanian feminine form of Sigitas which also got adopted into Latvian usage.
Derived from the Germanic name elements sigr "victory" and ketill "cauldron hat, helmet".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" combined with Old Norse kettil "kettle, cauldron" (see also Kettil).
From Tagalog sigla meaning "lively, vitality, energy".
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and laug "bathing for religious purification" but could also be derived from the Germanic element *-lauz- "enter into marriage, give holy vows".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" and leifr "descendant, heir".

This is the name of a Muslim Saracen killed by the Archbishop Turpin in "La Chanson de Roland," the poem about the noble defense of the French army against the Muslim Saracens. Siglorel was a sorcerer, who, allegedly, had "gone to the devil and back."
Latinate variant of Signy and Signý as well as a contracted form of Signilla. As a Swedish name it was first recorded in 1866 and is sometimes associated with the verb välsigna "to bless".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" combined with Old Norse harja or herr "army".
Diminutive of Signe. It literally means "little Signe".
Minnesota Swedish corruption of Signy or Signe.
Possibly from an Old High German name composed of the elements sigu "victory" and hild "battle", or perhaps derived from the Nordic name Signelill.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and njóta "to enjoy".
Derived from Spanish señora or Italian signora, both meaning "lady".
Short form of names beginning with the Germanic element sigu, such as Sigmund or Siegfried.
Variant of Sigisbert. Sigobert the Lame was a 6th-century king of Cologne and a grandson of Clovis I through his father Childebert I.
Possibly a feminine form of Sigerad. This was the name of a 7th-century Frankish saint, the mother of Saint Leodegarius and Saint Warinus.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and reifr "friendly, happy".
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert) combined with hraban or hramn "raven."

Old Norse name meaning "victory-bringer" or "inciter to victory", the first element from sigr "victory" (the second element perhaps related to drífa "driven snow, snowdrift"; compare Drífa). According to the 'Sigrdrífumál' of the Poetic Edda, this was an epithet of the valkyrie Brynhildr.
Possibly a variant of Sigrid or Signe.
Latvian and Lithuanian form of Sigrid.
Derived from the Germanic name elements sigr "victory" and ríkr "mighty, distinguished, rich".
Medieval English form of Old English Sigfriða, ultimately from Old Norse Sigríðr. This is a cognate to modern Scandinavian name Sigrid.

A name found on a presumed gaming piece of soap stone with a runic inscription, found under a road in Trondheim, Norway, and dating to the 12th century. Runologist Karen Langsholt Holmqvist has interpreted the inscription as a hitherto unknown name, Sigsífr. According to Niku Archaeology Norway, a direct translation of the name could be “Warriorbrother”, which could alternatively be seen as a name of the gaming piece itself. Alternatively, the name seems to use the elements of "sigr" which means victory in Old Norse, and "sifr", which means near relation/kinship. It could also be interpreted to mean Sif, the wife of Thor.
Derived from Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and þorn "thorn".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" combined with the name of the Norse god Þórr (see Thor).
Derived from Old Norse elements sigr 'victory' and Þórðr.

Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and *þrúðr, possibly from Proto-Norse *þrúþi "strength, power, force" (also appearing in myth as the name of the goddess Þrúðr, daughter of Þórr and Sif).
Variant of Sitona or a combination of sigr "victory" and Tona.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and tryggr "trusty, true, safe".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" combined with týr "god" (or the name of the Norse god Týr, which is identical).
Combination of Old Norse name elements sigr "victory" and unna "to love".
A knight slain by Tristan at a tournament in Ireland. Sigurano’s brother, Oris the Harsh, tried to avenge him but was also slain.
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and ást "love, affection".
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and the name Bára (which is derived from Old Norse bára "wave, billow").
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and bogi "bow (archery)". Coincides with the Icelandic word sigurbogi meaning "triumphal arch, gate of honour for parades to pass through".
Derived from Old Norse sigr meaning "victory" combined with ey meaning "island" or ey meaning "good fortune".
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" and gestr "guest". Also compare Gestur.
Derived from Old Norse sigr meaning "victory" and gríma meaning "mask, helmet".
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and the name Hanna 1.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and the name Hans. This was borne by Icelandic photographer Sigurhans Vignir (1894-1975).
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" and hjǫrtr "hart, stag, deer". Also compare Hjörtur.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and either lín "linen, flax" or Hlín.
Derived from Old Norse sigr meaning "victory" and logi meaning "flame, blaze". Also see Logi.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and the name Nanna 1.
Possibly a masculine form of Signý.
Combination of Old Norse sigr "victory" and the name Óli.
Siguròr, earl of Spain was the brother of Hríngr and Isolde the Dark. He gave his sister to Tristan (Tristram) when the latter conquered Spain.

Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" and ǫrn "eagle". This was the name given to a white-tailed eagle that was rescued from drowning by a 12-year-old girl in Kirkjufellslón lagoon in Iceland in 2006 (the eagle was found to have damaged tail feathers, was rehabilitated and returned to the wild); the incident received some media coverage in Iceland.
From the Old Norse elements sigr meaning "victory" and ósk meaning "wish" (compare Ósk).

Derived from the Icelandic words sigur meaning "victory" and rós "rose" (perhaps the Icelandic vernacular form of Rosa 1). The Icelandic band Sigur Rós is named for the younger sister of frontman Jónsi Birgisson (Sigurrós was born on the day the band was formed, and her name split into two words).
Faroese combination of sigr "victory" and sól "sun".
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr "victory" and sveinn "young man, boy, servant".
Derived from the Old Norse elements sigr meaning "victory" and veig meaning "strong, powerful". This is an Icelandic form of the Old Norse name Sigveig.
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" and veig "power, strength".
Old Norse variant and Norwegian form of Sigvæig.
Relatively new name (early 20th century) created by combining the popular name elements sig (Old Norse sigr) "victory" and vi (Old Norse vé) "holy".
Old Swedish and modern form of Sigviðr.
Derived from Old Norse sigr "victory" combined with Old Norse viðr "tree".
Modern form of the Old Norse name Sigvǫr, composed of the name elements sigr "victory" and vǫr "aware, cautious".
Formed from the Germanic name element sigu "victory" with an unknown second part.
Derived from Old High German sigu "victory" and wini "friend". This name was borne by two 9th-century dukes of Gascony.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سهام (see Siham) chiefly used in North Africa.
This is the name of King of Cambodia, Norodom Sihamoni.
Derived from Albanian si "as; like" and Gheg Albanian hanë, a variant of hënë "moon".
Ancient Egyptian masculine name meaning "Horus, he who seizes his power".
Means "have mercy on us" in Ndebele.

Proposed Amazigh (Berber) origin. Likely related to words for “spring; flowing water; springtime” — i.e., a natural water source and, by extension, renewal and fertility. In literary use, the name is famously borne by a character in Frank Herbert’s Dune (1965); within the novel’s Fremen lexicon it is glossed as “spring” / “springtime”, often interpreted as “desert springtime” (symbolizing life emerging in an arid landscape).In modern usage the name is rare; it appears primarily in discussions of Amazigh culture and in references to the Dune series.
Alternate transcription of Arabic سهام (see Siham) chiefly used in North Africa.
From Sino-Korean 時 (si) meaning "time, season, era, age" combined with 憲 (heon) meaning "constitution, statute, law". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Masculine name often found in Burkina Faso & neighboring regions.
From the Chinese 丝 (sī) meaning "silk" and 鸿 (hóng) meaning "wild swan, vast".
A medieval form of Sigtryggr. Sigtrygg Silkbeard was a Hiberno-Norse king of Dublin, known in Irish texts as Sihtric and Sitric.
From Sino-Korean 始 (si) meaning "begin, start" combined with 厚 (hu) meaning "thick". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 시헌 (see Si-heon).

column3: 시현(Korean Hangul)|時賢, 時憲, 施賢, 始炫, 是見, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 時 (si) meaning "time, era, season", 施 (si) meaning "grant, bestow, give", 始 (si) meaning "begin, start" or 是 (si) meaning "indeed, yes, right" combined with 賢 (hyeon) meaning "virtuous, worthy, able", 憲 (hyeon) meaning "law", 炫 (hyeon) meaning "shine, glitter" or 見 (hyeon) meaning "see, observe, perceive". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.

column3: 시현(Korean Hangul)|時賢, 時憲, 施賢, 始炫, 是見, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: Alternate transcription of Korean Hangul 시현 (see Si-hyeon).
Originally a short form of Siimon, used as a given name in its own right.
Estonian and Finnish form of Simon 1.
Variant of Sina or Zinaida. It can also be used as a diminutive for names ending -siina.

column3: 思憬, 思静, 思婧(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 憬 (jǐng) meaning "awaken", 静 (jìng) meaning "quiet, still, gentle" or 婧 (jìng) meaning "modest".
Feminine from of Sijmen. Some speculate that this name is the origin of the name Samantha.
Means "wealth opener" or "open the eyes of wealth" in Yoruba.
Alternate transcription of Urdu سکندر (see Sikandar).
Transferred use of the surname Sikena.
Means "one who rides a black horse" in Siksika.
Refers to a type of bird in the Wayuu language, spoken in South America.
Variant form of Sikke. Also compare Sico.
Belkis spelled backwards. It is used in Venezuela.
Croatian, Serbian, and Latvian form of Sixtus.
Means "attractive" in Telugu, Sindhi and Odia.

In the case of a male bearer, this name is probably (but not certain) a short form of a Germanic name containing the Old High Germanic element sigu "victory" (a younger form of Gothic sigis, see Sigisbert). It has also been spotted as a short name for Silvester. In the case of a female bearer, this name is most often seen as a short form for Cecilia.
Romanian and Italian form of Silas.

column3: ศิไลลักษณ์(Thai)
column12: Silailak (Thai: ศิไลลักษณ์) is a feminine Thai name derived from two Sanskrit-Pali roots: • “Silā” (ศิลา), meaning stone or rock, symbolizing strength, stability, and resilience. • “Lakkhana” (ลักษณ์), meaning mark, feature, or auspicious characteristic.Together, Silailak can be interpreted as “a woman with the noble qualities of stone” — someone who possesses enduring strength, inner beauty, and graceful character. The name reflects traditional Thai values that honor both fortitude and feminine elegance.
Means "virtues" in Caló. This name is used as the Caló form of Virtudes.
From Thai ศิลา (sila) meaning "stone, rock" and วรรณ (wan) meaning "colour, tint".
Spanish and Portuguese form of Silbannacus.
Possibly the name Silvanus with the suffix -acus. Silbannacus was an obscure Roman emperor or usurper.
This name is borne by Silda Wall Spitzer, wife of Eliot Spitzer.

Simply from the English word silence, from Middle English from Old French, from Latin silentium, from silere "be silent". A popular virtue name amongst the Puritans in the 17th century, it was usually given to girls (very occasionally to boys), ultimately taken from the admonition of Saint Paul: "Let the women learn in silence, with all subjection." Translated into Latin it became Tace, which "in its turn developed into Tacey". It was used by Pamela Belle for a Puritan character in her novels Wintercombe, Herald of Joy and Treason's Gift.
French form of Silenus. While as a mythologcial name, Silène is masculine, it is used as an exclusively feminine given name today.
Italian and Spanish form of Syleus.
The name Silesia is derived from the former Prussian province Silesia (in German: Schlesien).It is officially admitted in Germany.
Most likely a variant of Célésie. Note that Silésie conincides with the French word for "Silesia".
Etymology unknown. This is the name of the moon goddess of Nias Island, Indonesia.

Icelandic form of Silver. This is also the name of a rift formed in the Mid-Atlantic ridge between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates, located in the Þingvallavatn Lake in the Þingvellir National Park in Iceland.
Derived from Old Norse silfr "silver" and rún "secret lore, rune".
Means "silver" in Icelandic, from Old Norse silfr. It is a cognate of Silver.
Of uncertain origin and meaning. Theories include a variant of Selga, a variant of Ilga and a purely phonetic coinage.

A direct derivation of the Old Turkish word silig meaning "clean, pure, immaculate, flawless, and of high morals." It shares its linguistic heritage and structural elegance with historically famous cognates and sibling names such as Selçuk, Selcen, and Selin.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 恋 (liàn) meaning "love, yearn for".
Georgian form of Silvester via its hellenized form Silbestros.
Means "we are waiting" in Xhosa and Zulu.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 琉 (liú) meaning "sparkling stone".
Derived from the Latin word silo meaning "snub nose".

From the Macedonian mythology. It's a name of the mythical hero who transforms into stork and travels south in the distant lands. It has a bottle with magic liquid/water that transforms him back into human. But, one day he accidently breaks the bottle...
Simply form the English word silk.
Icelandic, Swedish and Sorbian form of Silke.
From the Scandinavian word silke meaning "silk".
From the word silken. Famous bearer is Canadian champion rower Silken Laumann (born 1964).
Medieval diminutive of Sibyl, via its short form Sill.
Up until the 17th century, Sill was a diminutive of Sybil and Silas. From the 17th century onwards, however, it became a diminutive of Puritan Silence.
Short form names ending in -silla and similar sounds, such as Priscilla and Drusilla.

A type of English frothy drink made of milk, cream, and wine.Sillabub also known as Jemina is a character in the musical Cats, written by Andrew Lloyd Webber based on the poetry of T. S. Eliot. The youngest member of the Jellicle cats, she is idealistic and very accepting of others. She becomes the first cat to accept the outcast Grizabella back into the tribe.
Pet form of Sigvaldr, Sighulfr, and other names starting with the name element sigr "victory".
From silma meaning "silver, shining white, crystal white" and rien, a variant of ien, meaning "maiden". This name was used by J.R.R. Tolkien.
Name of an 8th century Asturian king.

Derived from Siloé, which is the French, Portuguese and Spanish form of Siloam, the name of a spring mentioned in the New Testament which was the site of one of the miracles of Jesus: healing the man blind from birth.
From the utopian novel 'Titanus' (1959) by Eberhardt del'Antonio where Silona appears as an extra-terrestial medical doctor.The name was specifically used in German Democratic Republik (GDR).
Means "has kept us, has protected us" in Zulu.
Georgian form of Silvanus via its hellenized form Silouanos. A known bearer of this name was the Georgian sculptor Silovan Kakabadze (1895-after 1947).
Alternate transcription of Telugu శిల్పా, Kannada ಶಿಲ್ಪಾ, Malayalam ശിൽപ്പ or Tamil சில்பா (see Shilpa).

A name for the elder of the Two Trees of Valinor, the White Tree known most commonly as Telperion. This Tree shone with a shimmering light of silver-white, and that is the origin of the name Silpion, which comes from an old Elvish word sëlip for light of this kind. The Two Trees were destroyed, but Telperion ultimately gave rise to the Moon, and the word-forms behind the name Silpion lived on a name the Elves gave to the Moon: Isil.
Spanish form of Shilshah, which is borne by a male character in the Old Testament (1 Chronicles 7:37). It has occasionally been used as a Spanish feminine name.

Possibly derived from Latin silva, meaning "forest". Alternatively, it could be a contracted form of names derived from the same, such as Silvanus or Silvester, or, nicknames influenced by the English word silver, referring to the high value precious metal. Otherwise, the name may be a transferred use of the European surname Silva, itself derived from the same Latin root.The English name appears to have been most common in the late 19th to early 20th centuries, but has fallen out of common use in subsequent decades, likely due to the feminine connotation of related names like Silvia.
Derived from Silvanus. Used as a literary name in the 17th and 18th centuries; one example is the character of Silvander in Thomas Killigrew's play "Claricilla" (c 1641).
Variant of Silvana, this name was given in Brazil in the late 1970's.
Italian and Galician feminine form of Silverio.

A Disney character known as water-talent fairy who appears as a friend to Tinker Bell in Tinkerbell's cartoon films, in the ABC television show 'Once Upon a Time in Wonderland', and in Kinect Disneyland Adventures Pixie Hollow mini-game.Her name is a combination of the English words "silver" and "mist".
Languedocian and Gascon form of Silvester.
East Prussian German feminine form of Silvester as well as an obscure French feminine form of Sylvestre.
Romanian and Corsican form of Silvester.
Short form of Silvia, used as a given name in its own right.
English, German and Romanian form of Silvianus, also sometimes used in The Netherlands.
Romanian, Italian, Provençal, Spanish and Portuguese form of Silvianus.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Silvianus.
English and Picard form of Silvinus.

Possibly an elaboration of Old Norse silfr "silver" using the name suffix -lín, which may be derived from Old Norse lín "flax, linen". Alternatively it could be a Faroese form of Silvelin, a German diminutive of Silvia.
Vilamovian form of Silvester and Sylwester.
Anglicized form of Macedonian Силјан (see Siljan).
Derived from Aramaic שים "what is entrusted", this name is usually translated as "treasure, collection of valuable objects".
Spanish and Portuguese form of Symmachus.
Bulgarian, Croatian, Serbian and Slovene form of Symmachus.
si meaning "a little" and mala meaning "calamity" or "field, plantation".
Konkani form of Simon 1, via the Portuguese form Simão.
From Sanskrit स्मर (smara) meaning "memory, remembrance, recollection" and दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light".
From Sanskrit स्मर (smara) meaning "memory, remembrance, recollection" and जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਸਿਮਰਜੀਤ (see Simarjit).
From Sanskrit स्मर (smara) meaning "memory, remembrance, recollection" and ज्योतिस् (jyotis) meaning "light, brightness".
From Sanskrit स्मर (smara) meaning "memory, remembrance, recollection" and प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".
Means "treasure of life" in Mandaic, this is the name of the personification of life in Mandaeism and is also used as a feminine given name in Mandaean communities.

column3: 司马义, 司马宜(Chinese)|司馬義, 司馬宜(Traditional Chinese)
column12: Common Chinese transcription of Ismail used by Uygurs, inspired by surname Sima combined with given name Yi.
Variant of Sindbert. Derived from Old High German sind "way, path" combined with beraht "bright" meaning "bright path".
Italian and Spanish form of Simbert.
Means "One who strengthens or source of encouragement".
Possibly means "we need this", derived from Xhosa and Zulu dinga meaning "to need, to require".
Recently coined feminine form of Simon 1 and Simeon.
Possibly a rare feminine form of Similianus.
Perhaps a Slovene variant of Simon 1.
West Frisian form of Sigeman or Simon 1.
Feminization of Simeon with the popular suffix -ette.
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਸਿਮਰਜੀਤ (see Simarjeet).
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਸਿਮਰਜੀਤ (see Simarjeet).
Languedocian, Gascon and Russian form of Symphorianus.
Croatian and Slovene form of Symphorianus.
Lithuanian, Russian and Slovene form of Symphorosa.
From Sanskrit सिंहिका (sinhikā) referring to a willow-leaved justicia shrub (scientific name Justicia Gendarussa). In Hinduism this refers to the mother of Rahu and daughter of Daksha.
Languedocian, Provençal and Gascon form of Simeon as well as a Medieval Scandinavian variant of this name.

column3: 思渺, 丝淼, 鸶淼(Chinese)
column12: From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider", 丝 (sī) meaning "silk" or 鸶 (sī) meaning "eastern egret" and 渺 (miǎo) meaning "endlessly long, boundless" or 淼 (miǎo) meaning "wide expanse of water".
Possibly derived from Ancient Greek σιμός (simos) meaning "flat-nosed".
Feminine form and male diminutive form of Šime.

Means "follow me home" in Yoruba.Simidele Adeagbo is a Canadian-born Nigerian skeleton racer who competed at 2018 Winter Olympics. She is Nigeria and Africa’s first female skeleton athlete, as well as the first black female athlete in the sport of skeleton.
Possibly a variant form of Samael or even a short form of Jesimiel. According to Pope Saint Gregory I, this was the name of an archangel.
Derived from сим (sim) meaning "silver" and Khan.

In the "King Laurin Legend" Similde is the princess whom the dwarf king falls in love with and eventually abducts to his magical rose garden.Her name is a contracted form of Sigmilde, which is derived from Middle High German sige "victory" and milte "grace; clemency; kindness; endearment; tenderness; love".
Composed of the Lithuanian elements sim = simbolizuoti "to symbolize" and milti, pamilti "to love," hence "to symbolize love."
English form of Similianus. A bearer of this name was St. Similian of Nantes, a French bishop and saint from the 4th century AD. His feast day is on June 16.
Possibly derived from the Latin adjective similis meaning "similar, resembling, like".

column3: 思铭, 思明, 思鸣, 似铭, 似明, 似鸣, etc.(Chinese)|思銘, 思鳴, 似銘, 似鳴, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "to think" or 似 (sì) meaning "to resemble, to look like" combined with 明 (míng) meaning "bright, light, brilliant" or 鳴 (míng) meaning "to make a sound". Other hanzi combinations are also possible.
Elaborated form of the Romanian given name Simion.
Means "sun (shining) on the water" in Chuukese.
From the Persian sîm û zer meaning “silver and gold”.
Variant of Simias. This was the name of several Ancient Greek historical figures.
Diminutive of Simon 1, Simeon or other names with the sound sim.
Originally a short form of Simon 1, used as a given name in its own right.
Transferred use of the surname Simmons.
Short form of Simon 1 and perhaps also of Gerasime, Maksime, Onisime and Zosime.
Old Portuguese feminine form of Simão.
The name of the god of the river Simois, which passed the city of Troy on its way to join the Scamander river. Simoeis was a son of Oceanus and Tethys, and the father of Astyoche and Hieromneme.
Medieval Dutch form of Simon 1, which was most common in Flanders (Belgium).
Latinized form of Simoeis. In Greek mythology this was the name of a river flowing through Mount Ida near Troy, as well as the god or personification of the river.
Diminutive of Simona, used as a given name in its own right.
Feminine form of Simonas. In other words, this name is the Lithuanian equivalent of Simona.
Diminutive of Simone 1, as it contains the Dutch and Flemish diminutive suffix -ke.This name is exclusively used informally, meaning that it is not used as an official name on birth certificates.
Diminutive of Simone 2, as -etto is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix. Also compare Simonetta, which is the feminine equivalent of this name.

Serbian feminine form of Simonides. This name was borne by a daughter of the Byzantine emperor Andronikos II, Princess Simonida (1289-1340), born Simonis, who became the fourth wife of the Serbian king Milutin when she was five years old. She is the subject of a famous fresco and a Milan Rakić poem.
French form and Brazilian Portuguese variant of Simonida.
Possibly a blend of the name Simone 1 with Monique.

From Latin Simonis, which is the genitive of the third declension of Simon 1, the biblical Latin (and also Greek) form of the Hebrew name Shimon.In the Netherlands, this has been used as a Latin form of Simon (thus basically making it a latinization of a latinization) since at least late medieval times.
Italian name with the combination of Simon 1 and Luca 1. Famous bearer of this name is Italian football player Simonluca Agazzone.

Diminutive of Simonne, as it contains the Dutch and Flemish diminutive suffix -ke.A well-known bearer of this name is Simonne "Simonneke" Backx, one of the few remaining original characters from the Flemish soap opera Thuis (1995-). She is portrayed by the Flemish actress Marleen Merckx (b. 1958).
Combination of Simon 1 and Peter, given in reference to the Biblical character.
Medieval Italian diminutive of Simone 2, as -uccio is an Italian masculine diminutive suffix.
Medieval latinized form of Simon 1, which makes the name a double latinization, as Simon itself is already (biblical) Latin. Also compare Simonis.

As a masculine name (archaic), Simoon is a short form of Simonis and Simonus.As a feminine name (current), it is a short form of Simona and Simone 1. There are also cases where it is actually an alternate spelling of the latter name, made in order to ensure that the name is always pronounced in the French way (with two syllables) rather than in the Dutch way (with three syllables).
Diminutive of Simona, Simone 1 and Simoon, which is exclusively used informally.
Variant of Simua'i, si mua'i meaning "a first" in Samoan.
Variant of Sindbert.The name was borne as third given name by two Margraves of Baden-Baden.
Meaning "we have been given him/her" in Zulu.
this name goes far far back to around the begging of time
Roman cognomen which was derived from the Latin adjective simplex meaning "simple, plain".
French form of Simplicius. This was a middle name of Camille Desmoulins (1760-1794).
English form of Simplicianus. This was the name of a saint from the 4th century AD.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Simplician.
Italian and Spanish form of Simplicius.
This was the name of a Roman saint martyred during the persecutions of emperor Diocletian.
Transferred use of the surname Simpson.
From Punjabi ਸਿਮਰਨ (simran) meaning "continuous remembrance" (of Sanskrit origin) combined with Sanskrit दीप (dīpa) meaning "lamp, light".
From Punjabi ਸਿਮਰਨ (simran) meaning "continuous remembrance" (of Sanskrit origin) combined with Sanskrit जिति (jiti) meaning "victory, conquering".
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਸਿਮਰਨਜੀਤ (see Simranjeet).
From Punjabi ਸਿਮਰਨ (simran) meaning "continuous remembrance" (of Sanskrit origin) combined with Sanskrit प्रीति (prīti) meaning "pleasure, joy, love".
Means "service of the Father" in Ge'ez.
Variant transcription of Shimri, as used in 1 Chronicles 26:10.This transcription is used in The Webster Bible, Jubilee Bible 2000, King James Version, and Wycliffe Bible.
Means silver skin from 'sim' meaning silver and 'ten' meaning skin (both words are of Persian origin)
Bergamesque and Cremish Lombard form of Simon 1.
Norwegian variant of Sigmund, Sæmund and Simon 1 as well as a Judeo-Anglo-Norman adoption of this name.

From the name of a monstrous bird in Persian mythology, derived from Pahlavi sin "eagle" and murgh "bird". In the 11th-century epic the 'Shahnameh', Simorğ was a mighty bird who nursed the infant Zāl (father of Rostam).
Czech and Slovak diminutive of Simona. Also compare Simuška.
Czech and Slovak diminutive of Simona. Also compare Simuša.

In the Elamite pantheon, Simut was a herald god - although there are also sources who claim that he was a tutelary god (with one source even speculating that he might have been an astral deity). It is uncertain what the meaning of his name was in the Elamite language. He was married with the goddess Manzat and he was often referred to with an epithet that meant "God of Elam". At least three Elamite kings were named in his honour (which is consistent with the fact that nearly all rulers of Elam bore theophoric names).
Means "silver and gold", ultimately from Persian سیم (sim) meaning "silver", و (o) meaning "and" and زر (zar) meaning "gold".
Probably a form of the Gaelic Sìne or Síne, 'which normally becomes Sheena. Sina and Sinah were used in Britain between the 1890s and 1920s to some extent' (Dunkling & Gosling, 1986).
From Sino-Korean 信愛 (sin-ae), referring to devoted love (of God). Other hanja combinations are possible.
From native Korean 시내 (sinae) meaning "stream, brook, creek." It can also be a variant transcription of Sin-ae.
From Tagalog sinag meaning "ray of light, beam" and tala meaning "star".
Given in honor of the mountain from the book of Exodus.
Derived from place name Sinaí, which is the Spanish form of Sinai, the name of a mount and peninsula in Egypt.
German transliteration of Belarusian Зінаіда and Ukrainian Зінаїда (see Zinaida) as well as the Karelian and Estonian form of Zinaida.
Means "Sina with the crown" and "white/grey head" in Tongan. Sina is a variant of Hina 2.
Means "white lei of flowers" from sina "white, grey" and lei "flower garland".
Sinara is the secondary antagonist in the first half of the fifth season of Marvel's Agents of S.H.I.E.L.D..

Means "goddess or (white) moon of Samoa" from sina meaning "white" and masina meaning "moon". Sina is a goddess in Polynesian mythology. Or a contraction of Sinaoneosamoa meaning "white sand of Samoa". Sinasamoa is the daughter of chief Loa and chieftainess Sinaletigae in Samoan folklore. Sinasamoa is an archaic form of the word "cinnamon", modern word is kināmoni.
From Persian شناسی (shenāsī) meaning "science". This name was borne by İbrahim Şinasi, a 19th-century Ottoman intellectual and author.
Transferred use of the surname Sinatra.
From Σινατρούκης (Sinatroúkēs), A Hellenized of Old Iranian *sāna-taru-ka- meaning “enemy-conquering”. It could also be from Aramaic santū(ā) "senator" with an added Middle Iranian suffix -ūk.
Latinized form of Sinatroukes. This was the name of a king of the Parthian Empire from c. 75 BC to c. 69 BC.
Crimean Tatar name of unknown meaning.
Modern Hebrew name, a feminine form of Sinai. It was given to 8 baby girls born in the United States in 2011.
From the English word sincerely meaning "in a sincere manner".
Portuguese form of Syncletica. A bearer of this name was Sinclética Torres, was the first black woman to serve in the Portuguese parliament.
Etymology unknown, possibly from the Mandaic sinda meaning "seed, grain, dill, fennel".

Meaning uncertain. It might possibly be derived from Arabic or Persian سندار (sindar), which refers to a kind of large stone.One source states that this name means "bold, daring, courageous" but fails to explain the exact etymology.
Combination of Sindar with the Turkish military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".

Possibly a combination of a given name that starts with Sin- (such as Sinclair) with Darius.This name is best known for being the name of Sindarius Thornwell (b. 1994), an American professional basketball player.

Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with badu "battle."Mostly known from the tale "Sindbad the sailor" (The Book of One Thousand and One Nights). In this case, the name derives from the Persian name Sindbād ("Lord of the Sindh River").
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with Old High German beraht "bright."
Sindel is a fictional character in the Mortal Kombat fighting game series. She made her debut in Mortal Kombat 3 as the mother of Princess Kitana and the unwilling wife of the evil emperor Shao Kahn.
Referring to the refusal to sin.
Used in reference to denying sin and turning to God.
Derived from Gothic sinþs "way, path" and Ancient Germanic rēdaz, "counsel".Sindered was the last Archbishop of Toledo in Visigothic Hispania around the year 710.
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with rîcja "powerful, strong, mighty." The second element is also closely related to Celtic rîg or rix and Gothic reiks, which all mean "king, ruler."
From Sanskrit सिन्धु (sindhu) referring to the Indus River.

Ultimately derived from Sanskrit सिन्धु (síndhu) "Indus river, great river, sea" and राजन् (rā́jan) "king, prince". This was the name of an Indian king from the Paramara dynasty who is the father of Bhoja.
From Zulu sindisa meaning "save, redeem, rescue".
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with man "man."
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with Old High German mâri "famous."
Meaning unknown. Maybe a variant of Sandra or a feminine form of Sindri.
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with Old High German râd "counsel."
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with hraban or hramn "raven."
From the Gothic roots sinþs "way, path" and wulfs "wolf." This is the name of a 7th century hermit and saint who lived in the town of Aussonce near Rheims (France).
Derived from Gothic sinths "way, path" combined with Old High German wart "guard."

Short form of Germanic given names that contain the element sinths meaning "way, path", such as Chlodosind, Rudesind (see Rosendo) and Sindbald. But in the case of female bearers, the name can also be a short form of any name that ends in -sine, such as Gesine and Jensine.
Means "we have luck" in Zulu, from sine "we have" and inhlanhla "luck".
From Ottoman Turkish sine meaning "breast, bosom, heart" (from Persian سینه⁩) and Persian پرور⁩ (parvar), the present stem of پروردن⁩ (parvardan) meaning "to foster, nourish, cherish".
Spanish and Galician form of Synesius.

Unknown etymology, a modern hypothesis says that the name comes from the Old Norse signiutr or signjótr, where sig is "victory" and niutr or njótr is "enjoy". This name was borne by one of the brothers of Rurik, the founder of the Rurikid dynasty.

Variant of Sinfjötli. In Norse mythology, Sinfjötli was born from an incestuous relationship between Sigmund and his sister Signý. His stepmother Borghild poisons him, and his father takes his body to a fjord where Odin appears disguised as a ferryman and takes him to Valhalla.
Meaning unknown; possibly means "son of Seigeir or is a variant of Old High German Sintarvizzilo.
Italian and Spanish form of Symphora. There have probably also been cases where this name is a short form or contraction of Sinforiana, Sinforina and Sinforosa.
Spanish form of Symphoria. There have possibly also been cases where this name is a rare variant of Sinfora or a short form/corruption of Sinforiana and Sinforina.
Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Symphoriana.

Italian, Portuguese and Spanish form of Symphorianus. Known bearers of this name include the Spanish writer and politician Sinforiano López (1780-1815), the Spanish socialist politician Sinforiano Madroñero (1902-1936) and the Paraguayan archbishop Juan Sinforiano Bogarín (1863-1949).

Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Symphorina. There have possibly also been cases where this name is a corruption or a rare variant of Sinforiana.A known bearer of this name is the Mexican politician Irma Sinforina Figueroa Romero (b. 1945).
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Symphorinus. There have possibly also been cases where this name is a corruption or a rare variant of Sinforiano.
Spanish form of Symphorius. There have possibly also been cases where this name is a rare variant of Sinforo or a short form/corruption of Sinforiano and Sinforino.
Italian and Spanish form of Symphorus. There have probably also been cases where this name is a short form or contraction of Sinforiano, Sinforino and Sinforoso.
Italian, Spanish, Galician and Portuguese form of Symphorosa.
Masculinization of Sinforosa. A known bearer of this name was the Colombian botanist and politician Sinforoso Mutis Consuegra (1773-1822).
Greenlandic name derived from singarnaq meaning 'a yellowish grey wolf-like dog'.
From the name of the Southeast Asian country of Singapore.
Alternate transcription of Tibetan སེང་གེ (see Sangay).
Cantonese romanisation of Xingchi and other similarly pronounced names.
From a shortened form of Thai สิงหาคม (singhakhom) meaning "August", ultimately derived from สิงห์ (sing) meaning "lion, Leo (zodiac)" (itself of Sanskrit origin).
Singhe comes from the Sanskrit word siṃha, meaning "lion" or "hero."
From Lao ສິງ (sing) meaning "lion" and ຄຳ (kham) meaning "gold".
Transferred use of the surname Singleton.

The heroine of Swedish writer Viktor Rydberg's popular novel Singoalla (1858) (published in English as The Wind Is My Lover), about a gypsy girl who falls in love with a knight (set in the Middle Ages).
From the River Singwil in the Ranggira Region.
From Sino-Vietnamese 騁 (sính) meaning "to gallop, to run" or 娉 (sính) meaning "beautiful, charming".
Name - Sinh सिंह Origin- Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, sikh, Buddhist, Nepali, Sinhala MEANING - lion, "powerful one " ,eminent or heroic person
Name - Sinha सिंहा Origin - Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Sikh, Buddhist, Hindi MEANING - lions ,powerful one
Name- Sinhi सिंहीOrigin - Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, sikh, Buddhist, Nepali, Sinhala MEANING - lioness, a vein
From Sino-Vietnamese 生員 (sinh viên) meaning "student", composed of 生 (sinh) meaning "student" and 員 (viên) meaning "person".

Derived from the Old High German elements "sini" — meaning "victory" and "bald" — meaning "bold," "brave". While Sinibaldo is of Germanic origin, it came into use in Italy and other Romance-speaking regions during the Middle Ages. A famous bearer was Pope Innocent IV: Born Sinibaldo Fieschi, he was a canon of the Cathedral of Parma and later became Pope.
A War deity of the Berber
The name of a bandit killed by Theseus, who was the father of Perigune, who bore Theseus's son Melanippus.

Either a variant of Sintha, contracted form of Cynthia with popular suffix -ita; or a female variant of Sinnett from Anglo-Saxon name Sigenoth, also possibly a variant of Sunita, a Sanskrit name; or from sinittä, a plural form of Sini meaning "blue" in Finnish.
From Sino-Korean 信 "trust, believe" and 哉 "final exclamatory particle". A famous bearer is Korean author Kang Shin-jae (1924-2001).
Derived from the sino-korean 神 (sin) meaning "god, deity, spirit" and 靜 (jeong) meaning "calm, quiet".

The name of a giantess in the poem 'Fjǫlsvinnsmál' (a very late part of the Poetic Edda) whom scholars sometimes identify with the underworld goddess Hel. The second element of this obscure character's name is often thought to be Old Norse mara, which refers to a type of evil spirit or incubus in Germanic folklore. An alternative proposed meaning is "she who maims the sinews", based on Old Norse sina "sinew" and the hypothetic *mara "one who maims".
Means "rest in the lord" in Yoruba.
Variant of Cinnamon. This also coincides with a surname (see Sinnamon).

The name of a nymph of Mount Sinoe in Arkadia and the nurse of the god Pan. Her name is either derived from Mt Sinoe (or alternatively it may be named for her) or taken from the element σίνος (sinos) meaning "harm, hurt, mischief".
Derived from Macedonian синоличка (sinolička), a plant of the genus Viola.

Means "the mischievous", derived from Ancient Greek σίνος (sinos) "hurt, harm, mischief, injury", itself from σίνομαι (sinomai) "to hurt, damage, plunder". This was the name of the Greek warrior who convinced the Trojans to bring the Trojan Horse into their city, also called Sinopos.

From the name of the ancient city Sinope, derived from Hittite 𒅆𒉡𒉿 (Šinuwa) of unknown meaning. This was the name of a character from Greek mythology whom the city was supposedly named after, a daughter of Metope and Asopus, or in some accounts Ares. A moon of Jupiter was named after her.
Meaning unknown. The best known bearer of this name is Sinorice Moss (b. 1983), a former professional player of American football.

column3: 欣蓉, 新荣, etc.(Chinese)|新榮, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: Varient transcription of Xinrong (using Tongyong Pinyin).
From Tagalog sinta meaning "dear, darling, love, beloved".

Means "seven-eyed", deriving from the Hurrian elements šindi ("seven") and fur=i ("eye"). Name borne by a goddess associated with Šauška, who is mentioned as part of her entourage in several offering lists.
Meaning "what I have been through" or "what I have seen."
Means "iron tail" in Lakota. From the Lakota siŋté 'tail' and mázasapa (mah'-zah) 'iron'.
The name comes from Sint en Nicolaas or Klaas.

Sinthgunt is a figure in Germanic mythology, attested solely in the Old High German 9th- or 10th-century "horse cure" Merseburg Incantation. In the incantation, Sinthgunt is referred to as the sister of the personified sun, Sunna. The etymology of her name is uncertain: theories include a derivation based on Germanic *Sin-naχt-gund "the night-walking one". As a result of the pairing with Sunna, this etymology has been interpreted as a reference to the moon. This theory has since been disproved. Newer theories suggest a derivation from a Proto-Germanic compound *Senþa-gunþjō, the first element meaning "raid, (military) campaign", the second one "fight".
Slovene form of Cynthia and Hyacinthia.
Means "true, correct, right" in Toba Batak.

column3: 신우(Korean Hangul)|信雨, 信宇, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 信 (sin) meaning “truly, indeed, letter” combined with 雨 (u) meaning "rain" or 宇 (u) meaning "house, eaves, universe". Other hanja combinations can form this name as well.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 女 (nǚ) meaning "woman, girl".

From Egyptian zꜣ.nht meaning "son of the sycamore", derived from zꜣ "son" and nht "sycamore tree", a plant associated with the goddess Hathor. The last element has also been connected to the words nht "shelter, protection", nht "(magical) protection", nh "to escape (death)", and nhw "the protection of the king’s arm". This is the name of the titular character in ‘The Story of Sinuhe’, a work of ancient Egyptian literature dating back to at least 1800 BCE.
Spanish form of Sinuhe, which has occasionally been used as a given name in Mexico.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 诺 (nuò) meaning "promise, approve".
Means "cream-coloured" in Khmer. Also indicates a type of flower.
Short form or diminutive of Aksinya and Yevfrosiniya.

column3: 欣怡, 心怡, 馨仪, etc.(Chinese)|欣怡, 心怡, 馨儀, etc.(Traditional Chinese)
column12: Cantonese romanisation of Xinyi, or other names with the same pronunciation.
Means "Sin granted offspring", deriving from the Akkadian element zēru ("seed; offspring; sown, arable land").
Diminutive form of Sibéal or Isibéal.
Most likely related to the word "peace". Compare Siochain "peace" and Siodhachain

Derived from Irish síodhach "peaceful" or "otherworldly" combined with a diminutive suffix. The adjective síodhach is a variant of sítheach, from síth, basically meaning "settlement", hence both "peace" and "place inhabited by other world beings".

A minor goddess of love, or rather of young love, in Germanic Mythology.Some scholars argue that she might be identical with Sjöfn, Frigg's handmaid, from Norse mythology who in the Prose Edda book Gylfaginning is described as being "concerned to direct people's minds to love, both women and men."
Original Scottish Gaelic form of Sholto.

column3: 시언(Korean Hangul)|시온(Korean Hangul)|始溫, 詩溫, 始穩, 詩穩, etc.(Korean Hanja)

column12: Feminine form of Sion. This name was borne by Siona (or Sionah) Tagger (1900-1988), an Israeli painter who is regarded as the first Israeli-born woman artist.
Could be a variant of Sianne, influenced by Dionne. It could also be derived from the name of a town in France's Lorraine region.
Diminutive of any name ending in -cion.
The name of a Native American people, used as a variant of Sue. Considered offensive amongst some Natives.
Variant of Susie, made famous by the British rock band Siouxsie & The Banshees. This name is considered offensive to the Sioux Nation.
From the Egyptian tꜣ-špst meaning "the noblewoman".
Means "we are surviving hardships" in Ndebele.
Means "freedom, joyful, hard worker" in Xhosa and Zulu.
Means "they (cows) face each other" in Bandial.
Likely from the Frisian word sip meaning "Small" with kje added to indicate a diminutive.
Croatian and Georgian form of Zipporah.

Sippai (also spelled Saph) was a Philistine giant and descendant of the Rephaim, an ancient giant race. He's mentioned in the Old Testament as a formidable warrior who was slain by Sibbechai the Hushathite during a battle at Gezer. Not to be confused with Saph, short for Sapphire. This translates to "threshold," "basin," or "silver cup."
The stage name of blues singer Sippie Wallace, born Beulah Thomas. Sippie was a nickname she gained in childhood, as a gap between her two front teeth meant that she "sipped" on food and drink.
Scandinavian variant and Azerbaijani form of Zipporah.
Bosnian variant form of Zipporah attested in Bosnian Sephardic communities.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 茜 (qiàn) meaning "madder" or "reeds".

In Iñupiaq (also known as Inupiat), this name means "the return of the sun after the long darkness." In the TV series True Detective: Night Country, this is the cultural name bestowed on co-protagonist Evangeline Navarro by her deceased mother in a vision.

Possibly from the title "Sir", typically used to address any male whose name is unknown or out of respect, or who is of a higher rank, or who has been bestowed the title ('knighted') by royalty. Derived from the Old French sire 'master, sir, lord', from the Latin senior 'older, elder'.

column3: 시라(Korean Hangul)|始路, 始羅, etc.(Korean Hanja)
column12: From Sino-Korean 始 (si) meaning "begin, start" combined with 路 (ra) meaning "road, path, journey" or 羅 (ra) meaning "net, silk". Other hanja combinations are also possible.
Alternate transcription of Siraj, mainly used in Dutch-influenced regions of the continent.
Name of the book of the Bible in the Old Testament, from the name Sira.
Means "chronicle, biography, way of life, conversation" in Arabic.
Means "lamp of the religion" from Arabic سراج (sirāj) meaning "lamp, light, lantern" combined with دين (dīn) meaning "religion, faith".
Alternate transcription of Arabic سراج الدين (see Siraj ad-Din).
Alternate transcription of Arabic سراج الدين (see Siraj ad-Din), as well as the usual Dari Persian, Malay and Indonesian form.
Azerbaijani and Talysh form of Sherali.
French contracted or vernacular form of Sigiramnus.
From Armenian սէր (ser) meaning "love" and արփի (arpʿi) meaning "sun".
French transcription of Sirarpi. A known bearer was Sirarpie Der Nersessian (1896-1989), an Armenian art historian.
A respelling of Cyrus a Persian king from ancient Persia.
Kazakh, Tatar, Bashkir and Dagestani form of Siraj
Of debated origin and meaning. Current theories include a variant of Sigreda and a feminine form of Sired, the medieval English form of Old English Sigeræd.
Another name of Goddes LaXmi, Wife of Hindu lord VishnuSanskrit
Derived from Estonian sireli, the genitive form of sirel, "lilac".
Meaning uncertain. The name is possibly derived from Sirem, which is the Turkish name for Syrmia, a region of the Pannonian Plain in Europe.

Of debated origin.Some scholars argue that it might be a contracted form of Severine, others theorize a derivation from the Scandinavian name Sirin, while another theory assumes a derivation from Greek Seirenes (Σειρῆνας), the sirens or nymphs from Greek mythology.Whatever theory might be true, in Norway this name was first recorded in the late 1700s.

Derived from Spanish sirena "mermaid". The Spanish dramatist Jacinto Benavente used this name in his play 'Los intereses creados' (1907), where it belongs to a poor widow and matchmaker called Doña Sirena.
Russian transcription of Syrhiy or Sirhiy.
Means "wolf" or "lion" (a dialectal word) in Arabic.
From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" and ชัย (chai) meaning "victory".
From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" and โชค (chok) meaning "luck, fortune".
Derived from Sirius. This is the name of a pope (334-399).

column3: ศิริกานต์, สิริกานต์(Thai)
column12: From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" or สิริ (siri) meaning "fortune, grace, luck" and กานต์ (kan) meaning "dear, beloved".

column3: ศิริกานต์, สิริกานต์(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริกานต์ or สิริกานต์ (see Sirikan).

Means "glory of Kitiyakara" from Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" and กิติ์ (kit) referring to the royal house of Kitiyakara descended from Thai prince Kitiyakara Voralaksana. This was the name of a former queen of Thailand (1932-2025), who was the first wife of king Bhumibol Adulyadej.
Combination of Siri and hildr "battle, fight" or a combination of Siri and any name ending in -il.
English variant of Serena and Scandinavian variant of Sirin.
Probably from Thai สิริ (sì-rí) meaning "fortune, luck".
Alternate transcription of Thai สิริพรรณ (see Siriphan).
From Thai สิริ (siri) meaning "fortune, grace, luck" and พรรณ (phan) meaning "kind, variety, type".
Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริพล (see Siriphon).

column3: ศิริพร, ศิริพล(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริพร (see Siriporn). It can also be written as ศิริพล, which is a masculine name, from Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" and พล (phon) meaning "strength, power".
Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริพล (see Siriphon).

column3: ศิริพร, ศิริพล(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริพร (see Siriporn) or ศิริพล (see Siriphon).

column3: ศิริรัตน์, สิริรัตน์(Thai)
column12: From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" or สิริ (siri) meaning "fortune, grace, luck" and รัตน์ (rat) meaning "gem, jewel".
Mesopotamian goddess of beer and the mother of Zu; a large bird that can breathe fire and water.Her name is said to be derived from Akkadian sirašu "brewer".

column3: ศิริศักดิ์(Thai)
column12: From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" and ศักดิ์ (sak) meaning "power".
Another name for the Hindu goddess, Parvati.
Possibly an elaborated form of Syritha.

column3: ศิริวรรณ, สิริวรรณ(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริวรรณ or สิริวรรณ (see Siriwan).

column3: สิริวัณณวรี(Thai)

column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริวัฒน์ (see Siriwat).

column3: ศิริวิมล, สิริวิมล(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริวิมล or สิริวิมล (see Siriwimon).

column3: ศิริวิมล, สิริวิมล(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริวิมล or สิริวิมล (see Siriwimon).

column3: ศิริวรรณ, สิริวรรณ(Thai)
column12: From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" or สิริ (siri) meaning "fortune, grace, luck" and วรรณ (wan) meaning "colour, caste".
From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" and วัฒน์ (wat) meaning "prosperity, growth, development".

column3: ศิริวิมล, สิริวิมล(Thai)
column12: Alternate transcription of Thai ศิริวิมล or สิริวิมล (see Siriwimon).

column3: ศิริวิมล, สิริวิมล(Thai)
column12: From Thai ศิริ (siri) meaning "glory, splendour" or สิริ (siri) meaning "fortune, grace, luck" and วิมล (wimon) meaning "clean, clear, pure, chaste".
Finnish form and Estonian variant of Sirje.
Variant spelling of Cirka. From the Danish Word Cirka, meaning about or around (adverb.) This name submitted along with Cirka, because I'm not sure about how they spelled it.

Directly taken from the Finnish word sirkku "bunting (the bird)"."Prinsessa Lumisirkku ja kääpiöt" (Princess Lumisirkku and the dwarfs) used to be the Finnish title of the fairy tale "Snow White" before the princess' name was changed to Lumikki.
Short form of names containing the Turkmen şir meaning "lion".
Commonly understood as a variant of Sirje, this name may also be inspired by the Estonian word sirel "lilac".
Probably composed from the English words sir and lord.

Derived from Bulgarian сърма "golden thread; silver thread; filigree". Sirma Voyvoda (1776–1864), was a Bulgarian rebel soldier. Disguised as a man, she participated in the guerilla movement in Ottoman Vardar Macedonia between 1791 and 1813.
From Persian شیر (shir) meaning "lion" and مرد (mard) meaning "man".
Means "lazy". This is the name of a Jotunn.
Means "petite, graceful, delicate, slender" in Finnish. More commonly used as a surname
From the Arabic sarq meaning "east" it is the name of the strong, hot wind that blows from Africa across the Mediterranean.
Uzbek and Tajik form of Siraj al-Din.

Uncertain etymology. Possibly derived from Ancient Greek σειρά (seira) meaning "cord, rope", or perhaps σείριος (seirios) meaning "the scorcher; dog-star" (see Sirius). Siro was an Epicurean philosopher who lived in Naples. He was a teacher of Virgil.
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider" and 蓉 (róng) meaning "hibiscus".
Polish form of Siroslav, a variant of Syroslav.
Referring to "Sirs, what must I do to be saved?"
Finnish version of Sigrid. In Finnish language it means "fragment".
Its origin in Kurdish and Persian is called "Sirwan", meaning 'roaring sea' or 'shouting river', as well as being the name of an ancient city near Ilam city in Iran.
Old High German sisu "lament, song" + Old High German beraht, Old Saxon berht "bright" from Proto-Germanic berhtaz.
Irish form of Cecil, from Latin Caecilius, thus making it a masculine form of Síle.

The first element of this Germanic name is derived from sis, which is probably a contraction of sigis (see Sigisbert). However, this is not completely certain - the element might also come from Old High German sisesang "sad song" or from Old Swedish sisu "solemn lament." The second element is derived from Old High German bald "bold, brave."

The first element of this Germanic name is derived from sis, which is probably a contraction of sigis (see Sigisbert). However, this is not completely certain - the element might also come from Old High German sisesang "sad song" or from Old Swedish sisu "solemn lament." The second element is derived from Old High German beraht "bright."

The first element of this Germanic name is derived from sis, which is probably a contraction of sigis (see Sigisbert). However, this is not completely certain - the element might also come from Old High German sisesang "sad song" or from Old Swedish sisu "solemn lament." The second element is derived from Gothic biutan "to offer" or Old High German boto "bid, offer."
Variant of Sisebod. Sisebut was the name of a 7th-century king of the Visigoths in Hispania.
Italian and Spanish form of Sisebut.

The first element of this Germanic name is derived from sis, which is probably a contraction of sigis (see Sigisbert). However, this is not completely certain - the element might also come from Old High German sisesang "sad song" or from Old Swedish sisu "solemn lament." The second element is derived from Old High German mund "protection."

The first element of this Germanic name is derived from sis, which is probably a contraction of Gothic 𐍃𐌹𐌲𐌹𐍃 (sigis) "victory" (see Sigisbert). However, this is not completely certain - the element might also come from Old High German sisesang "sad song" or from Old Swedish sisu "solemn lament." The second element is derived from Gothic nand "bravery" (or from Gothic nanthjan "to venture, to risk, to dare"). Sisenand was the name of a 7th-century king of the Visigoths in Hispania.
Italian, Spanish and Portuguese form of Sisenand.
Sisera was commander of the Canaanite army of King Jabin of Hazor, who is mentioned in Judges 4-5 of the Hebrew Bible.
Old High German sisu "lament, song" + Old High German rih "ruler".
From the Chinese 思 (sī) meaning "think, consider, ponder" and 珊 (shān) meaning "coral".
Variant of Cici, more often used for names beginning with or containing the letter s.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Sisyphos via its latinized form Sisyphus.
Italian form of Sisyphos via its latinized form Sisyphus.
Latinized form of Saessyllt and Seisyllt. This was the name of three legendary Kings of the Britons as accounted by Geoffrey of Monmouth.
Feminine form of Sisinio. St. Sisinio is a Catholic saint celebrated on November 23rd.
Spanish and Portuguese form of Sisinnius.
Sardinian form of Late Latin Sisinnius.
Means "it is a gift" in Zulu and Xhosa.
Means "being torn apart". It was given to protect child from evil spirits.
Variant of Cisly. It might also be a borrowing of Sisile.
Old High German sisu "lament, song" + Old Saxon mund, Old High German munt "hand, protection"
Hellenized form of Sisoy.A notable bearer of this name is the Coptic saint Sisoes the Great († 429 AD).
From Lao ສີສົມ (sisom) meaning "orange (the colour)" and ພອນ (phone) meaning "blessing".

Meaning unknown. It is perhaps related to the Old Georgian compound word სისვისფერს (sisvispers) meaning "colourful, full of colour". The modern Georgian equivalent of the elements in that word are სისავსის (sisavsis) meaning "of fullness" (genitive of სისავსე (sisavse) meaning "fullness") and ფერი (peri) meaning "colour". Also compare the modern Georgian compound word ცისფერი (tsisperi) meaning "sky blue" or more literally, "celestial colour".A known bearer of this name was the Georgian outlaw Sisona Darchia (1860-1891).
Derived from Egyptian Ṯȝy-ḏy meaning "the bearer of the hairlock", which was an epithet of Harpocrates.
Originally an Old Norse diminutive of Sigþrúðr, this name is now a diminutive of Cecilia. As a Swedish name, it was traditionally found in Scania.

Diminutive of Cecilia, Elisabet and names beginning Si-. Specifically, it is a nickname of Empress Elisabeth of Austria popularised through the film "Sissi" (1955).Sissi is also Finnish for "guerrilla" and a type of training in the Finnish Defence Forces and the Finnish Border Guard.
Most likely a combination of Sissie and Retta. This name was borne by Sissieretta Jones (1868-1933), an American opera singer (whose mother's name was Henrietta).
Diminutive of Athanasia, Anastasia and Aspasia.

Derived from the English noun sister meaning "sister". Like in most countries with a culture and language that is ultimately Germanic in origin, this name first started out as an affectionate nickname for a female sibling (who was often older in age, such as the first-born daughter and therefore eldest sister) and over time (due to frequent usage) transformed into an actual given name.Also compare the names Suster, Syster and Zuster, which are all cognates of this name.

From Italian sistino "of or pertaining to Pope Sixtus", referring to the Sistine Chapel in the Apostolic Palace, which was named after Pope Sixtus IV (1414-1484), for whom it was built. This is borne by American actress Sistine Stallone (b. 1998), the daughter of actor Sylvester Stallone (b. 1946).
Corsican and Sicilian form of Sixtus.
From Thai ศรี (si) meaning "glory, honour, splendour" and สุดา (suda) meaning "daughter, woman, lady".
Irish adoption of Cecily. Unlike Síle, however, this name does not seem to have survived the Middle Ages.
Old High German sisu "lament, song" + Old High German wolf, Gothic wulf "wolf".
From Javanese siswa meaning "student, pupil", ultimately from Sanskrit शिष्य (śiṣya).
From Javanese siswa meaning "student, pupil" combined with either the masculine suffix -na or the word ana meaning "being, having, holding".
Sisygambis was an Achaemenid queen consort, the mother of Darius III, and was a friend of Alexander the Great and Hephaestion. This name is of uncertain etymology.
French form of Sisyphos via its latinized form Sisyphus.
Variant transcription of Sitt. This name was borne by Sit al-Berain, the mother of Anwar Sadat, 3rd President of Egypt.

Possibly means "diversion of God", derived from Hebrew סְטִייָּה (setiya) meaning "diversion, digression, deviation" combined with אֵל (ʾel) meaning "God". This is the name of an angel belonging to the order of the Seraphim. He is one of the 72 angels bearing the explicit name of God (the Shem HaMephorash), as interpreted by some Christian Kabbalists.

Hellenised form of the Thracian name *Sitalkas, derived from Thracian *si and‎ *talkas meaning "striker, pusher". Possibly influenced by Ancient Greek Σιτάλκας (Sitalkas) meaning "protector of wheat". This was the name of two Thracian kings.
Telugu feminine name derived from the name of the goddess Sita and the word అమ్మ (amma) meaning "mother".
