From Kyrgyz сүйүн (süyün) meaning "joyful, glad, happy" combined with the Turkic military title beg meaning "chieftain, master".
音 - Sound 鈴 - Bell 羽 - FeatherA famous bearer is the time-traveller Amane Suzaha from the anime and visual Steins;Gate

column3: 朱雀(Japanese Kanji)|すざく(Japanese Hiragana)|スザク(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name is used as 朱雀, referring to the Vermilion Bird, one of the Four Symbols of the Chinese constellations, that is said to rule over the southern heavens. It is made up of 朱 (shu, ake, su) meaning "vermillion, cinnabar" and 雀 (jaku, jan, saku, shaku, suzume) meaning "sparrow."Fictional bearers of this name include Suzaku Kururugi (枢木 スザク) from the anime series Code Geass: Lelouch of the Rebellion and Suzaku (朱雀), one of the Four Beasts from the manga and anime series Yū Yū Hakusho.This name is rarely used.
English variant and Gallo form of Suzanne.

Suzel is the name of a main character in 'L'amico Fritz', an opera by Pietro Mascagni, premiered in 1891 from a libretto by P. Suardon (Nicola Daspuro, with additions by Giovanni Targioni-Tozzetti) based on the French novel 'L'ami Fritz' by Émile Erckmann and Pierre-Alexandre Chatrian.
A word meaning pure, cleanest. The root of the word comes from the verb "to filter(in Turkish süz-".Nowadays (as a misuse) it is also used to mean drawn out, sick, tired.It is Old Turkic

column3: 素真, 素珍, 素嫃, 素贞, etc.(Chinese)
column12: From Chinese 素 (sù) meaning "plain, simple" combined with 真 (zhēn) meaning "real, genuine, true", 珍 (zhēn) meaning "precious, rare", 嫃 (zhēn), a meaningless character used in feminine names, or 贞 (zhēn) meaning "virtuous, chaste, loyal". Other character combinations can form this name as well.

Suzine Har Nicolescu (March 21, 1931 – February 22, 2013) was an American librarian who was one of the founders of the Asian Pacific American Librarians Association (APALA). She served fourteen years as the chief librarian at Medgar Evers College and fought against discrimination in the library profession.

column3: 鈴空, 鈴愛, 鈴亜, 涼愛, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell" or 涼 (suzu) meaning "cool, refreshing" combined with 空 (a) meaning "sky", 愛 (a) meaning "love, affection" or 亜 (a) meaning "second, Asia". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: すずえ(Japanese Hiragana)|鈴江, 鈴絵, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" and 枝 (e) meaning "bough, twig, branch" or 江 (e) meaning "inlet, river". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: おぶない(Japanese Hiragana)|涼羽, 紗羽, 涼葉, 鈴巴, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 紗 (suzu) meaning "gossamer, silk gauze" and 巴 (ha) meaning "comma". Other kanji combinations can be used.
From 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" and 日 (hi) meaning "day, sun". Other kanji combinations can be used.
From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell" combined with 彦 (hiko) meaning "boy, prince". Other kanji combinations are also possible.
From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" combined with 姫 (hime) meaning "princess". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 涼一, 鈴人, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" and 人 (hito) meaning "person". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: すずほ(Japanese Hiragana)|鈴宝, 紗峯, 篠歩, 涼帆, 凉穂, 錫星, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 涼 (suzu) meaning "cool breeze, refreshing" and 宝 (ho) meaning "treasure, valuable objects". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 鈴依, 鈴井, 鈴姫, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell" combined with 依 (i) meaning "rely on", 井 (i) meaning "well" or 姫 (i) meaning "princess". Other kanji combinations are also possible.
From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" combined with 一 (ichi) meaning "one". Other kanji combinations are possible.
From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "chime, bell" and 鹿 (ka) meaning "deer". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: 涼風, 鈴風, etc.(Japanese Kanji)|すずかぜ(Japanese Hiragana)|スズカゼ(Japanese Katakana)
column12: From 涼風 (suzukaze) meaning "cool breeze." The first kanji can be replaced with one that is read suzu (or two kanji that make up that reading), e.g. 鈴 meaning "bell."This name is extremely rare.

column3: スズキ(Japanese Katakana)|すずき(Japanese Hiragana)|鈴木(Japanese Kanji)
column12: Transferred use of the surname Suzuki.
From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "chime, bell" and 子 (ko) meaning "child". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: スズミ(Japanese Katakana)|鈴美, 涼海, 凉美, 鈴見, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" or 涼/凉 (suzu) meaning "cool, refreshing" combined with 美 (mi) meaning "beautiful". Other kanji combinations are also possible.
From Japanese 進 (suzumu) meaning "advance, make progress", as well as other kanji or kanji combinations having the same pronunciation.This name is another form of Susumu.

column3: すずな(Japanese Hiragana)|スズナ(Japanese Katakana)|すず菜, すず奈, すず那(Kanji/Hiragana)|鈴菜, 鈴苗, 涼梨, 涼那, 涼雪, 朱々奈, 珠々奈, 珠洲菜, 寿々七, 寿々奈, 素寿南, 珠沙, 涼茄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "chime, bell" combined with 菜 (na) meaning "vegetables, greens". Other combinations of kanji characters can form this name.

column3: すずね(Japanese Hiragana)|鈴音, 涼音, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" and 音 (ne) meaning "sound". Other kanji combinations can be used.

column3: すずの(Japanese Hiragana)|紗乃, 錫乃, 清乃, 涼乃, 鈴乃, 錫野, 涼野, 鈴望, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 紗 (suzu) meaning "gauze, thin silk", 錫 (suzu) meaning "tin", 清 (suzu) meaning "pure", 涼 (suzu) meaning "cool, refreshing" or 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell" combined with 乃 (no), a possessive particle, 野 (no) meaning "area, field" or 望 (no) meaning "hope". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: すずお(Japanese Hiragana)|スズオ(Japanese Katakana)|鈴男, 鈴夫, 鈴雄, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 鈴 (suzu) meaning "chime, bell" combined with 男 (o) meaning "male", 夫 (o) meaning "man, husband" or 雄 (#o) meaning "hero, manly". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: すずら(Japanese Hiragana)|珠洲羅, 涼良, 鈴蘭, 鈴良, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 珠 (su) meaning "pearl", 洲 (zu) meaning "continent" combined with 羅 (ra) meaning "lightweight fabric". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 鈴蘭, 涼蘭(Japanese Kanji)|すずらん(Japanese Hiragana)|スズラン(Japanese Katakana)
column12: This name can used as 鈴蘭, referring to the flower known as the lily of the valley, made up of 鈴 (rin, rei, suzu) meaning "bell" and 蘭 (ra, ran) meaning "orchid." Alternatively, the first kanji can be replaced with 涼 (ryou, suzu.mu, suzu.shii/yaka, usu.i, hiya.su, makotoni) meaning "cool, refreshing."

column3: 錫太郎, 鈴太郎, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 錫 (suzu) meaning "tin" or 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell", 太 (ta) meaning "thick, big" combined with 郎 (rou) meaning "son". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 涼夜, 鈴夜, 鈴弥, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From Japanese 涼 (suzu) meaning "cool, refreshing" or 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell" combined with 夜 (ya) meaning "night" or 弥 (ya) meaning "universally". Other kanji combinations are possible.

column3: 鈴代, 涼代, etc.(Japanese Kanji)
column12: From 鈴 (suzu) meaning "bell, chime" or 涼 (suzu) meaning "refreshing, cool" combined with 代 (yo) meaning "generation". Other kanji combinations can be used.A notable bearer is Suzuyo Takazato who is a Japanese politician.
Variant of Souzy, influenced by the unrelated English name Suzy.
Variant and feminine form of Svæinn.
Ancient Scandinavian with the combination of sveinn "young man, boy" and heiðr "honour".

Meaning uncertain, possibly "Swabian woman" or "woman from Schwaben" from Old Norse svabar "Swabians", from the name of a Germanic (Suebic) tribe which allegedly derived from Old German swēba "free, independent". In the Eddic poem 'Helgakviða Hjörvarðssonar', this was the name of a Valkyrie who would be reborn as Sigrún.
Derived from the Lithuanian noun svaja meaning "dream, daydream". Also see Svajonė.
It's a Lithuanian name derived from the Lithuanian word “svajonė” (“dream”) or the verb “svajoti” (“to dream”).
MEANING : beautiful eyed, a name of lord Vishnu, having beautiful axle .Here सु means beautiful + अक्ष means eye, axle

From the Norwegian word svale meaning "swallow", which in turn comes from the Old Norse svala of the same meaning (see Svala ). It also coincides with the Scandinavian word sval meaning "cool", "chill". It is borne by a popular Norwegian pop singer Sval Rosenlöw Eeg.
Derived from Old Norse svala "swallow (bird)". This name is also considered a short form of Svalaug.
the Norwegian word for a bird part of the Hirundinidae family the swallow.
Derived from Old Norse svala meaning "swallow (bird)" and rún meaning "secret lore, rune".
Derived from Hindi svāmī (स्वामी) meaning "master, lord, owner," from Sanskrit svāmin (स्वामिन्), used as an honorific title for yogis initiated into the religious monastic order in Hinduism.
Newer form of Svanlaug, a combination of Old Norse svanr "swan" and laugr "promised".
Norweigan and Faroese younger form of Svanbjǫrg.
From Old Norse svanr meaning "swan" combined with bjǫrg meaning "help, save, rescue".
From the Old Norse elements svanr meaning "swan" and bjǫrn meaning "bear".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and bjartr "bright".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" combined with bjǫrg "help, salvation" or possibly borg "stronghold, fortification, castle".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and dís "goddess; woman, lady; seeress".
Combination of the Old Norse name elements svanr "swan" and ey "island; flat land along a coast" or ey "good fortune".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and fríðr "beautiful, beloved".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and holmr "small island".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and hvítr "white". In Norse mythology this was an epithet of the valkyrie Hlaðgunnr.

Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and laug possibly meaning "vowed, promised, bound in oath", a derivative of Proto-Germanic *-lauʒ- "to celebrate marriage; to swear a holy oath; to be dedicated; promised (in names)".
Old Norse name and byname, from Old Norse svanr meaning "swan".
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and rós "rose".
Norwegian combination of svanr "swan" and rún "secret".
Combination of Old Norse svanr "swan" and Þór.
Derived from the Old Norse elements svanr "swan" and þrúðr "strength".
Short form of Svanhild and other names beginning with Svan or Swan.
From the Sanskrit स्वर (svara) meaning "noise, sound, musical pitch".
Means "slayer". This is a kenning for both Odin and "snake".
Name of Little Svarog, god of fire and war. This is also English variant name for god (compare Svarozhits).
Bulgarian variant of Svarozhich. This is also English name for Svarozhich.
Ukrainian and Belarusian form of Svarozhich.
Serbo-Croat-Bosnian form of Svarozhich. This is also German name of Svarozhich.
Slovene and Slovak form of Svarozhich. Also Dutch name of Svarozhich and Czech variant of Svarožic.
Combination of Old Norse svartr "black" and geirr "spear".
Means "slippery place". In Norse mythology Svadi is a giant, the father of Hadda and the owner of Svaðilfari.
Masculine form of Svava and younger form of Svávarr.

Means "waving one" in Old Norse. Sveigðir was a legendary Swedish king, son of Fjǫlnir and father of Vanlandi. He appears in the epic works 'Heimskringla' and 'Ynglinga saga' written in the 13th century by Snorri Sturluson. Sveigðir also appears in the 9th century poem 'Ynglingatal', possibly written by the Norwegian skald Þjóðólfr ór Hvini.
Old Norse form of Svyatoslav. It was used to refer to Svyatoslav I Igorevich.
Derived from the Old Norse elements sveinn "boy" and herr "army", perhaps inspired by Einar.
Derived from the Old Norse elements sveinn "boy, servant" and bjartr "bright".
Derived from the Old Norse elements sveinn meaning "boy" and bjǫrg meaning "help, save, rescue". Also compare the Swedish name Svenborg.
From the Old Norse name Sveinbjǫrn, which was derived from the Old Norse elements sveinn "young man" and bjǫrn "bear".
From the Old Norse elements sveinn "young man" and dís "goddess".
From Old Norse sveinn meaning "young man" combined with ey meaning "island" or ey meaning "good fortune".
From Old Norse sveinn "young man" and fríðr "beautiful".
Combination of Old Norse sveinn meaning "young man, youth" and the name Jón.
Former Norwegian dialectal variant of Sveinulf.
Derived from Old Norse sveinn "young man" and rún "secret lore, rune".
From Old Norse sveinn "young man" combined with the name of the Norse god Þórr (see Thor). In other words, this is a combination of Sveinn and Þór.
Norwegian combination of sveinn "boy" and ulfr "wolf"
Derived from the Old Norse elements sveinn "boy, servant" and veig "strength".
Possibly means "noise". This is the name of a Valkyrie.
From Serbian све (sve) meaning "all" and мила (mila) meaning "dear" thus the name means "dear to all".
Derived from Old Norse sveinn "young man" and bjǫrg "help, save, rescue". A known bearer of this name was Anna Svenborg Billing (1849-1927), a Swedish painter.

Medieval Slavic form of Svæinaldr. Sveneld is a semi-legendary 10th-century Varangian warlord in the service of Svyatoslav I of Kiev and his family. Although he seems to have been the richest and the most influential Rus' leader after the ruling prince, his relation to the House of Rurik, if it existed, has not been positively established.

Svengali is a fictional character in George du Maurier's 1895 novel Trilby. Scholars call Svengali a classic example of anti-Semitism in literature because he is Jewish, of Eastern European origins, and he seduces, dominates and exploits Trilby, a young English girl, and makes her into a famous singer. The word "svengali" has come to refer to a person who, with evil intent, dominates, manipulates and controls a creative person such as a singer or actor. In court, a "Svengali defense" is a legal tactic that purports the defendant to be a pawn in the scheme a greater, and more influential, criminal mastermind.
Swedish combination of sveinn "boy" and harðr "hard, strong".
Swedish name with the combination of sveinn "boy" and hildr "battle, fight".
Diminutive of Sven as well as a feminine form.
Diminutive of Sven. It is also a slang word for "Swede", mostly used ironically or derogatory.
Derived from Old Norse sveinungr meaning "descendant of Sven".
Diminutive of Sven as well as a feminine form.
Modern form of Svartgeirr meaning "black spear".
Diminutive of Svetlana that people in the English-speaking world sometimes use. It also means "light" in Russian.
Derived from the elements svet meaning "holy" оr "world" and boriti, meaning "to fight, to battle".
Diminutive of Svetlana and its short form Sveta.
Masculine form of Svetlana. A known bearer of this name is the Bulgarian former soccer player Svetlan Kondev (b. 1976).
Variant of Svetlan. A known bearer of this name is the Bulgarian artist Svetlin Rusev (b. 1933).
Derived from the Slavic element svet meaning "light, world" and combined with miru meaning "peace, world".
A dithematic name composed from the Slavic name element světŭ "light" and an unidentified second part.
Diminutive of Světlana, Světluše or Světla.
Short form of Svetozar, Svetoslav and other names beginning with svet meaning "blessed, holy, bright".
Derived from the Slavic elements svet, which could mean "holy, saint" or "world", or from the element svetli, "bright", and lik, meaning "image".
Diminutive of Svetlana and its short form Sveta, as it contains the Georgian diminutive suffix -უნა (-una).
Variant Belarusian Taraškievica Łacinka transcription of Śviatlana.
"One's own" ;"my own" ; "peculiar"Origin - Sanskrit Other spell - Swika
From Serbian свила (svila) meaning "silk" and коса (kosa) meaning "hair". Therefore the name means "silk haired".

Medieval Georgian form of Simon 1, which is still in use today (albeit barely).This was the name of a 5th-century archbishop of Mtskheta as well as of several Catholicoi of Iberia and later Georgia (the earliest of which lived in the 6th century, the last in the 16th century).
Form of Svimon with the Georgian nominative suffix -ი (-i). It is only used in Georgian when the name is written stand-alone.

The first element of this name is possibly derived from Proto-Slavic svin'a or svinьja meaning "swine, pig, hog". Also compare Serbo-Croatian svinja, Polish świnia and Slovak sviňa, all of which mean "swine, pig, hog". The second element is derived from Slavic mir "peace". Also note that according to some sources, this name is an older (or a variant) form of Zvonimir.
Derived from svipr ("sudden sweeping movement") and dagr ("day, lifetime"). In Norse mythology Svipdagr wishes to marry Menglǫð.

Means "changeable" in Old Norse. This name belongs to a Valkyrie in both the skaldic poem 'Darraðarljóð' and the Poetic Edda book the 'Skáldskaparmál' (where it is used as a kenning (synonym) for "battle" - presumably in reference to the changeable nature of fate, of which the Valkyries are represented as directors).

A possible combination of the lithuanian radical švitr/svir, from Lithuanian švisti or švigeti, meaning "to shine", with -gaila#, a common suffix in medival baltic and slavic, meaning "strong, powerful." Therefore, the meaning of this name could be understood as "a strong glow" or "shining and strong".
From Slavic root свѣтъ (světŭ), meaning "light, world". Could be considered variant of Svitlana. Usage possibly influenced by unrelated Bulgarian name Tsvetana.

Derived from the Lithuanian adjective švitrus meaning "nimble, agile" as well as "fast, quick, brisk" combined with old Lithuanian gailas, which usually means "strong, potent" but has also been found to mean "sharp, jagged" as well as "angry, fierce, violent" and "miserable, sorrowful, remorseful". Also compare the modern Lithuanian noun galia meaning "power, might, force".This name was borne by a 15th-century Grand Duke of Lithuania.
Means "the vanishing one". This is the name of a dwarf.
Estonian transcription of Russian Святослав (see Svyatoslav).
Croatian variant form of Svetlan. A known bearer of this name is Svjetlan Junaković (b. 1961), a Croatian painter, sculptor and illustrator.
From Serbian свобода (svoboda), an archaic form of слобода (sloboda) meaning "freedom".
Means "cooler; the cooling one". This is a by-name for Odin.
Means "holy mountain". Svyatogor was Russian bogatyr who was son of Mother Earth in Slavic mythology.
Short form of François. Also compare Swat.This name is extremely rare as an official name on birth certificates; it is almost always used informally.
Means "road" in Bariba, this name is given to a child born on a journey.
According to Hindu beliefs, this is one of the "nakshatras" in the sky. When a drop of water from Swaati falls upon the shell in the sea, it turns to a pearl.
Proto-Norse combination of svabar "Swabians" and herr "army".
Transferred use of the surname Swade.
Means "I welcome you, Lakshmi", from the Sanskrit स्वागत (svāgata) meaning "welcome" combined with the name Lakshmi. A known bearer is Swagatalakshmi Dasgupta, a Bengali actress.
Transferred use of the surname Swain.

MEANING - one's own, one of one's own people, a relation, kinsman, friend, one's own people, friends ,one's own goods property, wealth, riches. It is feminine of स्वकOrigin : Sanskrit Usage : Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
स्वक्षी / Swakshi means beautiful eyed girl
Possibly derived from the Old Norse name Svala.

From the English word which refers to a small, migratory bird of the Hirundinidae family with long, pointed, moon-shaped wings and a forked tail. It is mainly used by Chinese bearers as a translation of 燕子 (yànzi).

Derived from Hindi स्वामी (svāmī) meaning "master, lord, owner," from Sanskrit स्वामिन् (svāmin), used as an honorific title for yogis initiated into the religious monastic order in Hinduism.This name was introduced, or popularised at least, in Italy by television presenter, model and actress Elenoire Casalegno (1976-) who gave this name to her daughter in November of 1999.
Short form of names beginning with the element Swan-, such as Swanhild.
Derived from Old High German suan "swan" combined with Old High German bald "bold, brave."
Derived from Old High German suan "swan" combined with Old High German beraht "bright."

The first element of this name is derived from Old High German suan "swan." The second element is derived from Gothic bairgan (bergan in Old High German) "to keep, to save, to preserve", or from Old High German burg "fortress."

The first element of this name is derived from Old High German suan "swan." The second element is derived from gardan "to hedge in, to enclose, to fence in" or from Gothic gards "house, garden, (court)yard."
Derived from Old High German suan "swan" combined with Gothic gild "sacrifice."
Variant of Swanhild. Swanahild was the second wife of Charles Martel, a Frankish king from the Carolingian dynasty.

American English regional name (Appalachian) influenced by Swan with the addition of the suffix -ie which is a common suffix added to names throughout Appalachia. It may also be influenced by the Shawnee indigenous tribe of Oklahoma located in Oklahoma and within Appalachia.
Either a short form of Swannetje or a combination of a name starting with Sw- (such as Swaantje and Swana) with Annet.
Pet form of names that contain the Old High Germanic element suan meaning "swan", such as Swanhild and Swanaburg.
MEANING : messenger from Paradise, Angel. Here स्वर्ग means swarga or paradise + दूत means messengerUsage - Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil, Telugu, Nepali, Sinhala, Hindi, Sikh, Buddhist
Name - Swargadooti स्वर्गदूतीMEANING : messenger from Paradise,female Angel. Here स्वर्ग means swarga + दूती means female messenger Origin - Sanskrit, Indian, Tamil
Alternate transcription of Punjabi Gurmukhi ਸਵਰਨ (see Swaran).
This gorgeous name means in Bengali “gold” or “golden.”
Means "divine self" or "divine form" in Sanskrit.
Possibly derived from Old English sweart "black" and either col "coal, charcoal" (see kol) or the Old Norse byname Kollr "top (of the head), skull".
From Sanskrit स्वरूप (svarūpa) meaning "one's own form, nature, character".
From Sanskrit स्वस्तिक (svastika) meaning "lucky or auspicious object, mystical mark denoting good luck".
Flemish short form of François. The best known bearer of this name is the Belgian former soccer player François "Swat" Van der Elst (1954-2017).
Combination of Swayde with the popular name suffix, lee
Old Prussian god of light whose name is derived from Old Prussian swāigstan "light; shine".His functions were akin to those of the Roman god Sol.
Transferred use of the surname Swayze as a given name. Usage of the name is likely due to popular American actor Patrick Swayze (1952-2009).
Means "relative, kin, family" or "friend" in Burmese.

Used by author Leif Enger in the 2001 novel Peace Like A River. Swede is the protagonist's younger sister, who is fascinated with the American Old West and composes poems about a heroic cowboy known as Sunny Sundown.
From the name of the European country of Sweden.
Dutch and German form of an ancient Germanic name that was composed of the Gothic element svinths (swind in Old High German) "strength" and the Old High Germanic element hari "army".
Hokkien and Teochew romanization of Rui.
Originally a transferred use of the surname Sweet, it is found as a given name from the 1600s onwards.
From the English pet name "sweetheart". This is the middle name of Tobey Maguire's daughter Ruby Maguire.
From the term of endearment, meaning "sweet".
From old English swet "sweet" and lufu "love".
Usually a common term of endearment to describe someone cute and lovable
Old English form of Sweyn, derived from Old Norse Sveinn. This was the name of Sweġn Godwinson; Earl of Hereford and brother of Harold Godwinson.

Medieval English form of Sveinn. Swein Forkbeard (17 April 963 – 3 February 1014) was king of Denmark from 986 to 1014. In 1013, shortly before his death, he became the first Danish king of England after a long effort.
African variation of Swela, from Arabic name Suela, meaning "beautiful and even".
Dutch form of Zwentibold. According to some, it might even also be a germanized form of the Slavic name Svatopolk, which means "holy people" (see also Svyatopolk).
Bengali and Odia form of Shweta.
Derived from Middle English swete "sweet; pleasant, likeable; loved, dear, precious" combined with a diminutive suffix.
Variation of Swetlufu used in the Medieval English times.
Derived from Middle English swete "sweet; pleasant, likeable; loved, dear, precious" combined with a diminutive suffix. This name was also used as a secular form of Asher.
Possibly derived from Old English elements swete meaning "sweet" and lufu meaning "love".

predominantly a male Arabic given name can be derived from the Arabic root "شفا" (shafa), meaning "cure," "healing," or "remedy". Or from the word Sayf (سيف), which literally means "sword" in Arabic. Most commonly a shortened Indonesian and Malay given name or nickname derived from Arabic roots beginning with Shaykh/Shayf or, more typically, the triliteral root sh-y-f related to shifā’, “healing.” In Southeast Asia it appears as a clipped form of longer Arabic-Islamic names such as Syafii/Syafi’i (from al-Shāfi‘ī, the eminent jurist; meaning “intercessor”), Syafik/Syafiq (“compassionate, kind”), Syafaq (from shafaq, “twilight”), Spelling varies with transliteration: Syaf sits alongside Shaf, Syaf’, Syaf’, Shyaf, and in Arabic-influenced contexts Shafi, Shafee, or Shafie; related feminine forms include Syafa/Syifah (from shifā’, “healing”).Because it is frequently a hypocoristic, Syaf serves as an everyday call-name for longer forms: Muhammad Syafiq becomes Syaf; Nur Syafira becomes Syaf or Fira; Al‑Syafi’i becomes Syafie/Shafie. Common nicknames include Syaf, Shaf, Syafie, Fiq (from Syafiq), and Fira (from Syafira). In South Asian usage, parallel variants like Shafi, Shafiq, and Shafeeq are more prevalent, while in Arab contexts forms such as Ash‑Shāfi‘ī (a nisba) and Shafī‘/Shafīq underpin the same semantic field of “intercession,” “compassion,” and “healing.” Overall, Syaf encapsulates a family of Arabic-derived meanings-mercy, remedy, advocacy-filtered through Malay-Indonesian phonology and naming customs.it is often used within longer, compound Arabic names, and it is frequently used in Malaysia, Singapore, Egypt, and Indonesia.

From Ancient Greek συλεύς (syleus) meaning "privateer", derived from συλάω (sylao) meaning "to plunder, to rob, to strip (off)". Also compare σύλη (syle), a term used to refer to the right of seizing a ship. In Greek mythology, Syleus was a Lydian who was killed, along with his daughter (Xenodoce or Xenodice), by Heracles for forcing passing travellers to work in his vineyards. In one version of the myth, Syleus was a son of Poseidon, and Heracles married his daughter instead of killing her.
Possibly an elaborated form of Sylvie using the common Haitian name suffix -ise.
The given name of the Rwandian politician Sylidio Dusabumuremyi who was stabbed to death in September 2019.
Uncertain etymology. In Greek mythology, this was name of a nymph of the town of Sikyon, the mother of Zeuxippos by Apollo.

Meaning uncertain. Also see Syleus. Syloson was the name of a tyrant of Samos, who lived in the 6th century BC.

Derived from the name of the North Frisian island of Sylt whose name is a corruption of the Old Frisian name Silendi "sea-land" and thus ultimately derived from Proto-West Germanic *saiwi and *land. This name is borne by German actress Sylta Fee Wegmann (b. 1987).
Sylvanas Windrunner is a fictional character who appears in the Warcraft series of video games.

Polish form of Symphorianus. A known bearer of this name is Symforian Ducki (1888-1942), a Polish Capuchin friar who was beatified by the Roman Catholic Church in 1999.

Dutch form of Symphorosa. In Dutch literature, Symforosa is the name of the main character of the 1918 novel De zeer schone uren van Juffrouw Symforosa, begijntjen written by the Flemish author Felix Timmermans (1886-1947).
Variant of Samir 1 resembling names like Tymir and Kymir.

Derived from Ancient Greek συμφέρω (symphero) meaning "to bring together, gather, collect, contribute" as well as "to be of use, profitable, useful, beneficial". It is ultimately derived from σύν (syn) "beside, with" combined with φέρω (phero) "to bring, to carry, to bear". As such, one could say that this name is essentially a variant of Symphora.
Latinized form of Sympherousa. This name was used as a feminine cognomen in the Roman empire, especially in Roman Greece and Sicily. Also compare Symphorosa.
Means "symphony" in French. It is also an English variant of Symphony.

Feminine form of Symphoros and its latinized form Symphorus. Also compare the Greek noun συμφορά (symphora) meaning "a bringing together, collecting, contribution" as well as "misfortune, tragedy".In modern times, there may be cases where this name is a short form or contraction of Symphoriana, Symphorina and Symphorosa.A well-known bearer of this name is the French sportswoman Symphora Béhi (b. 1986).

French form of Symphorus (masculine) and Symphora (feminine). This name has always been predominantly used on men, and today there are no known living female bearers.It should also be noted that there may be (or have been) cases where this name is (or was) a short form of names like Symphorien (for men) and Symphorienne and Symphorose (for women).
Feminine form of Symphorius. It should also be noted that like Symphorina, this name is sometimes encountered as a corruption (or perhaps short form in this case) of Symphoriana.
English and German form of Symphorianus. This name was borne by a saint from the 2nd century AD.
Variant of Symphorienne, which is the standard French form of Symphoriana.

Roman cognomen which was derived from the Greco-Roman name Symphorus.The earliest known bearer of this name is a 2nd-century martyr and saint from Augustodunum in Roman Gaul (now Autun in eastern France), who is better known in English as saint Symphorian of Autun. He was born into an affluent family, to a Roman nobleman or senator named Faustus and his wife Augusta, who presumably was at least partially of Gaulish descent, since her last words to her son are recorded as having been in Gaulish.

French form of Symphorianus. Known bearers of this name include the French physician and humanist Symphorien Champier (1471-1539) and the French police chief and senator Symphorien Boittelle (1813-1897).
French and German form of Symphorinus. There have probably also been cases where this name is a corruption or a rare variant of Symphorien (French) and Symphorian (German).
Feminine form of Symphorinus. It should also be noted that this name is sometimes encountered as a corruption of Symphoriana.
French form of Symphorina. There have probably also been cases where this name is a corruption or a rare variant of Symphorienne.

Essentially means "of Symphorus", since it contains the Latin masculine adjectival suffix -inus. This suffix later developed into a diminutive suffix, so one could also say that this name is a diminutive of Symphorus.Lastly, it should be noted that this name is sometimes encountered as a corruption of Symphorianus.
Variant form of Symphorus. It should also be noted that like Symphorinus, this name is sometimes encountered as a corruption (or perhaps contraction in this case) of Symphorianus.

Derived from the Greek adjective σύμφορος (symphoros) meaning "accompanying", which is derived from the Greek verb συμφορέω (symphoreo) meaning "to bring together, to collect, to heap up", a variant of the more common verb συμφέρω (symphero) meaning "to bring together, to gather, to collect" as well as "to be of use, to be useful". Both verbs are ultimately derived from Greek σύν (syn) meaning "beside, with" combined with respectively Greek φορέω (phoreo) and φέρω (phero), which both mean "to bring, to carry, to bear".

Either a latinate variant of Symphora that was created by adding the Latin feminine augmentative suffix -osa to it, or a corruption of Sympherusa, which is the proper Latin form of the Greek name Sympherousa.This name is best known for being the name of the 2nd-century saint Symphorosa of Tibur (now Tivoli in central Italy), who was martyred during the reign of the Roman Emperor Hadrian, together with her seven sons.
Latinized form of Symphoros. This name was used as both a first name and a cognomen (often on slaves) in the Roman empire, especially in Roman Greece and Sicily.

Probably derived from Greek σύμφρων (symphron) meaning "of one mind, brotherly; favouring, propitious" or συμφρονέω (symphroneo) "to agree, think with, be in harmony; notice, understand", both derived from σῠν (syn) meaning "with, together" and φρήν (phren) "mind, heart, emotions".
Means "refusal, denial". This is the name of a goddess, the guardian of the gates. Her name is also used as a kenning for "woman".

Albanian form of Cynane, the name of a half-sister of Alexander the Great. She was the wife of Amyntas IV of Macedon and mother of Eurydice II of Macedon, but is more noted as a powerful woman-warrior and politician.
Variant of Sincere commonly used by African Americans.
Combination of Syn and Claire. Possibly a variant of Synclair or Sinclair.

Latinized form of the Greek feminine given name Συγκλητική (Synkletike), which is derived from Ancient Greek συγκλητικός (synkletikos) meaning "senatorial, of senatorial rank" as well as "summoning, beckoning, calling".The word is ultimately derived from Greek σύγκλητος (synkletos) - also found spelled as sugkletos - which originally meant "called together, summoned" but later came to mean "senate, council, assembly" (possibly in reference to the Byzantine Senate). It is a compound word that consists of Greek σύν (syn) "beside, with, together" combined with Greek κλητέος (kleteos) meaning "to be called, to be named". The latter element is ultimately derived from the Greek verb κλέω (kleo) meaning "to call". Also compare the Greek verb κλητεύω (kleteuo) meaning "to summon into court".Syncletica is the name of two saints of the Orthodox Church, one of which is Syncletica of Alexandria (4th century AD).
Possibly an altered form of Sandra. (See also Cindra.)

Possibly derived from Ancient Greek συνέχεια (synécheia) meaning "continuation, continuity", συνέχω (synecho) meaning "to hold together, secure, contain", or συνηχέω (synecheo) meaning "to sound in accord, ring with, echo to".

This name is best known for being the name of the British interior decorator Syrie Maugham (1879-1955), who was born as Gwendoline Maud Syrie Barnardo. She was given the name in honour of her mother, whose name was Sarah Louise "Syrie" Elmslie.

From Syringa, the name of a genus of plants commonly known as lilacs, which is derived from Greek σῦριγξ (syrinx) meaning "hollow tube, pipe" (compare Syrinx), referring to the broad pith in the shoots of some species. A known bearer of this name was Syringa Marshall-Burnett (1935-2014), a Jamaican nurse, educator and politician.

From Greek σῦριγξ (syrinx) meaning "tube" or "panpipes", referring to a musical instrument played by mouth and comprising tubes arranged in order of length. In Greek myth this was the name of a nymph and follower of Artemis who asked to be turned into hollow river reeds to escape the pursuit of the god Pan. Pan then fashioned these reeds into the first panpipe.
From Syrith, an Anglo-Scandinavian form of Sigríðr.
SYRLENE CLARKE was competing in the SECOND series of "Gladiators" which took place in 1993. She got as far as the QUARTER-FINALS before being eliminated by Georgina Berger.

There are several possible explanations for the meaning of the first element of this name. An other explanation is that it is derived from Proto-Slavic širokъ meaning "wide, broad" (also compare Czech široký, which also means "wide, broad"). Lastly (but most unlikely), it could have been derived from Russian sirota or syrota (сирота) meaning "orphan" (compare Croatian sirotan and Polish sierota, both of which mean "orphan"). The second element of this name is derived from Slavic slav "glory".
Derived from the Greek noun σύρφαξ (syrphax) meaning "rabble, riffraff". This was the name of a Greek tyrant of Ephesus, who lived in the 4th century BC.
Derived from Kazakh сыр (syr) meaning "dye, ink, paint" or "secret".
